Where Article 5 engaged, containment must be necessary, proportionate, and time-limited. d: Containing a crowd within a police cordon ('kettling') for about seven hours during a volatile demonstration wasn't a deprivation of liberty under Article 5, in the specific and exceptional circumstances.

f.facts: During a May Day demonstration in London in 2001, police held up to 2,000 people inside a cordon at Oxford Circus for up to seven hours, with no access to food, water or toilets. A protester and three passers-by complained that this deprived them of their liberty.
f.held: No violation of Article 5 (by majority; three judges dissenting). European Court of Human Rights (Grand Chamber), 15 March 2012: Article 5 isn't concerned with mere restrictions on movement, and the context and purpose of a measure are relevant. The cordon was the "least intrusive and most effective means" of protecting people from serious injury in volatile conditions, and the police kept trying to release people. Crowd control mustn't be used to stifle or discourage protest.

why: Containment is a last resort for preventing serious injury or damage. Keep it as short as possible, release people (especially those not involved) as soon as you safely can, provide for basic needs, and record the decisions and reasons.

d: Burglary of a dwelling violates the constitutional inviolability of the home. A householder needn't retreat and may use force to drive off, immobilise or detain an intruder, judged with the victim's shock and fear in mind. A burglar's self-defence is very narrow: a burglar who kills the householder is guilty of at least manslaughter.

f.facts: The accused and another man broke into a house in Co. Waterford, believing it was empty. The elderly householder came home and was fatally stabbed by the accused. In inconsistent statements to Gardaí he claimed self-defence after being attacked; he didn't give evidence. He pleaded guilty to burglary and was convicted of the killing.
f.held: Court of Criminal Appeal, 21 December 2006 (Hardiman J, with Hanna and Feeney JJ): leave to appeal refused. Burglary of a dwelling is an invasion of the constitutional right to inviolability of the dwelling. A householder need not retreat and may use force to drive off, immobilise or detain an intruder, judged subjectively as well as objectively — he isn't in the position of a calm, reasonable person weighing options. A burglar has only narrow scope for self-defence (essentially against an attempt to kill him just for being a burglar), and a killing of a householder by a burglar can never be less than manslaughter. The judge's misdirection on the burden of proof was cured on recharge.

why: At a burglary scene, record what the householder saw, feared and did — their fear and shock are central to judging their force. For a burglar who uses violence, burglary is a crime against the person and the home, not just property.

f.facts: A man was arrested in France on a European Arrest Warrant and surrendered to Belgium, where he was investigated for murder. Under a general Belgian statutory rule he was questioned by police and an investigating judge without a lawyer, and later his lawyer couldn't attend interviews. His detailed statements were used at his trial.
f.held: Violation of Article 6(1) and 6(3)(c), unanimously. European Court of Human Rights (Grand Chamber), 9 November 2018: applying the two-stage test from Ibrahim, the Court asks whether there were compelling reasons for restricting access, and whether the proceedings as a whole were fair. d: Bulk interception isn't in itself incompatible with the Convention, but it needs 'end-to-end safeguards'. The UK's regime lacked them and breached Articles 8 and 10, and so did its scheme for getting communications data from service providers.

f.facts: After the 2013 Snowden disclosures, campaign groups, NGOs and journalists challenged three UK regimes: bulk interception of communications from fibre-optic cables under s.8(4) RIPA; receipt of intercepted material from foreign intelligence services; and acquisition of communications data from service providers.
f.held: Violations of Articles 8 and 10 (bulk interception; communications data), no violation for intelligence sharing. Grand Chamber, 25 May 2021: bulk interception to protect national security can be lawful, but only with end-to-end safeguards, including independent authorisation at the outset and independent oversight; access to communications data should be limited to serious crime and subject to prior independent review, and confidential journalistic material needs authorisation by a judge or independent body.

d: Under the s.15A drugs regime, the minimum sentence must be imposed unless there are circumstances that are both exceptional and specific making it unjust. Value, not the type of drug, sets the threshold — cannabis isn't treated differently. Courier's 5-year sentence upheld.

f.facts: A courier arrived at Dublin Airport from Paris in July 2002 carrying four slabs of cannabis weighing just over 20kg, worth just over €52,000. He had agreed to bring the bag to Dublin for a fee. He pleaded guilty under s.15A of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1977, made a full statement to Gardaí, and was sentenced to five years. He argued the sentence was too heavy compared with other couriers, pointing to his age, finances, plea and co-operation.
f.held: Court of Criminal Appeal, 19 January 2004 (Hardiman J, with O'Sullivan and Herbert JJ): appeal dismissed. The trial judge was entitled to ask about sentences in similar cases — past decisions under these specific provisions are useful guidance. The plea and assistance to Gardaí could be considered. But s.27 significantly limits the court's discretion: the minimum must be imposed unless there are exceptional and specific circumstances making it unjust, and the two words are conjunctive. Cannabis isn't a separate category: the threshold is set by value, not type of drug.

why: In s.15A cases, evidence of value drives everything: get a proper valuation of the drugs and record the weight. Record the suspect's co-operation and admissions accurately — they can count in mitigation, but the minimum still applies unless the circumstances are exceptional and specific.

Facts: The applicant's daughter and granddaughter were killed by the daughter's partner, who had been convicted of threats to kill them and had been ordered to undergo psychiatric treatment - but the treatment had not been provided. He killed them and himself shortly after release. Holding: Violation of Article 2. The authorities had specific knowledge of the threat and had failed to take the steps that the court orders required (provision of psychiatric treatment), with foreseeable lethal consequences. Reasoning: The Court applied the Osman test. The threat was specific and known; the State response was inadequate (failure of statutory psychiatric treatment); the failure was causally connected to the deaths. d: Croatia breached Article 2: it knew a man's threats to kill his former partner and their baby were serious, but didn't make sure the court-ordered psychiatric treatment was given or assess his risk before release, and he killed them.

f.facts: A man was jailed for threatening to kill his former partner and their infant daughter, and a court ordered psychiatric treatment. Psychiatrists warned of a strong likelihood he would reoffend without treatment. In prison he saw a doctor only for unrelated illnesses. Weeks after his release he shot both of them dead and then himself.
f.held: Violation of Article 2. European Court of Human Rights, 15 January 2009: the authorities knew the threats were serious and should have taken all reasonable steps to protect the victims; the Government didn't show the ordered treatment was actually and properly given, and there was no risk assessment before his release. €40,000 was awarded to the family.

why: Threats to kill in a domestic setting are a warning sign of homicide. Record them, assess the risk, and make sure bail or release conditions and supervision are known and acted on, especially around the time an offender is released.

f.facts: Five men took part over about ten years in consensual sadomasochistic activities in private. Police discovered them during an unrelated investigation, and the men were charged under ss.20 and 47 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861. f.held: House of Lords, 11 March 1993, by 3 to 2 (Lords Templeman, Jauncey and Lowry; Lords Mustill and Slynn dissenting): consent is no defence to actual bodily harm or wounding outside recognised exceptions such as properly conducted sport and reasonable surgery. f.facts: The accused was arrested under s.30 of the Offences Against the State Act 1939 on suspicion of a firearms offence linked to a robbery, and interviewed at a Garda station in three sessions. In the first, after Gardaí read him a co-accused's statement and asked him to tell the truth, he said 'Haven't ye got the story there?' The Special Criminal Court ruled the first two sets of admissions inadmissible but admitted the third, and convicted him of robbery.
f.held: Court of Criminal Appeal, 31 July 1989 (Finlay CJ): conviction upheld. The trial court was right to admit the third statement, because the earlier admissions had been ruled inadmissible on grounds other than oppression, threat or inducement — so there was no continuing taint carrying over into the later statement.

d: A later admission isn't automatically inadmissible because earlier admissions were excluded. Where the earlier ones were excluded for reasons other than oppression, threat or inducement, a later properly taken statement can be admitted. Robbery conviction upheld.
why: If an interview goes wrong, a later interview can still be admissible — but only if it's clean and the earlier problem wasn't oppression, a threat or an inducement whose effect may continue. Start the later interview fresh: new caution, break, solicitor access, and record it all.

f.facts: In May 1997 Gardaí arrested the accused after he drove to a spot near Drogheda shortly after a man was seen dumping sacks of cannabis in a ditch. About six kilos of cannabis were involved, and £27,920 in cash was found at his home after his arrest. He didn't give evidence at his trial in Dundalk Circuit Criminal Court. s.t: 2. The Proper Approach in Irish Law The People (DPP) v Cumberton [2020] IECA 136 Holding. The leading modern restatement. The case (the fatal shooting of Michael Barr at the Sunset House, Summerhill Parade, Dublin 1) was wholly circumstantial. The Court of Appeal reiterated and clarified how circumstantial evidence is to be approached: the tribunal must assess the evidence as a whole, not strand by strand in isolation, and convict only if satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that guilt is the only reasonable inference from the proven facts taken together. Individual strands need not each be proved beyond reasonable doubt; it is the ultimate inference of guilt that must reach that standard — save that a fact which is an indispensable link in the chain of reasoning must itself be proved beyond reasonable doubt. d: A wholly circumstantial murder case — DNA on a cap and a mask in a partly burnt getaway car, ballistics linking a pistol from the car to the fatal shots, and an attempt to fly abroad the next day — was enough. f.facts: In April 2016 two masked men shot a man dead in a licensed premises in Dublin 1, in a killing linked to a gangland feud. A car was later found partly burnt, with firearms, masks and other items inside. The accused was linked by DNA to a cap and a mask from the car; ballistics showed one of the pistols fired the fatal shots; and the day after the shooting he tried to fly to Bangkok, then got an emergency passport to travel the following day. The Special Criminal Court convicted him of murder in January 2018 after a 21-day trial.
f.held: Court of Appeal, 19 May 2020 (Edwards J, with McCarthy and Kennedy JJ): appeal dismissed. Of 28 grounds, four were dropped and none of the rest succeeded. Many concerned the court of trial's treatment of the circumstantial evidence; the court restated the Irish approach to circumstantial evidence and how it applies in practice, and was completely satisfied that the trial was satisfactory and the verdict safe.

why: Serious crime is usually proved by strands, not one decisive item. Treat a burnt-out car as a major scene, get weapons to ballistics, and check travel bookings and passport applications — an attempt to leave can itself be a strand of the case.

f.facts: As part of Operation Amethyst, Gardaí obtained a warrant to search the home of a serving Circuit Court judge in Tralee. The warrant was valid for seven days. They searched on 27 May 2002 — the eighth day, one day after it expired — and seized a computer, discs, storage devices and other material. He was charged with possession of child pornography and pleaded not guilty.
f.held: Circuit Criminal Court, 23 April 2004 (Judge Carroll Moran): the warrant had expired, so the evidence was inadmissible. Time limits on warrants must be strictly observed; evidence obtained outside them could be admitted only in accidental or unintentional cases or extraordinary circumstances, and the prosecution accepted none applied. With no admissible evidence, the judge directed a not guilty verdict. He called the prosecution's arguments on the warrant 'untenable and nonsensical', said the law was crystal clear, and refused the accused's costs application.

d: A search warrant is valid only for its stated period. Gardaí searched a judge's home on the eighth day of a seven-day warrant; the computer and other material seized were excluded, and the trial judge directed an acquittal on a charge of possessing child pornography. The prosecution accepted that no exception — accident, inadvertence or extraordinary circumstances — applied.
why: Check the issue date and validity period before you execute any warrant, and execute it within time. A warrant executed a day late gives no authority to enter — the evidence, and the case, can be lost.
topic: Executing a search warrant after it expires
st: The rule — execute within the warrant's period — is unchanged. The exclusion test has since moved: under People (DPP) v JC (2015), evidence taken in breach of constitutional rights may be admitted if the breach was inadvertent. Don't rely on that: an expired warrant gives no authority to enter.

f.facts: The two accused were convicted in the Special Criminal Court of shooting with intent to commit murder (s.14, Offences Against the Person Act 1861), and of robbery and firearms offences. d: A Garda may use such force as is reasonably necessary to make an arrest and keep it. Force used for another purpose — here, to stop a young man going to look after his companions — isn't in the execution of duty and is unlawful. Damages of £3,500.

f.facts: A young man was stopped at a supermarket for shoplifting potatoes and held by the assistant manager until a Garda arrived to arrest him. At the patrol car he resisted being put in without his two younger companions; a scuffle followed and his wrist was injured. He sued for damages.
f.held: High Court, 1985 (Barron J): the plaintiff succeeded and was awarded £3,500. But the Garda was holding him to stop him looking after his companions, not to arrest him or keep him in custody, so he wasn't acting in the execution of his duty and the force was unlawful. d: For s.15A sentencing, first fix a notional sentence as if the minimum didn't exist; if it's over ten years, that's the sentence. A late guilty plea will rarely, if ever, be 'exceptional and specific' enough to go below the minimum. Twelve years upheld for a paid driver of ecstasy worth over €2 million.

f.facts: The accused was paid €1,000 to collect and drive a car containing ecstasy tablets worth roughly €2.1–2.7 million; Gardaí stopped the car within minutes. He pleaded guilty but gave no information about his contacts, citing fear. He had about forty previous convictions, mostly road traffic, and a troubled childhood. The Dublin Circuit Court imposed twelve years — two above the ten-year minimum.
f.held: Court of Criminal Appeal, 15 July 2005 (Geoghegan J, with Budd and O'Neill JJ): leave to appeal refused. The court should set the sentence as if the minimum didn't exist, bearing the life maximum in mind; if that exceeds ten years, that is the sentence, and if it's below ten, the minimum applies unless the exceptional and specific circumstances test is met. A late plea would rarely, if ever, meet that test, and the plea mustn't be counted twice. The minimum remains a guide to gravity (Renald).

d: A murder conviction was quashed because the judge misdirected the jury on intoxication. Voluntary intoxication can reduce murder to manslaughter (it's no answer to manslaughter); the question is whether the accused in fact formed the intent to kill or cause serious injury — not whether he had the capacity to — and correct speeches by counsel can't cure a wrong direction on the law.

f.facts: In March 2011 the accused, then 19, killed his mother in Co Mayo in a frenzied knife attack. He had used alcohol and drugs heavily since the age of 13 and had hallucinations and paranoid delusions in the week before. His offer to plead guilty to manslaughter wasn't accepted. At trial he relied on diminished responsibility, which the jury rejected, and on intoxication: a psychiatrist said he was grossly intoxicated and psychotic, which would have affected his capacity to form the specific intent. He was convicted of murder and lost an earlier appeal.
f.held: Supreme Court, 20 December 2019 (McKechnie J; Charleton J concurring; unanimous five-judge court): conviction quashed as unsafe. The judge wrongly told the jury that intoxication is not a defence in law; put the question as capacity to form intent instead of whether he in fact formed it; and omitted that intoxication can be a partial defence to murder. Counsel's closing speeches couldn't supply the correct law — that is the judge's duty. The DPP was left to choose between accepting the manslaughter plea and a retrial.

why: Intent is judged on what the suspect actually intended at the time, and intoxication evidence is weighed against it. In homicide and serious assault cases record intoxication in detail, and gather the evidence of purpose: threats, weapon, targeting, and conduct before and after.
topic: Intoxication and the intent for murder
st: Yes. The Supreme Court's statement of how juries must be directed on voluntary intoxication in murder: actual intent, not capacity.

d: Someone who picks up a bag intending to steal only if they find something worth taking, finds nothing, and puts it back hasn't stolen the bag or its contents: a conditional intention isn't enough for the full offence. Conviction quashed.

f.facts: In a cinema, the defendant picked up a handbag that had been left there, went through its contents looking for anything worth stealing, found nothing he wanted, and put it back with everything still in it. He was convicted of theft of the handbag and its contents.
f.held: Court of Appeal, 1971: conviction quashed. Intending to steal only whatever turned out to be worth taking was not an intention to permanently deprive the owner of the handbag or the items actually in it. A conditional intention of that kind isn't enough for theft.

d: A suspect in garda custody keeps the right to refuse to answer questions, and no adverse inference may be drawn from that refusal unless a statute expressly allows it. Evidence of the silence shouldn't be used against him at trial.

f.facts: Gardaí stopped a man's car after his passenger alleged that he had raped her. At the roadside he said the intercourse was consensual. Detained under the Criminal Justice Act 1984, he consulted a solicitor and, when interviewed, made no further statement. At trial he gave an account of consent; the judge let the prosecution put his silence in custody before the jury and cross-examine him about it. He was convicted of rape.
f.held: Conviction quashed and a retrial ordered. Supreme Court, 17 June 1999 (Keane J, for a unanimous court): the 1984 Act didn't abolish the right to refuse to answer questions in custody, and the right would be significantly eroded if juries could draw adverse inferences from its exercise. d: The statutory presumption of corruption put only an evidential burden on the accused, not a legal one: making him prove he wasn't corrupt would be a clear inroad on the presumption of innocence. Conviction quashed.

f.facts: An elected local councillor received payments from a person with an interest in planning applications for land in a neighbouring council's area. The prosecution alleged he tried to influence that council's decisions and the zoning of the land. He was charged under s.1 of the Prevention of Corruption Act 1906, and the prosecution relied on the presumption in s.4 of the Prevention of Corruption (Amendment) Act 2001: a benefit received by an office holder from someone with an interest in their functions is deemed corrupt unless the contrary is proved.
f.held: Supreme Court, November 2018 (O'Malley J): conviction quashed. Section 4 shifts only an evidential burden. If the accused had to prove, on the balance of probabilities, that the money wasn't received corruptly, he would effectively have to disprove an essential element of the offence. The jury must be told the prosecution has to prove every other element beyond reasonable doubt; if it does, the jury may treat corrupt intent as proved unless the evidence leaves them in doubt about it.

why: A statutory presumption 'unless the contrary is proved' isn't proof of guilt. Investigate the element it covers anyway, put the evidence to the suspect, and record their explanation — evidence that raises a doubt can displace the presumption.

Facts: Applicant attended a major protest in Moscow which descended into clashes between protesters and police. Mass arrests followed. Issue: state's handling of the assembly and the absence of dialogue with organisers. Holding: Violation of Article 11 (assembly). The authorities failed to maintain communication with the organisers and missed opportunities for dialogue and de-escalation. The state has a positive obligation to facilitate peaceable assembly including by constructive engagement with organisers. Reasoning: The Court emphasised that policing of mass assemblies is not merely a passive containment function. Active engagement, dialogue, accommodation are part of the Article 11 obligation. Significance: Positive obligation to engage. Failure to dialogue may itself constitute violation. Operational Application: Garda

d: Police must keep open communication with protest organisers and try to contain trouble before ending a whole assembly. Arresting, holding for 36 hours and jailing a peaceful protester breached Articles 11, 5 and 6.

f.facts: At an authorised rally in Moscow on 6 May 2012, turnout exceeded expectations. Riot police blocked the expected route into the park; organisers, unable to negotiate, staged a sit-in. Police ordered the meeting closed — the crowd couldn't hear — and dispersed it by force, with clashes. A peaceful protester was held for 36 hours and given 15 days' administrative detention for obstructing traffic and disobeying police orders.
f.held: Violations of Articles 11, 5 and 6. European Court of Human Rights, 5 January 2016: the authorities failed to keep a reliable channel of communication with the organisers or take simple steps at the first signs of conflict; ending the whole meeting wasn't shown to be necessary when trouble was confined to one area; there was no pressing social need to arrest and punish a peaceful participant; the 36-hour detention was arbitrary; and the courts refused to hear the defence evidence.

f.facts: A man convicted of murder challenged the Communications (Retention of Data) Act 2011, under which phone companies had to retain all traffic and location data for two years and gardaí could access it on the authorisation of a chief superintendent. The High Court granted a declaration in 2018, and the Supreme Court referred questions to the Court of Justice of the EU.
f.held: CJEU (Grand Chamber), 5 April 2022: general and indiscriminate retention of traffic and location data is precluded even to combat serious crime (only a genuine and present threat to national security can justify it, temporarily). Targeted retention, general retention of IP addresses and identity data, and 'quick freeze' orders are allowed. Access decided centrally by a police officer, reviewable only afterwards by a court, is precluded. A national court can't limit the temporal effects of a declaration of invalidity, and admissibility of the evidence is a matter for national law.

d: In English law, an appropriation can happen even with the owner's consent — here, consent obtained by deception. Ireland's theft offence is different: it requires the absence of the owner's consent, but consent obtained by deception or intimidation is not consent (s.4(1) and (2), 2001 Act).

f.facts: An assistant manager of an electrical goods shop arranged to supply goods to an acquaintance in return for two stolen building society cheques. He got the manager to authorise the sale by falsely saying the bank had accepted the cheques. The goods were handed over and the cheques were dishonoured. The employees were convicted of theft; the Court of Appeal held there had been no appropriation.
f.held: Prosecution appeal allowed and the convictions upheld. House of Lords, 3 December 1992 (Lord Keith, with Lords Jauncey, Browne-Wilkinson and Slynn; Lord Lowry dissenting): an act can be an appropriation even though it is done with the owner's consent (following Lawrence). Lord Roskill's statement in Morris that appropriation requires an adverse interference with the owner's rights was disapproved.

why: In Ireland, theft requires appropriation 'without the consent of its owner', but consent got by deception or intimidation doesn't count (s.4(2) of the 2001 Act). Where goods are handed over because of a lie, theft can still be charged — record exactly what was said to get them. Also consider deception offences.
topic: Appropriation with the owner's (deceived) consent
st: English authority. In Ireland the 2001 Act sets its own rule: no consent required for appropriation to be theft only where consent was obtained by deception or intimidation.

Significance: Though concerning journalistic source protection under Article 10, Goodwin establishes the broader principle that the protection of confidential sources is a value of high importance, interference with which requires an overriding requirement in the public interest. d: Ordering a journalist to disclose his source breached Article 10: protection of sources is "one of the basic conditions for press freedom", and disclosure can be ordered only where there is an overriding public interest.

f.facts: A trainee journalist was phoned, unsolicited, with information from a confidential corporate plan about a company's finances. The company got an injunction stopping publication, and the courts also ordered him to disclose his notes identifying the source. He refused and was fined £5,000 for contempt.
f.held: Violation of Article 10. European Court of Human Rights (Grand Chamber), 27 March 1996: "protection of media sources is one of the basic conditions for press freedom"; forced disclosure has a chilling effect on the press as public watchdog and is justified only by an overriding requirement in the public interest. Here the injunction already protected the company, so the disclosure order wasn't necessary.

d: Appropriation is a continuing act, so force used after a thief has picked up the property, while the theft is still going on, can make it robbery. The jury decides when the appropriation ended.

f.held: Robbery convictions upheld. Court of Appeal, 1978: appropriation is a continuing act; it doesn't end abruptly, and it is for the jury to decide when it ended, looking at the whole course of conduct. So tying her up could be force used at the time of stealing.

R v Hancock and Shankland [1986] AC 455 (HL — persuasive) Holding: Foresight of a virtually certain consequence amounts to intention. The greater the probability the accused foresaw, the stronger the inference of intent. Why It Matters: Useful in serious cases (arson with intent) where intent must be proved circumstantially. Ethics Touchpoints (Foundations) • Std 3 — victim impact often understated for criminal damage; treat the IP as a victim of significant intrusion. • Std 4 — graffiti, low-value damage, repeat offenders — same investigative threshold as higher-profile cases. 4.1 Simple Criminal Damage (s.2(1) CDA 1991) SIMPLE CRIMINAL DAMAGE: Damaging property of another without lawful excuse, intentionally or recklessly. Contrary to s.2(1) Criminal Damage Act 19

d: Foresight of a consequence isn't the same as intending it — it's evidence from which a jury may infer intention, and the more probable the consequence, the stronger that evidence. Murder convictions replaced with manslaughter.

f.facts: During the 1984–85 miners' strike, the defendants dropped a concrete block from a bridge to frighten a working miner being driven to work below. It struck the taxi carrying him, and the driver was killed. They offered to plead guilty to manslaughter; the prosecution went for murder, and they were convicted.
f.held: House of Lords, 27 February 1986: prosecution appeal dismissed; the Court of Appeal's manslaughter convictions stood. Murder requires an intent to kill or cause serious harm. Foresight of consequences is no more than evidence of that intent, to be weighed with all the other evidence. The trial judge's direction was defective because it didn't tell the jury that the probability of death or serious injury matters: the greater the probability, the more likely it was foreseen, and the more likely it was intended.

why: In serious cases, intent must be proved, not assumed. In interview, cover what the suspect knew and expected — the height, the weight of the object, the traffic, the risk — and gather evidence of how likely the harm was. In Ireland, see s.4 of the Criminal Justice Act 1964.
topic: Intention and foresight of consequences
st: English authority, persuasive in Ireland. Irish law has its own rule: s.4 of the Criminal Justice Act 1964 (intent to kill or cause serious injury; a rebuttable presumption of intending natural and probable consequences).

s.t: Part D - ECtHR Authority on Expression, Assembly, and Force D.1 Handyside v United Kingdom (1976) 1 EHRR 737 Citation: Application No. 5493/72, judgment 7 December 1976. Facts: Handyside, publisher of 'The Little Red Schoolbook', was prosecuted under the Obscene Publications Act. He claimed breach of Article 10 (freedom of expression). Holding: Freedom of expression under Article 10 is one of the essential foundations of a democratic society. It applies not only to information or ideas that are favourably received or regarded as inoffensive but also to those that offend, shock, or disturb the State or any sector of the population. Restrictions must be: prescribed by law; pursue a legitimate aim; be necessary in a democratic society. Reasoning: The Court's analysis: 'such are the demands of that pluralism, tolerance and broadmindedness without which there is no democratic society'. The proportionality assessment is the operative test for

d: Freedom of expression covers ideas that offend, shock or disturb — but States have a margin of appreciation to restrict it to protect morals, especially children's. A conviction over a sex-education book aimed at school pupils didn't breach Article 10.

f.facts: A publisher bought the British rights to a book for school pupils aged about 12 to 18, with a chapter on sex. After complaints, police seized over a thousand copies. He was convicted under the Obscene Publications Acts of having obscene books for publication for gain and fined, and his appeal failed.
f.held: European Court of Human Rights, 7 December 1976: no violation of Article 10. The conviction interfered with free expression but was prescribed by law and pursued the legitimate aim of protecting morals. With no European consensus on morals, national authorities have a margin of appreciation. 'Necessary' isn't the same as 'indispensable', but it isn't as flexible as 'reasonable'. Given the young readership, the direct style, wide circulation and cheap price, the measures were necessary in a democratic society.

why: That something offends, shocks or disturbs isn't enough on its own to stop it being said, written or displayed — at a protest, for example. Any restriction needs a legal basis, a legitimate aim and real necessity: act on a specific offence and record why.
topic: Freedom of expression: offensive ideas and the margin of appreciation
st: Still the foundation of Strasbourg's Article 10 case law, cited constantly.

d: On a DPP review of an 'unduly lenient' sentence, the Court of Criminal Appeal must consider the whole chain of events in which the DPP took part that led to the plea and sentence — including discussions in the judge's chambers. The original sentences were restored.

f.facts: The accused pleaded guilty in the Dublin Circuit Criminal Court to sexual offences against children, after the trial judge had met counsel in chambers before sentencing. Concurrent sentences of six and three years were imposed. The DPP applied for a review under s.2 of the Criminal Justice Act 1993, and the Court of Criminal Appeal substituted ten years, declining to take account of the chambers meeting.
f.held: Supreme Court, 5 April 2001 (Keane CJ, with Denham, Murphy, Murray and Hardiman JJ): appeal allowed; the Court of Criminal Appeal's order was discharged and the Circuit Court sentences affirmed. The Court of Criminal Appeal was wrong to disregard the discussions in chambers: it had to consider the whole chain of circumstances, in which the DPP participated, leading to the plea and sentence. There was no double jeopardy issue as such.

s.t: B.3 The People (DPP) v Heffernan [2017] IESC 5 - Sustained Provocation Citation: [2017] IESC 5 (Supreme Court). Facts: Heffernan killed his wife in circumstances that involved a sustained pattern of conflict, mental health issues, and an immediate precipitating event. The defence raised provocation including the cumulative impact of the relationship dynamics. Holding: Provocation in Irish law accommodates cumulative or sustained provocation, not only immediate provocation. The killer's state of mind at the time of the killing is the inquiry; the contribution of sustained prior provocation is relevant. Reasoning: The Supreme Court extended the MacEoin / Davis subjective framework to accommodate cumulative provocation. The immediate event may be the trigger; the accumulated abuse / pressure is part of the subjective state-of-mind picture. Significance: Important development for the DV-homicide scenario where the killer is the long-term IP

d: The accused must establish diminished responsibility (s.6 Criminal Law (Insanity) Act 2006) on the balance of probabilities — raising a reasonable doubt isn't enough. That doesn't breach the presumption of innocence: the prosecution still proves murder beyond reasonable doubt, and the defence only reduces the consequences of a proven offence.

f.facts: In 2011, near Ennis, Co Clare, the accused killed a man he had met briefly in a bar that evening, then rang Gardaí and said he had killed a man. He believed he had removed a devil from the world; the key question was whether he was truly delusional or exaggerating. He relied on diminished responsibility, and the judge told the jury the defence had to prove it on the balance of probabilities. He was convicted of murder in June 2013, and the Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal in 2015.
f.held: Supreme Court, 7 February 2017 (O'Malley J; Charleton J concurring): appeal dismissed. By requiring the defence to 'establish' diminished responsibility, the Oireachtas intended a burden on the accused beyond raising a reasonable doubt, and the balance of probabilities direction was correct. This doesn't breach the presumption of innocence (Article 38.1; Article 6(2) ECHR): the prosecution must still prove every element of murder beyond reasonable doubt, and diminished responsibility is a separate mitigating defence that reduces the consequences of a proven offence.

why: Where mental state is in issue, experts on both sides will test the claimed disorder against what the suspect actually said and did. Record the suspect's words, behaviour and demeanour before, during and after the incident — verbatim and timed.

s.t: Hill v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire [1989] AC 53 (persuasive) Garda generally owes no duty of care in negligence for operational decisions in pursuit/investigation. Operational immunity exists but does not protect bad faith or gross negligence.

d: The police owed no duty of care in negligence to a murder victim's family for failing to catch her killer sooner: there was no special risk to her, and public policy weighed against liability.

f.facts: A serial killer murdered a young woman in 1980, the last of his victims. Her mother sued the police in negligence, alleging their investigation had been flawed and that he should have been caught before her daughter was killed.
f.held: Claim struck out. House of Lords, 28 April 1988 (Lord Keith giving the leading speech; unanimous): she was one of many members of the public at risk and faced no special, distinctive risk, so there was insufficient proximity; and public policy (the risk of a "detrimentally defensive frame of mind" and the diversion of resources) weighed against a duty of care.

why: English authority, persuasive in Ireland. Hill doesn't give the police immunity: Robinson (2018) holds they owe a duty not to cause harm by their own positive acts, such as during an arrest. And under Article 2 (Osman), the State must act on a known real and immediate risk to life.

st: Still the English starting point on police omissions, but narrowed by Robinson v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire [2018] UKSC 4.

s.t: R v Hinks [2001] 2 AC 241 (HL) Appropriation may exist even where property passed with consent or by gift. Expands theft reach beyond physical taking; relevant to deception-by-relationship cases.

Dishonesty is now assessed objectively against ordinary standards, with reference only to what the defendant actually knew or believed about the facts. Defence counsel in Ireland will cite both; know which the court is applying. R v Hinks [2001] 2 AC 241 (HL) Principle: Appropriation may exist even where property passed with consent or by gift. A defendant who induced a vulnerable person to make 'gifts' was held to have appropriated the property dishonestly. Relevant to theft-by-deception and elder-abuse cases.

d: In English law, a person can 'appropriate' property even by receiving a gift that's valid in civil law. A woman who got a vulnerable man to hand over about £60,000 was rightly convicted of theft (3–2).

f.facts: The defendant befriended a 53-year-old man of limited intelligence and described herself as his main carer. Over about seven months in 1996 he withdrew around £300 from his building society almost every day, and about £60,000 went into her account. She said the money was a gift. She was convicted of theft.
f.held: House of Lords, 26 October 2000 (Lord Steyn, with Lords Slynn and Jauncey; Lords Hutton and Hobhouse dissenting): appeal dismissed. Acquiring an indefeasible title to property is capable of being an appropriation. Following Lawrence and Gomez, appropriation is a neutral word covering any assumption of the rights of an owner; the owner's consent isn't decisive, and the mental elements of theft — dishonesty and intention to permanently deprive — give enough protection.

why: In Ireland, theft needs appropriation without consent, so a genuine gift isn't theft — but consent obtained by deception or intimidation doesn't count (s.4(2), 2001 Act). d: A breach of the peace happens whenever harm is actually done, or is likely to be done, to a person or (in their presence) their property, or someone is put in fear of such harm by an assault, affray, riot, unlawful assembly or other disturbance. You can arrest without warrant for a breach in your presence, a breach you reasonably believe is about to happen, or a renewal you reasonably believe is threatened.

f.facts: The free reports available set out the court's statement of the law, not the facts of the incident.
f.held: Court of Appeal (Watkins LJ): there is a breach of the peace whenever harm is actually done or is likely to be done to a person, or in his presence to his property, or a person is in fear of being so harmed through an assault, affray, riot, unlawful assembly or other disturbance. There is a power of arrest without warrant where (1) a breach is committed in the presence of the person making the arrest; (2) the arrester reasonably believes the person will commit a breach in the immediate future, although none has yet been committed; or (3) a breach has been committed and the arrester reasonably believes a renewal of it is threatened.

why: Breach of the peace means violence or threatened violence — not just noise, swearing or annoyance. For a preventive arrest, record why you believed harm was about to happen. The power doesn't get you into a home (DPP v O'Brien (2021)).

d: Suspicion is 'a state of conjecture or surmise where proof is lacking', so reasonable suspicion for arrest needn't amount to a prima facie case. But it must extend to the offence itself: here the arrest was premature.

f.facts: In Malaysia, a piece of timber fell from a passing lorry and killed a person in a car. The next day police arrested the lorry driver and his attendant for causing death by reckless or dangerous driving. They didn't know which of the two had been driving, and suspected that their alibis were false. The men were later released and sued for false imprisonment.
f.held: Privy Council, 7 October 1969 (Lord Devlin): reasonable suspicion doesn't require prima facie proof, and can take into account matters that couldn't be put in evidence. The power to arrest is a discretion. But although it was reasonable to suspect that one of the two men was the driver, it wasn't yet reasonable to suspect that the lorry had been driven recklessly or dangerously, so the arrest was premature.

why: You don't need proof to arrest, but you need reasonable suspicion of the offence itself, not just of who was involved. Irish law says the same: under s.4(3) of the Criminal Law Act 1997 you must suspect, with reasonable cause, both that an arrestable offence was committed and that the person is guilty of it.

f.facts: In December 2004 an evening newspaper published articles about a man who had just appeared in the District Court charged with murder. The DPP brought criminal contempt proceedings against the publisher, the editor and a journalist, seeking committal or sequestration and an injunction. In May 2005 the High Court gave the respondents a direction and refused the application, finding only a remote possibility, not a real risk, of prejudice — though the judge criticised parts of the articles. The respondents argued that no appeal lay against what was in effect an acquittal.
f.held: Supreme Court, 5 March 2008 ([2008] IESC 8, Fennelly J): in contempt matters the High Court was not sitting as the Central Criminal Court, so the DPP could appeal. Supreme Court, 5 March 2009 ([2009] IESC 20, Geoghegan and Hardiman JJ; Murray CJ, Fennelly and Finnegan JJ agreeing): appeal allowed and the High Court order set aside. The judge should have decided whether there was at least a prima facie case, and there clearly was an arguable case of contempt. The fade factor matters when deciding whether to stop a trial, not whether a publication was a contempt. Given the time that had passed, no new hearing was ordered.

d: Newspaper articles about a man just charged with murder raised an arguable case of criminal contempt. The DPP can appeal a refusal of a contempt application; the judge should have decided whether there was a prima facie case; and the 'fade factor' (publicity fading before trial) is irrelevant to whether a publication was a contempt — that is judged when it is published.
why: Once someone is charged, publicity about them can be a crime in itself and can derail the prosecution. Keep all media contact to official Garda Press Office statements — no background, character, previous convictions or evidence, and no off-the-record briefings.

f.facts: In 2014 a national newspaper published articles and commentary portraying a man as dishonest and lacking moral judgment, knowing he had already been charged with fraud-related offences. The articles didn't deal with the subject of the charges, and others had published similar material before he was charged. In 2015 the High Court found the publishing company and three other respondents guilty of contempt, granted an injunction, and fined two of them €50,000 each and another €100.
f.held: Court of Appeal, December 2017 (Edwards J; Finlay Geoghegan J agreeing; Hogan J dissenting): conviction appeal dismissed. The question is whether the publication created a real risk to the fairness of the trial; 'calculated to interfere' means likely to interfere, and actual interference needn't be proved. Publication after charge, with knowledge of it, was decisive; the story could have been reported factually without naming him or adding prejudicial comment. Court of Appeal, 30 July 2018 ([2018] IECA 301): the offending was of moderate gravity, and the two €50,000 fines were replaced with €25,000 each.

d: Articles published after a man was charged, attacking his character though not dealing with the charges, created a real risk to his trial and were contempt. Actual prejudice and intention to prejudice needn't be shown; earlier coverage by others before charge was no excuse; and the chance of a jury direction doesn't answer whether contempt was committed. Fines were later cut to €25,000 each.
why: Anything that reaches the media about an accused after charge — from any source — can be contempt and can stall or collapse the trial. Gardaí should never comment on an accused's character or background, and all media contact should go through the Garda Press Office.

s.t: Ivey v Genting Casinos [2017] UKSC 67 Ghosh modified — second subjective limb removed; dishonesty assessed objectively against ordinary standards. Persuasive in Ireland; defence counsel will cite both Ghosh and Ivey — know which the court is applying.

European and Comparative Authority R v Ghosh [1982] QB 1053 (CA, England) Test: The classic two-limb dishonesty test — (1) was the conduct dishonest by the ordinary standards of reasonable and honest people; (2) did the defendant realise it would be regarded as dishonest by those standards. Persuasive in Ireland and frequently cited. Ivey v Genting Casinos [2017] UKSC 67 Test: The UK Supreme Court modified Ghosh — the subjective second limb is removed. Dishonesty is now assessed objectively against ordinary standards, with reference only to what the defendant actually knew or believed about the facts. Defence counsel in Ireland will cite both; know which the court is applying.

d: Edge-sorting at a casino was cheating, whether or not it was dishonest. The Supreme Court also restated the test for dishonesty: establish what the person actually knew or believed, then judge the conduct by the standards of ordinary decent people. The person needn't realise it was dishonest.

f.facts: A professional gambler won about £7.7 million playing Punto Banco at Crockfords casino in August 2012 by 'edge-sorting': he had the croupier, who didn't understand why, turn certain cards so that tiny manufacturing differences on their edges showed which were valuable. The casino refused to pay, and he sued.
f.held: Appeal dismissed unanimously. UK Supreme Court, 25 October 2017 (Lord Hughes): getting the croupier to arrange the cards unwittingly was in effect fixing the deck, which was cheating. On dishonesty: first ascertain the person's actual knowledge or belief as to the facts, then decide whether the conduct was dishonest by the standards of ordinary decent people. The second stage of Ghosh 'does not correctly represent the law'.

why: Persuasive only in Ireland, where 'dishonestly' means 'without a claim of right made in good faith' (s.2(1) of the 2001 Act). In fraud cases, establish what the suspect actually knew and believed.
topic: Cheating, and the modern English test for dishonesty
st: Its dishonesty test was confirmed for English criminal cases in Barton and Booth (2020).

d: The first jury conviction for coercive control (s.39, Domestic Violence Act 2018). Individual acts are understood within the wider pattern of behaviour, with the assaults reinforcing the control. A cumulative 10½ years for coercive control, assaults, intimidation on bail and perverting justice on remand was upheld.

f.facts: Over about 20 months, the accused subjected his partner to repeated violence, threats, intimidation and humiliation, and controlled her contact with family and friends. In November 2020 a jury convicted him of coercive control, twelve counts of assault causing harm, intimidation (committed while on bail) and perverting the course of justice (committed while on remand). The Circuit Criminal Court imposed an effective 10½ years. He appealed the length of the cumulative sentence.
f.held: Court of Appeal, 23 March 2023 (Kennedy J): appeal dismissed; no error in principle. Following English authority, the individual acts in coercive control are understood within the wider pattern of behaviour; the offence is a distinct wrong, and the assaults reinforced it. The s.40 aggravating factor (intimate relationship) applied to the assaults but not the coercive control, where the relationship is already an element. Consecutive sentences were properly imposed — the assaults weren't isolated, and intimidation attracts a mandatory consecutive sentence. The overall offending was egregious and the sentence not disproportionate.

why: Coercive control is proved by the pattern, so build the whole picture: a timeline of every incident, the controlling conduct (isolation from family and friends, monitoring, threats, humiliation), its effect on the victim, and corroboration (messages, medical records, witnesses). Charge the individual assaults too, and watch for intimidation while on bail or remand.

d: Presenting a credit card is a representation that you have the bank's actual authority to use it. Using a card after that authority has been withdrawn is a deception, and the shop's reliance on it can be inferred even if the assistant can't remember the sale. Conviction restored.

f.facts: The defendant held a credit card with a £200 limit and went well over it. The bank asked for the card back; she agreed to return it but didn't, and a week or so later used it to buy goods worth £10.35 in a Mothercare shop in Luton. She was convicted of obtaining a pecuniary advantage by deception; the Court of Appeal quashed the conviction.
f.held: House of Lords, 25 June 1981 (Lord Roskill, the other four Law Lords agreeing): appeal allowed, conviction restored. Presenting the card represented actual authority from the bank to make the contract — nothing to do with her credit standing. The question was whether the assistant would have completed the sale had she known the truth, and plainly she wouldn't. Where a witness can't remember a routine transaction, the jury may infer reliance from the other evidence. The cheque-card case Commissioner of Police v Charles (1977) applied equally to credit cards.

why: In card-misuse cases, prove the card's authority had been withdrawn (or never existed) — get the bank's records and letters — and get a statement from the shop that it would never have completed the sale had it known. Even if staff don't remember the sale, reliance can be inferred.

d: Under the English Theft Act 1968, a taking can be an appropriation even though the owner consented to it: consent goes to dishonesty, not to whether there was an appropriation. Taxi driver's theft conviction upheld.

f.facts: A foreign student who had just arrived at Victoria Station, with little English, showed a taxi driver a note of his destination. The driver said it was a long and expensive journey and took £6 from the student's open wallet. The proper fare was 10s 6d (52.5p). The driver was convicted of theft.
f.held: House of Lords, 30 June 1971: conviction upheld. The 1968 Act deliberately left out the old words 'without the consent of the owner', so the prosecution doesn't have to prove an absence of consent. Any assumption of the rights of an owner is an appropriation; whether the owner consented, or the taker believed he did, goes to dishonesty — and there was ample evidence of dishonesty here.

why: In Ireland the rule is different: theft requires appropriation without the owner's consent, but consent obtained by deception or intimidation isn't consent (s.4(1)–(2), 2001 Act). For an overcharging or 'help yourself' scam, record exactly what was said to get the money.

Cork Circuit Criminal Court imposed four years with the final two and a half suspended. The DPP applied for a review.
f.held: Court of Criminal Appeal, 18 April 2007 (Denham J): sentence quashed as unduly lenient; seven years imposed. The court should first determine the appropriate notional sentence, then consider aggravating and mitigating factors. The trial judge didn't address the gravity shown by the life maximum and the ten-year presumptive sentence, and applied the mitigating factors twice. The plea carried less weight because he was caught red-handed. On a DPP review, only a substantial departure from the appropriate sentence justifies intervention.

why: A plea from someone caught red-handed earns less credit — so record exactly how they were caught and what was found on them. Record any assistance precisely: 'limited' assistance counts for less.

f.facts: A Polish national arrested in Ireland in May 2017 on three European Arrest Warrants for drug trafficking objected to surrender, arguing that Poland's judicial reforms put him at real risk of an unfair trial. The High Court (Donnelly J) referred questions to the Court of Justice of the EU.

d: In drugs sentencing, the quantity and value of the drugs are critical factors in judging seriousness. A two-year sentence for possessing over €111,000 of cocaine was unduly lenient.

f.facts: The accused, in his early twenties, pleaded guilty to possessing about 1.6kg of cocaine worth €111,370, found at his family home while he was out. He said he was holding it for someone he owed €500. A psychological report described him as immature and vulnerable; he had no drug convictions. The sentencing judge said the value wasn't a material factor and imposed two years. The DPP sought a review as unduly lenient.
f.held: Court of Criminal Appeal, 10 October 2008 (Kearns J, with Budd and Clarke JJ): DPP's application allowed, with a new sentence to be substituted after further submissions. Quantity and value are critical factors in evaluating the overall seriousness of a drugs offence — that's implicit in the Act. Value isn't determinative, and the type of drug may also count, but the judge was wrong to treat value as immaterial. The court also stressed the importance of giving reasons.

why: Value and quantity drive the sentence, so prove them properly: weigh the drugs, get a professional valuation, and record where and how they were found. Record what the suspect says about holding them for someone else — it goes to culpability, not to whether the offence is complete.

d: Guards may use firearms against an unlawful or riotous crowd only where it's necessary as a last resort to preserve life. Detectives who fired at a crowd at a cattle sale in Cork, killing the plaintiff's son, weren't justified, and damages were awarded.

f.facts: Cattle seized under an Irish Land Commission warrant were to be sold by the sheriff at a yard in Cork, and a demonstration was expected. About 200 Guards, including about 12 armed detectives, were posted outside and 40 inside. A crowd gathered and a lorry carrying men broke through the barriers and gates. Special Branch detectives then opened fire, and the plaintiff's son, who had followed the lorry, was killed. His father sued three detectives and the Chief Superintendent under the Fatal Accidents Act 1846.
f.held: At trial Hanna J held the shooting unjustified: armed forces of the State may fire on an unlawful or riotous assembly only where it is necessary as a last resort to preserve life, and this firing wasn't done to protect life. Damages were awarded against Guards involved. The case is reported with the Supreme Court's 1938 decision, but the free sources don't show the full judgments or the result of the appeal.

why: A firearm is a last resort to preserve life — never a way to disperse a crowd or protect property. Today read it with Article 2 ECHR (McCann v UK (1995)): force must be no more than absolutely necessary, and operations must be planned to minimise the risk to life.

d: After a murder trial ends in manslaughter, the sentencing judge should state clearly the facts accepted, consistent with the verdict; a judge shouldn't probe the jury's reasoning, save exceptionally a limited question where the verdict is ambiguous. Producing a knife, absent a deadly attack, is a serious aggravating factor. Seven years for a knife manslaughter upheld.

f.facts: In 2013 the accused stabbed his partner's son in the abdomen during a confrontation outside a Dublin apartment; the young man died in hospital. The accused said it was an accident. He had brandished the knife, left without seeking help and disposed of the weapon. He had offered to plead guilty to manslaughter before trial. In 2016 a Central Criminal Court jury acquitted him of murder and convicted him of manslaughter; he got seven years, which the Court of Appeal upheld in December 2017.
f.held: Supreme Court, 11 April 2019 (Charleton J, for a unanimous court): appeal dismissed. A judge should not question a jury about its reasoning; only rarely, where a verdict is ambiguous, may the judge ask a limited question about which version it accepted, and declining to do so wasn't wrong. The sentencing judge should give a clear narrative of the facts accepted. Unless there is a deadly attack or reasonable grounds to fear one, producing a knife is a serious aggravating factor. The trial judge had taken a lenient view, and seven years was within the medium range (four to ten years) for manslaughter.

why: Weapons drive verdict and sentence. Evidence of who brought the knife, how it was produced and used, and what was done after — fleeing, failing to get help, getting rid of the weapon — shapes the outcome. Gather it, and recover the weapon.
topic: Sentencing manslaughter after a murder trial; knives as aggravation
st: Yes. Supreme Court guidance on the factual basis for sentencing after a manslaughter verdict, the manslaughter range, and knives as a serious aggravating factor.

f.facts: An antiques dealer was prosecuted for handling stolen goods. At his trial the prosecution admitted that some evidence came from tapping his phone under a warrant from the Home Secretary. His civil action in England failed in 1979, because no law made the tapping unlawful.
f.held: Violation of Article 8, unanimously. European Court of Human Rights (plenary), 2 August 1984: 'in accordance with the law' "relates to the quality of the law". d: Delay alone doesn't stop a trial. A man charged in 2009 with two killings from 1997 — after another man had confessed and been charged, and after new DNA testing of retained clothing — failed to prohibit his trial. Breach of the right to a timely trial, publicity, lost witnesses and forensic disputes are generally for the trial judge; prohibition needs a serious factor that clearly outweighs a trial on the merits.

f.facts: In March 1997 two women were killed in sheltered accommodation at a Dublin psychiatric hospital. Another man confessed and was charged, but the charges were withdrawn. In August 1997 the applicant, arrested on other matters, also made admissions; both men retracted, and a later inquiry criticised Garda handling of the confessions. In 2009 new DNA testing of retained clothing linked the applicant to the victims, and he was charged in October 2009. He sought to prohibit his trial for delay, publicity, missing witnesses and evidence, and the forensic issues. The High Court (Moriarty J) refused.
f.held: Supreme Court, appeal dismissed on 10 December 2014 with reasons on 29 January 2015 (Clarke J giving the lead judgment; Hardiman and Charleton JJ also giving judgments): breach of the right to a timely trial doesn't by itself bar a trial, because the Constitution values charges being determined on the merits; a serious factor must clearly outweigh that. The trial judge's role in securing a fair trial is paramount, and publicity, lost evidence and the DNA issues were best tested at trial. He was convicted in April 2015, and his appeals failed.

why: Old cases can still be prosecuted — but only if the exhibits survive and can be trusted. Package, seal, log and store exhibits so they can be retested years later without a contamination argument. And test every confession against the facts: a withdrawn confession by another man sent this investigation the wrong way.
topic: Prohibiting a trial for delay: the trial judge's role
st: Yes. A leading Supreme Court authority that delay, publicity and evidential problems are generally for the trial judge rather than grounds to prohibit a trial. His later claim for damages for delay also failed.

The exception is where disclosure is necessary to establish the accused’s innocence (“innocence at stake”), in which case the privilege must yield. Operational point. Keep the intelligence-to-evidence divide clean — the sterile corridor (see Volume 10). Source identity stays in the intelligence system; build the evidential case on independently obtainable material so source identity is never put in issue at trial. Public interest immunity (PII). Sensitive material — methods, premises, third-party safety — may be withheld where the public interest in non-disclosure outweighs the defence’s interest in disclosure. f.facts: A driver arrested for drink-driving in December 2001 was required at the station to give two breath specimens. On three attempts she couldn't seal her lips around the mouthpiece, and the machine recorded each specimen as incomplete. She was charged with failing to comply 'in the manner indicated by the Garda' and convicted in the District Court. On appeal, the Circuit Court stated a case.
f.held: Supreme Court, 28 July 2005, by 2 to 1 (Kearns J giving the decision): it was not an offence to refuse or fail to comply with the requirement to give the specimens in the manner the Garda indicated — s.13 is a penal provision and must be strictly construed. But a driver must give specimens sufficient to enable the concentration of alcohol in the breath to be determined; merely exhaling into the device isn't compliance. The conviction on the 'manner indicated' charge couldn't stand.

d: Failing to give breath specimens 'in the manner indicated by the Garda' wasn't an offence under s.13 of the Road Traffic Act 1994 (strictly construed). But a driver must give specimens sufficient to determine the alcohol concentration — just blowing into the machine isn't compliance. Conviction couldn't stand (2–1).
why: Charge the right failure: that the person failed to provide specimens sufficient to determine the alcohol concentration — not that they didn't follow your method. Record each attempt, the machine's printout, what you told them, and whether they were genuinely trying.

f.facts: The accused was charged in 1996 with historic sexual offences alleged to date from the 1970s, including indecent assault under s.62 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861. In the Circuit Criminal Court he applied to quash the counts, arguing s.62 was inconsistent with the Constitution and the European Convention on Human Rights. The judge stated a case to the Supreme Court.
f.held: Supreme Court, 2 April 2003 (Keane CJ, Denham, Murray, McGuinness and Hardiman JJ): the Circuit Criminal Court had no jurisdiction to decide a constitutional challenge to a pre-1937 statute; a court of local and limited jurisdiction must apply legislation unless the superior courts have found it invalid. Because the Convention hadn't then been incorporated by legislation, no court had jurisdiction to decide whether a statute was inconsistent with it.

why: Constitutional challenges to criminal statutes belong in the High Court, not the District or Circuit Court — so a prosecution under a statute goes ahead unless a superior court has struck it down. Keep your file moving.

A garda took a walkie-talkie from his right jacket pocket; when he went for the left pocket, the man pushed his hand away. The garda arrested him under s.30, cautioned him and told him why, and the man handed over the contents of the pocket: explosives. The continued search after arrest and explanation was lawful, and nothing linked any earlier irregularity to the find.

s.t: D.3 Bukta and Others v Hungary (2007) Application No. 25691/04 Citation: Application No. 25691/04, judgment 17 July 2007. Facts: Applicants attended a spontaneous demonstration in response to a sudden political event. Police dispersed the assembly because notification had not been given as required by domestic law. Holding: Dispersal of a spontaneous peaceable assembly solely for failure to give prior notification breaches Article 11. Where the assembly is a response to a current event and prior notification was not practicable, the right to peaceful assembly attaches. Reasoning: The Court emphasised that strict application of notification requirements to spontaneous assembly defeats the purpose of the right. Assemblies responding to immediate events must be accommodated where peaceable. Significance: Spontaneous assembly protection. Operational implication for Irish public order policing of unplanned protests. Operational Application:

d: Dispersing a peaceful demonstration solely because the organisers hadn't given the required prior notice was disproportionate and breached Article 11, where the event it responded to was announced too late for notice to be given.

f.facts: The day before a government function, the Prime Minister announced he would attend. Domestic law required three days' notice of a demonstration, which couldn't be met. About 150 people demonstrated outside the function without notice, and police dispersed them. There's no indication in the summary of disorder.
f.held: Violation of Article 11. European Court of Human Rights, 17 July 2007: a notice requirement can pursue legitimate aims (preventing disorder, protecting others' rights), but dispersing a peaceful assembly solely because notice wasn't given, where it couldn't be, was disproportionate. Authorities must show a certain degree of tolerance towards peaceful gatherings.

why: A peaceful protest isn't unlawful just because it's spontaneous or unannounced. Facilitate it, engage with organisers, and act on specific conduct (for example, a s.8 direction for a listed offence), not on the lack of paperwork.
topic: Spontaneous demonstrations and dispersal for lack of notice
st: Still cited for tolerance of peaceful, spontaneous assemblies. Read with Kudrevičius (2015) on deliberate disruption.

s.t: D.4 Kudrevicius and Others v Lithuania [GC] (2015) Application No. 37553/05 Citation: Application No. 37553/05, Grand Chamber judgment 15 October 2015. Facts: Farmers protested by blocking major roads for two days. Significant disruption to road users. Convicted of rioting under domestic law and sentenced to suspended imprisonment. Issue on Article 11. Holding: Article 11 protects peaceful assembly but the State has a wider margin where the assembly causes substantial disruption to public life. Conviction and sanction for sustained, deliberate, significantly disruptive blocking of major roads did not breach Article 11. Reasoning: The Grand Chamber emphasised the balance between assembly rights and the rights of others (public order, freedom of movement, economic activity). Significant deliberate disruption falls outside the most protected core of Article 11. Significance: Defines the limit of Article 11 protection in disruptive protest

d: Convicting protest leaders for deliberately blocking major highways for two days didn't breach Article 11: intentional serious disruption isn't at the core of the right of peaceful assembly, and the authorities had shown tolerance.

f.facts: In May 2003 farmers held authorised demonstrations beside major highways, then blocked three highways without authorisation until talks with the government ended the protest. Five organisers were convicted of inciting and taking part in riots and given suspended sentences.
f.held: No violation of Article 11, unanimously. European Court of Human Rights (Grand Chamber), 15 October 2015: the protest was peaceful, so Article 11 applied and the convictions were an interference; but deliberately disrupting others' lawful activities, to a greater extent than normal for a protest, was "reprehensible" conduct, and the authorities had tolerated the blockades for a long time, so the sanctions were necessary and proportionate.

why: Peaceful protest is protected even when disruptive, but deliberate, serious obstruction of roads can justify directions and prosecution. Show tolerance first, give clear directions, and record the disruption caused.

topic: Protest blockades of roads and the right of peaceful assembly

s.t: Section 30(1) provides as follows: “A member of the Garda Síochána (if he is not in uniform on production of his identification card if demanded) may without warrant stop, search, interrogate, and arrest any person, or do any one or more of those things in respect of any person, whom he suspects of having committed or being about to commit or being or having been concerned in the commission of an offence under any section or sub-section of this Act or an offence which is for the time being a scheduled offence for the purposes of Part V of this Act or whom he suspects of carrying a document relating to the commission or intended commission of any such offence as aforesaid or whom he 2: a person whom it is decided not to charge should be released forthwith: Wiltshire v. Barrett [1966] 1 QB 312 3: Hussein v. Chong Fook Yam [1970] AC 942; [1969] 3 ALL ER 1626 4: O’Hara v. Chief Constable, Royal Ulster Constabulary [1992] AC 286; [1997] 1 AL

d: An arresting officer must genuinely suspect the person and have reasonable grounds for that suspicion, judged on the information in his own mind at the time. A briefing can supply the grounds, but a bare order from a superior to arrest isn't enough.

f.facts: In December 1985 a constable in Northern Ireland arrested a man without warrant under s.12(1)(b) of the Prevention of Terrorism (Temporary Provisions) Act 1984, in connection with a murder. His only basis was a briefing from a superior officer that the man was involved. The man was questioned, released without charge in January 1986, and sued for unlawful arrest and false imprisonment.
f.held: Appeal dismissed. House of Lords, 12 December 1996: the test is partly subjective (the officer must genuinely suspect) and partly objective (there must be reasonable grounds), judged on what was in the arresting officer's mind. Information from others, such as a briefing, a tip-off or an informer, can provide reasonable grounds even if it later proves wrong. But the discretion to arrest is the arresting officer's, so a mere order from a superior isn't enough. The trial judge was entitled to infer, on scanty evidence, that the briefing gave reasonable grounds.

why: The arrest is your decision. Before arresting on a briefing, make sure you know the grounds yourself, and record them: what you were told, by whom, and why you suspected the person. Irish arrest powers (for example s.4 of the Criminal Law Act 1997) also require you to suspect 'with reasonable cause'.
topic: Reasonable suspicion for arrest, and arresting on a briefing
st: The leading UK authority on reasonable suspicion, persuasive in Ireland. Applied in Raissi (2008): officers can't simply assume their superiors had good grounds.

why: CCTV and bodycam footage is personal data. Release images to the media or public (for example, in an appeal) only through the proper channels, when necessary and proportionate, and mask anyone who doesn't need to be identified.

d: The Judges' Rules are not rules of law but rules of practice for those taking statements; a statement obtained in breach of them may be excluded in the trial judge's discretion. The case also raised the duty to tell a s.30 detainee of the right to a solicitor.

f.facts: The accused was convicted in the Special Criminal Court in 1976 of causing an explosion (s.2, Explosive Substances Act 1883) — a bomb in Pettigo, Co. Donegal, in 1973 — and sentenced to 15 years. The only evidence linking him was verbal statements and one written statement made while he was detained under s.30 of the Offences Against the State Act 1939 for over 24 hours. He argued the statements should have been excluded because he wasn't told of his right to consult a solicitor or medically examined before questioning.
f.held: Court of Criminal Appeal, 29 July 1977 (O'Higgins CJ, Gannon and D'Arcy JJ). The Judges' Rules are not rules of law; they are administrative directions for the guidance of those taking statements, and a statement obtained contrary to their spirit may be rejected by the trial judge (following People v Cummins (1972)). The court noted that s.30 detention can't override constitutional rights such as access to legal advice. The free sources available don't show the final order.

why: Today the Custody Regulations, the Code of Practice on access to a solicitor and electronic recording govern interviews — but the principle stands: breaches give the court grounds to exclude. Tell every detainee of their rights, record that you did, and follow the rules on recording statements.

s.t: It was held by Court of Criminal Appeal that the reply was not voluntary as the failure or refusal to answer would constitute an offence involving serious penalties. The Court expressed no opinion on the position which would have existed if the charges had been for offences under the Road Traffic Act, 1961 - The People v. Gilbert [1973] I.R. 383. 4.16. Examples of confessions held to be voluntary A member said to the accused (in custody on another charge): "What about Premier Tailors, I believe you did it?" The member was referring to an alleged burglary and did not administer the caution before asking the question. At the time the member had no evidence implicating the accused but claimed that because of his experience and knowledge of the accused and the nature of the crime, it was his belief. The reply of the accused - which amounted to a confession - was found by the Supreme Court to have been voluntary -

d: An admission made in answer to a s.107 Road Traffic Act demand — after a warning that refusing to answer is an offence — isn't voluntary, and shouldn't have been admitted on a charge of receiving a stolen car. The court left open its use for Road Traffic Act offences.

f.facts: Before the trial, a Garda sergeant invoked s.107 of the Road Traffic Act 1961, warning the accused that refusing to answer was an offence carrying serious penalties, and the accused admitted using the car. He was then tried in the Circuit Court for receiving a stolen motor car, knowing it to be stolen (s.33(1), Larceny Act 1916), the admission was put in evidence, and he was convicted.
f.held: Court of Criminal Appeal, 13 April 1973 (Pringle J): the statement wasn't voluntary, because the sergeant had warned that refusing to answer was an offence with serious penalties, so the trial judge shouldn't have admitted it on the Larceny Act charge. The court expressly gave no opinion on the position for offences under the Road Traffic Acts. A trial judge has no discretion to admit a confession found to be involuntary (Cummins (1972)).

why: A s.107 answer ('who was driving?') given under threat of prosecution is compelled. You can use it for the Road Traffic Act offence (Burke (2019)), but don't rely on it for theft, handling or other non-road-traffic offences — get the evidence another way, after a caution.

st: Still good law for non-road-traffic offences. For Road Traffic Act prosecutions, the Court of Appeal held s.107 answers admissible in DPP v Burke (2019).

s.t: Subsequently the witness’s recollection of the culprit and their recollection of the photograph may become merged so that the witness cannot separate them leading to the possibility of a wrong identification. The Court of Criminal Appeal in The People v. Mills [1956] I.R. 106 acknowledged that it is permissible for a Garda who has received a description of a person suspected of a particular offence to show photographs to the person giving the description for the purpose of confirming such description. Where photographs are used for this purpose, numerous photographs of possible suspects and not merely one or two should be shown to the witness . A detailed description should first be obtained from the witness as a means of recording the parameters of the witness’s memory prior to the inspection of the photographs The Court of Criminal Appeal in

d: A Garda may show photographs to a witness who has given a description, to confirm it — but a witness who has seen a suspect's photograph before an identification parade gives weaker identification evidence, because the photo can merge with the memory.

f.facts: A woman's wallet with £104 10s was stolen while she was jostled in a bus queue in North Earl Street, Dublin, in December 1955. The next day she described the man to two detectives, who returned that day with six or eight photographs, including one of the accused; she picked his. The following day she identified him at an identification parade. The photographs came out only in cross-examination. She was the only identifying witness; the accused gave an alibi.
f.held: Court of Criminal Appeal (Maguire CJ). Later cases describe Mills as treating the evidence of a witness who has previously seen a photograph as less reliable than other identification evidence, and as accepting that Gardaí may show photographs to a witness who has given a description, to confirm it. The free sources available don't show the final order.

why: Get a full description first and record it. If photos are used, show a fair, numerous selection — never one or two — and record exactly what was shown and said. Once a witness has seen a suspect's photo, any later parade identification is weaker, so think before you show photos.
