s.t: The employer would clearly be in authority in the case of a charge against their servant of embezzlement or arson of their property, but not against the servant on a charge of murdering their own child. A confession made to, but not induced by, a person in authority is admissible, while, conversely, a confession induced by, but not made to, such a person will be rejected. An inducement not held out by a person in authority but in their presence is the same as an inducement held out by a person in authority unless the person in authority disassociates themselves completely from the inducement - People v Murphy [1947] I.R. 236. 4.12. Inducement, threat or promise The use or threat of violence by a person in authority would plainly render a confession inadmissible. There are numerous recorded decisions showing that the vaguest hint of a threat or promise may be fatal in this respect. Crime Investigation Techniques Manual 7

Murphy (supra). In the People v. Pringle, 2 Frewen 57, the Court of Criminal Appeal held that the effect of an inducement on the accused had dissipated by the time he made his statement of admission because he had a consultation with his solicitor prior to making the statement. 4.14. The accused at a stage when he was a suspect asked a police officer: "If I make a statement will you give me bail now?" The police officer answered "Yes". App. R. 97. A member investigating the unlawful taking of a motor car invoked sta

d: The prosecution must prove a statement was voluntary. If an inducement was held out earlier, the trial judge must be satisfied it had ceased to operate on the accused's mind before the statement was made. A statement isn't inadmissible merely because it was made in answer to police questions.

f.facts: During a murder investigation, the accused made a statement in answer to questions by a police officer. Before that, a remark had been made to him — 'you are all right' — that was argued to mean 'you will be all right', an improper inducement.
f.held: Court of Criminal Appeal, 23 January 1947: the onus is on the prosecution to establish that a statement was voluntary. Where an inducement has been held out, the trial judge must be judicially satisfied that it had ceased to operate on the accused's mind before the statement is admitted. A statement made in answer to police questions isn't, on that account alone, inadmissible. The free headnote available doesn't show the final order.

why: Don't hold out hopes or promises — 'you'll be all right', 'it'll go easier on you', 'just tell us and you can go home'. If someone else has, record it, and make sure any later statement is made free of it (break, fresh caution, solicitor). The prosecution must prove voluntariness.

d: Offering to sell someone else's property as if you own it is an appropriation, so the theft is complete at that moment, even if nothing has been moved. Buyers who then took the goods were handling stolen goods 'otherwise than in the course of the stealing'. Appeals dismissed.

f.facts: A man offered to sell furniture in the house of a friend who was in prison to the two defendants, with no authority to do so. They agreed to buy it and helped take it away. They were convicted of handling stolen goods and appealed, arguing that anything they did was 'in the course of the stealing'.
f.held: Court of Appeal: appeals dismissed. The offer to sell was an assumption of the rights of the owner, so the appropriation — and the theft — took place at that point, even though nothing had been moved and the owner hadn't yet lost anything. The defendants' later dealings with the furniture were therefore not in the course of the stealing, and they were rightly convicted of handling.

why: Where someone offers property that isn't theirs, the theft can be complete at the offer. People who then receive or move the goods, knowing or reckless that they're stolen, can be charged with handling (s.17, 2001 Act). Record what was offered, by whom, for how much and when.
topic: When theft is complete: offering to sell another's property; handling
st: English authority, persuasive in Ireland. Ireland's handling offence (s.17, 2001 Act) also applies only 'otherwise than in the course of the stealing'.

d: Police generally need a warrant to search the digital contents of a phone taken from a person on arrest. They may examine the phone physically to make sure it can't be used as a weapon.

f.facts: Police stopped a car for expired registration and arrested the driver for driving on a suspended licence. An officer looked through his smartphone at the scene, and about two hours later a detective searched it at the station, finding a photograph linking him to a shooting weeks earlier. In a companion case (United States v Wurie), police searched an arrested man's flip phone, which led them to drugs and a firearm.
f.held: US Supreme Court, 25 June 2014, unanimously (Chief Justice Roberts): the search-incident-to-arrest exception doesn't extend to the data on a phone. Data can't be used as a weapon, the risk of remote wiping can be met by other means (such as a signal-blocking bag), and modern phones hold 'the privacies of life'. Officers must generally get a warrant, though exigent circumstances, such as a child abduction or an imminent bomb, can still justify a search, case by case.

why: Persuasive only, but Irish law points the same way: in Quirke (2023) the Supreme Court required specific authority to search a device's contents. Secure the phone and get proper authority before looking through it.

f.facts: In 1988 a man was charged with entering a building as a trespasser and stealing, and with malicious damage. The District Court refused bail. The President of the High Court granted it, holding that he couldn't consider the DPP's only objection: that the man would continue to commit crime if released. The DPP appealed.
f.held: Appeal dismissed. Supreme Court, 18 November 1988 (Finlay CJ): following O'Callaghan, the likelihood that an accused will commit offences on bail isn't a valid ground for refusing bail. It wasn't a ground at common law before 1922, and Article 40.3 doesn't provide one. The answers to offending on bail lie in police surveillance, speedy trials and deterrent sentences.

why: When objecting to bail, be clear which ground you rely on: the O'Callaghan grounds (flight; interfering with witnesses or evidence) or s.2 of the Bail Act 1997 (necessary to prevent a serious offence). Bring specific evidence for each.

f.facts: In April 1992 a man was detained by police on suspicion of aiding the PKK. Less than a day later he was taken to hospital and declared dead on arrival. The autopsy and investigation were inadequate, and police questioning of the applicant about her application interfered with her right of petition.

why: Everyone in your custody is your responsibility. Record their condition on arrival, every check and any injury, and get medical help at once. If someone is injured or dies in custody, the State has to explain it.

s.t: 3.1 Persuasive authority on “reasonable firmness” R v Sanchez (1996) — English; persuasive only Holding / principle. On affray, the violence relied on must be such as would cause a notional bystander of reasonable firmness to fear for their personal safety. Where the violence was confined to two individuals in an open outdoor space, with ample room for any bystander to withdraw, an affray conviction was quashed — there was no real risk to a person of reasonable firmness. Operational point. Useful for understanding the objective element common to all three offences: it is not enough that two people fought; the prosecution must show the conduct was such as would frighten a notional bystander of reasonable firmness. In the inner city the setting usually supplies this (a crowded street, projectiles, weapons) — but it must be articulated in the evidence, not assumed. English authority; not binding here. Working reference - not legal advice -

d: For affray in England, where violence is aimed at one person, the hypothetical 'person of reasonable firmness' must be a bystander, not the victim — and the jury must ask whether that bystander would have feared for their own safety. Conviction quashed.

f.facts: In a car park, the defendant lunged at her boyfriend with a knife. She was convicted of affray.
f.held: Court of Appeal, 6 March 1996 (Simon Brown LJ sitting): appeal allowed. Where the violence is directed at one person, the person of reasonable firmness is a hypothetical third party, not the victim. The judge hadn't directed the jury to consider whether such a bystander would have feared for their own safety, so the conviction couldn't stand.

why: In Ireland affray (s.16, 1994 Act) needs two or more people using or threatening violence towards each other, such that a person of reasonable firmness there would fear for their own or another's safety. f.facts: In a routine search at a courier compound at Dublin Airport in 2007, Gardaí found five large parcels of herbal cannabis. Using the consignee details they arranged a meeting and handed the parcels over to a father and son, who were arrested. The son said a friend had asked him to collect parcels supposedly containing computer parts, using a new phone and an assumed name, and that he'd asked his father to drive; they expected about €300. Evidence of their movements and behaviour before arrest was led to show they knew. Both were convicted of possession for sale or supply, including under s.15A.
f.held: Court of Criminal Appeal, 18 May 2010 (Charleton J): appeal allowed, retrial ordered. The trial judge rightly treated s.29(2) as subjective, but wrongly told the jury the burden never shifted to the defence, leaving the jury with inconsistent directions. The prosecution must prove possession and that the substance is a controlled drug beyond reasonable doubt; the burden then shifts to the accused to show a reasonable doubt that he didn't know and had no reasonable grounds to suspect — a legal burden discharged on the lowest standard. He may do so by pointing to weaknesses in the prosecution case, his statement to Gardaí, or his own evidence.

d: Under s.29(2) of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1977, once the prosecution proves possession and that the substance is a controlled drug, the accused bears a legal burden — on the lowest standard — to show a reasonable doubt that he didn't know, and had no reason to suspect, it was a drug. Telling the jury the burden 'never shifted' was wrong. Retrial ordered.
why: In controlled deliveries and courier cases, knowledge is the battleground. Record the suspects' movements and behaviour before arrest (counter-surveillance, false names, new phones, payment), and put the s.29 issues to them in interview: what they thought was inside, and why.

f.facts: Gardaí got a search warrant from a Peace Commissioner and searched the accused's home. Nothing incriminating was found, but he was arrested there and detained under s.4 of the Criminal Justice Act 1984, and made a statement that became the main prosecution evidence on charges of assault, possession of an article with intent to injure, and robbery. The trial judge held there was no evidence the warrant was valid without the Peace Commissioner's evidence, held the arrest and detention invalid, and directed an acquittal. The DPP referred the point of law to the Supreme Court.
f.held: Supreme Court, 16 February 1999 (Barrington J, for Hamilton CJ, O'Flaherty, Denham and Keane JJ): the Peace Commissioner had to give evidence in person to establish his state of mind when issuing the warrant. The warrant is a document that may affect constitutional rights and doesn't speak for itself. Only that point was referred, so the Court didn't rule on the arrest; O'Flaherty J added that the arrest didn't depend on the warrant, as Gardaí may arrest on reasonable suspicion of an arrestable offence.

why: A warrant is only as good as the issuer's satisfaction behind it. Make sure your sworn information gives the issuer real grounds, and that whoever issued the warrant can be called to prove they considered it. Don't rely on a warrant to justify an arrest — have independent grounds.

f.facts: A driver was charged with drink-driving under s.49 of the Road Traffic Act 1961. The prosecution proved his arrest and detention, the taking of a urine sample and the Medical Bureau certificate — but there was no evidence he had been told of his rights under the 1987 Custody Regulations. The District Court stated a case to the High Court asking whether the Regulations applied, whether compliance had to be proved, and whether a breach made the custody unlawful or the evidence inadmissible.
f.held: High Court, 8 February 1995 (O'Hanlon J): the words 'of itself' in s.7(3) of the Criminal Justice Act 1984 matter — a breach of the Regulations doesn't of itself affect the lawfulness of custody or the admissibility of evidence. Whether a breach does so in a particular case is for the trial court to decide on the facts, case by case; it isn't an automatic ground for exclusion.

s.t: Constructive possession applies where the suspect item is in the actual possession of some other person over whom the accused has control so that it would be available to them if they wanted it (Minister for Posts and Telegraphs v Campbell [1966] I.R. 69 at 73). d: To 'keep or have in possession' an article, a person must have control of it. Being the occupier of the premises where it's found is evidence of that, but control — not mere presence — is what possession requires.

f.facts: An inspector from the Department of Posts and Telegraphs visited a cottage near Clane, Co. Kildare, spoke to a woman there and found a television set on a table. A valuation certificate named the defendant as the occupier. He was charged under s.3 of the Wireless Telegraphy Act 1926 with unlawfully keeping or having in his possession a television set without a licence. He didn't appear. The District Justice stated a case to the High Court on the evidence and onus of proof.
f.held: High Court, 13 May 1966 (Davitt P), on a consultative case stated: a person must have control of an article to be said to keep it or have it in his possession — a statement later cited by the Supreme Court. The free sources available don't show how the questions were answered on the facts.

why: In any possession case (drugs, weapons, stolen goods), evidence of control is the key: who occupies or controls the premises, vehicle or bag; who has keys; whose belongings are with the item; what was said. Presence alone isn't possession.

d: For an attempt, the jury must be told that a mere desire to commit the crime isn't enough — and neither is a desire followed by an intention to act. Asking a doctor whether there wasn't 'some drug' didn't prove an attempt to obtain it. Conviction quashed.

f.facts: The accused was convicted at Galway Circuit Court of attempting to procure a drug, knowing it was intended to procure a miscarriage. The evidence was that he went to a doctor who was treating a young woman, asked for a prescription to end her pregnancy, was refused, and then asked whether there wasn't some drug named ergot. He gave no evidence, and was acquitted on the other counts.

d: A power to arrest someone 'committing' an offence covers a person apparently committing it, judged on the facts as they appeared to the officer at the time — a later decision not to prosecute doesn't make the arrest unlawful. If inquiry then shows the person is innocent, release them at once.

f.facts: Police stopped a driver late at night in December 1962 on suspicion of drink-driving. He refused to get out, and they arrested him for being unfit to drive through drink; he was injured in the struggle. A police doctor found he wasn't unfit, and he was released without charge. He sued the constable for assault, and the trial judge treated the arrest as unlawful.
f.held: Court of Appeal, 1965 (Lord Denning MR, Davies and Salmon LJJ): a constable was justified in arresting a driver who was apparently committing the offence; the question is whether the facts, as they appeared to him at the time, warranted it. A later acquittal, or a decision not to prosecute, doesn't make the arrest unlawful. If, after arrest, the person is found on inquiry to be innocent, he should at once be set free — there's no obligation to take him before a court.

why: Your arrest is judged on what you perceived at the time, so record what you saw, heard and smelt. And if inquiries clear the person, release them straight away and record when and why.
topic: Arresting someone apparently committing an offence; releasing them when cleared

The Winterwerp v Netherlands (1979) framework establishes: Unsoundness of mind established by objective medical expertise. Of a kind / degree warranting compulsory confinement. Validity of continued confinement depends on persistence of disorder. Periodic review by independent body. The framework has been substantially supported by judicial decisions while also being subject to ongoing reform. C.3 Bournewood Principle -

d: Except in emergencies, a person may be detained as of 'unsound mind' only if a true mental disorder is reliably shown by objective medical expertise, it warrants compulsory confinement, and it persists. Detention must be reviewed periodically by a court.

f.facts: A man was committed to a psychiatric hospital under the Dutch emergency procedure in 1968. Detention was then authorised by a court on a GP's declaration without hearing him, and prolonged yearly by court order ten times. He also lost the legal capacity to administer his property without being heard, and his requests for discharge got nowhere.
f.held: No violation of Article 5(1)(e), but violations of Articles 5(4) and 6(1). European Court of Human Rights, 24 October 1979: a person may be detained as of unsound mind only if reliably shown to be so by objective medical expertise, the disorder warrants compulsory confinement, and continued confinement "depends upon the persistence of such a disorder"; periodic court review is required; and mental illness "cannot warrant the total absence" of the right to a court.

why: When you take someone into custody under the Mental Health Act 2001 (s.12), act on clear grounds of serious and immediate risk, get a medical assessment at once, and record what you saw. Emergency powers are short-term only.

s.t: The Architecture of Proof 1.1 Burden and standard of proof The prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. This is the “golden thread” running through the criminal law — Woolmington v DPP [1935] AC 462 — carried into Irish law and grounded in the right to trial in due course of law under Article 38.1 of the Constitution. “Beyond reasonable doubt” is a high standard: not proof beyond all doubt, but proof to the point where the tribunal is sure. The accused is presumed innocent; if at the end of the case the tribunal is left with a reasonable doubt, the accused is acquitted. Two distinct burdens must be kept apart: • Legal (persuasive) burden — the obligation to prove a fact to the required standard. On the ingredients of the offence this rests on the prosecution from start to finish and never shifts. f.facts: A farm labourer shot his wife dead at her mother's house after she had left him. He said he had meant only to frighten her by threatening suicide, and that the gun went off by accident. House of Lords, 23 May 1935 (Viscount Sankey LC, for a unanimous House): "it is the duty of the prosecution to prove the prisoner's guilt", subject only to insanity and statutory exceptions, and a reasonable doubt arising from any part of the evidence means acquittal: the 'golden thread' of the criminal law.

When deciding under s.4(7) of the Immigration Act 2004 whether to renew or vary a long-term resident's permission, the Minister must consider Article 8 ECHR (private and family life) at that stage — not leave it until deportation. Minister's appeal dismissed.

f.facts: A Mauritian national came to Ireland in 2006 under a State education scheme that allowed part-time work, and lived here with his family, self-supporting, with children in Irish schools. A 2011 change of policy put time limits on non-EEA students registered before 2011, and the family was directed to leave by December 2013. The High Court refused judicial review; the Court of Appeal held the Minister had erred by not considering Article 8.
f.held: Supreme Court, April 2018 (MacMenamin J, heard with Luximon v Minister for Justice): Minister's appeal dismissed. In s.4(7) decisions the Minister must consider whether Article 8 rights are engaged; it isn't enough to leave them to the deportation stage. The applicants were lawful, long-duration residents whose position changed because of a policy shift, not anything they did. The Minister can still set limits on how long people may stay, and the ruling shouldn't be stretched beyond its facts.

d: A refusal of asylum can be a sufficient basis for a deportation order, and the Minister may treat the integrity of the asylum and immigration systems as part of the common good when refusing humanitarian leave to remain. Leave for judicial review refused.

f.facts: Each applicant applied for asylum, was refused and appealed unsuccessfully. They then asked the Minister to let them remain on humanitarian grounds under s.3(3)(b) of the Immigration Act 1999, and argued that the Minister hadn't given intelligible reasons for deciding to deport them.
f.held: Supreme Court, 30 July 2001 (Hardiman J, for Keane CJ, Denham, Murphy and Murray JJ): the High Court's refusal of leave to seek judicial review was upheld. Refusal of asylum may be a sufficient basis for deportation. The humanitarian applications were appeals to mercy that didn't meet any requirement for special consideration, and the Minister was entitled to identify maintaining the integrity of the asylum and immigration systems as an aspect of the common good. The State has a legitimate interest in controlling the entry and residence of non-nationals.

d: A deportation order under s.3(1) of the Immigration Act 1999 isn't unconstitutional because it has no end date: the Minister can amend or revoke it under s.3(11), and must deal with that proportionately. Appeal dismissed.

f.facts: A Georgian man arrived in 2001 and a deportation order was made against him that December. He avoided deportation by deceptive means until November 2011. He had married in Ireland in 2009 and had two children, who weren't Irish citizens; his wife had temporary humanitarian leave to remain, which she admitted was obtained with a false story. The family argued that an order of indefinite duration disproportionately interfered with family rights, and that s.3(11) was an unlawful delegation of legislative power.
f.held: Supreme Court, 23 June 2015 (Murray J, with Hardiman, O'Donnell, Clarke and MacMenamin JJ): appeal dismissed. A deportation order isn't necessarily unlimited in time, because the Minister can amend or revoke it under s.3(11), and must use that power proportionately, with fair procedures and in line with the Constitution and the ECHR. A non-national with no right to be here doesn't acquire one with the passage of time, so a fixed end date would be inappropriate. The power to exclude non-nationals is inherent in a sovereign State; the Act just names the Minister to exercise it.

f.facts: A single mother came to Ireland in 2007 with her young children and sought asylum, describing violence and threats at home. Her account was found not credible in 2010. In 2011 the Minister refused subsidiary protection and humanitarian leave to remain, and the family was removed from the State that December. From abroad, they sought judicial review, arguing they should have had an oral hearing and that judicial review wasn't an effective remedy.
f.held: Supreme Court, 21 December 2017 (Charleton J, with Dunne and Hogan JJ): the refusal of leave on the broader grounds was affirmed. Judicial review — with proportionality applied where fundamental rights are engaged (Meadows) — gives a thorough review of a refusal of subsidiary protection, and so is an effective remedy; EU law doesn't expressly require a separate merits appeal. Following the CJEU in MM, as a rule there's no right to an oral hearing for subsidiary protection where an asylum oral hearing has already taken place.

n: U.M. (a minor) v Minister for Foreign Affairs
d: Revoking a parent's refugee status doesn't operate backwards. A child born in Ireland while the father's refugee declaration was in force is a citizen, even though the declaration was later revoked because it was obtained by fraud. Supreme Court unanimous.

f.facts: A child was born in Ireland in June 2013. The father had been granted refugee status in 2006, but it emerged that his fingerprints matched a man refused asylum in the UK in 2005, and his refugee status was revoked with effect from August 2013. A passport application for the child was refused because the father's refugee application had been fraudulent. The Court of Appeal held that permission obtained by fraud couldn't count towards the child's citizenship under s.6A of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956.
f.held: Supreme Court, June 2022 (Dunne J; O'Donnell CJ concurring; unanimous): the Court of Appeal was overturned. A declaration of refugee status remains valid until it is revoked, and the Minister's discretion over revocation allows account to be taken of people, like a child, who acquired rights before then. Without clear statutory words, revocation takes effect from its own date and doesn't change the legal character of what went before.

why: Don't assume a child isn't an Irish citizen because a parent's status was later revoked — citizenship depends on the position when the child was born. Refer questions of citizenship to the immigration authorities or the Passport Office.

f.facts: An 18-year-old held under s.30 of the Offences Against the State Act 1939 over a firearm linked to an attempted armed robbery began making a statement after hours of questioning. A solicitor engaged by his family arrived and asked to see him, but gardai kept the solicitor out until the statement was finished, regarding interruption as 'bad manners'.
f.held: The Supreme Court dismissed the DPP's appeal against a directed acquittal. Reasonable access to a solicitor is a constitutional right, meant to ensure the detainee knows his rights and can decide freely how to respond to questioning. Deliberately keeping out a solicitor who had arrived and asked to see him breached it, making later admissions inadmissible; as their timing could not be fixed, the acquittal stood.

f.facts: Arrested on suspicion of murder one Sunday afternoon and detained under s.4 of the Criminal Justice Act 1984, he asked for a solicitor. Gardai tried in good faith to reach one, but questioning continued for about two hours before the solicitor arrived that evening. His admissions came later that night and the next morning.
f.held: Where gardai made bona fide efforts to contact the requested solicitor, they were not required to postpone questioning until the solicitor arrived, and admissibility remained a matter for the trial judge. Exclusion required a conscious and deliberate breach of the right and a causative link between breach and statement; neither was shown, so the admissions stood.

d: A conscious and deliberate denial of reasonable access to a solicitor renders the detention unlawful while it continues, and statements taken in that period are inadmissible.

f.facts: A detained suspect wanted legal advice. The gardai were found to have acted mala fide in arranging it, in effect contacting a solicitor unlikely to reach the station for a considerable time. Statements were taken both while he was without advice and after a solicitor became available.
f.held: A conscious and deliberate denial of reasonable access to a solicitor renders the detention unlawful while it continues, and statements taken in that period are inadmissible. The unlawfulness ends once genuine access is given, so later statements not causally linked to the breach may be admitted. Deliberately calling a solicitor likely to take a long time to arrive can amount to such a denial.

Gardaí have a common-law power to stop vehicles without prior suspicion when acting in good faith to detect or prevent crime, including drink-driving, and evidence obtained after such a stop is admissible. Facts: The case concerned evidence obtained in breach of constitutional rights and the question of admissibility. The Supreme Court considered whether the strict exclusionary rule of People (DPP) v Kenny [1990] 2 IR 110 should be modified. Holding: The court modified the Kenny rule. Where evidence is obtained in breach of constitutional rights, it is presumptively inadmissible, but the breach may be excused where it was inadvertent and excusable. Deliberate or conscious violation results in exclusion; inadvertent breach by an officer acting in good faith may not. Reasoning: The court balanced the deterrent / rights-protective function of exclusion against the cost of excluding probative evidence in cases of accidental breach. d: A mere error, especially one not calculated to mislead and which did not mislead, does not invalidate a warrant.

f.facts: A peace commissioner issued a s.26 Misuse of Drugs Act warrant for '4 Marrowbone Close, Dublin 8'. The real address was 4 Marrowbone Lane Close; the address on the warrant did not exist. About €300,000 of heroin was found. The trial ruled the warrant invalid and the DPP appealed.
f.held: A mere error, especially one not calculated to mislead and which did not mislead, does not invalidate a warrant. Invalidity arises where a statutory precondition for issue was not met or the warrant fails on its face to show it was met; a misdescription that leaves the intended premises obvious is not fundamental. Balfe had not been overruled by Edgeworth. Appeal allowed (O'Donnell J, 3 March 2011).

d: A 16-year-old charged with intoxication in a public place argued it was unequal that adults can get a fixed charge notice but children can't. Relief refused: the Oireachtas could reasonably prefer children to be dealt with under the Children Act 2001 instead.

f.facts: A 16-year-old was charged with being intoxicated in a public place (s.4 CJPOA 1994). f.held: Where a case depends wholly or substantially on disputed identification, the judge must warn the jury of "the special need for caution" and explain why — including "the possibility that a mistaken witness can be a convincing one" and that several witnesses can all be mistaken. The jury should examine the circumstances: how long the witness had the accused under observation, at what distance, in what light, whether the view was impeded, whether the witness had seen the accused before and how often, any special reason to remember, the time before the identification to police, and any discrepancy with the first description. f.facts: Section 27A(8) Firearms Act 1964 (as substituted by s.59 Criminal Justice Act 2006) imposed a five-year minimum sentence on anyone convicted of a s.27A(1) firearms offence who had a previous conviction for a listed offence. The High Court and Court of Appeal upheld it; Mr Ellis appealed.

Supreme Court, 15 May 2019 (Finlay Geoghegan J; Charleton J concurring separately): the minimum applied not to everyone convicted of the offence but "only on a limited group of such offenders" identified by one characteristic, removing the court's sentencing discretion for them. d: Informer privilege is "of ancient origin" and remains intact "subject only to the innocence at stake exception".

f.facts: In a 1998 murder trial in the Special Criminal Court the prosecution claimed privilege over about 40 statements from 20 informants, with Garda evidence that disclosure would put them at risk. The Special Criminal Court held that information given to Gardaí in confidence is not privileged merely for that reason, and offered to show the relevant statements to the defence solicitor and counsel only, on terms that they not disclose them to the accused. The High Court (Carney J) quashed that ruling and the matter went to the Supreme Court.
f.held: Informer privilege is "of ancient origin" and remains intact "subject only to the innocence at stake exception". Supreme Court, 20 July 1998 (O'Flaherty J): an order letting defence lawyers but not the accused see privileged material was an "unprecedented and wholly undesirable breach" of the duty counsel owe their client. Instead the trial court can itself review the documents if necessary to decide whether they would assist the defence, and prosecuting counsel have a duty to ensure overall fairness.

why: Informant identity and informant material are protected — keep them out of the main investigation file, flag them to the prosecutor, and expect the trial judge to read them if the defence claims they could help show innocence.

Holding: Violation of Article 3 (prohibition of torture, inhuman or degrading treatment). The use of force was excessive, unnecessary, and constituted ill-treatment. Italy also breached the procedural obligation under Article 3 to investigate effectively. Reasoning: The Court found the conduct rose to the threshold of torture given the severity and the lack of necessity. The investigative response was inadequate. Article 3 imposes both substantive limits on force and procedural duties of investigation. Significance: Force at demonstrations engaging Article 3 where excessive. Procedural obligation to investigate alleged ill-treatment by police. Operational Application: Force in

d: The beating "amounted to 'torture' within the meaning of Article 3" and was gratuitous.

f.facts: During the G8 summit in Genoa in July 2001, riot police stormed the Diaz-Pertini school, which the city had made available to demonstrators as a night shelter. The 62-year-old applicant was sitting against a wall with his arms raised when officers beat him, causing multiple fractures. The officers were never identified and the injury offences became time-barred, so no one was convicted for his ill-treatment.
f.held: The beating "amounted to 'torture' within the meaning of Article 3" and was gratuitous. European Court of Human Rights, 7 April 2015: Article 3 was also breached in its procedural limb — the officers had never been identified, and the Italian criminal law applied was inadequate and "devoid of the necessary deterrent effect". The Court described the problem as structural and awarded €45,000.

why: Force must be necessary and proportionate to the person's own conduct — force used on someone who is compliant is unlawful and can amount to torture. Officers must be identifiable (shoulder numbers) and must cooperate with any investigation into use of force.

st: Leading Strasbourg case on police ill-treatment during public-order operations.

f.held: An officer arresting without warrant must, in ordinary circumstances, "inform the person arrested of the true ground of arrest" — he may not withhold the reason or give a different one, or the arrest is unlawful. f.facts: After a bomb attack in 1990, two men suspected of IRA membership were arrested under s.30 Offences Against the State Act 1939 and refused to account for their movements when required to under s.52. f.facts: A husband and wife took part in an armed bank robbery and escaped by car. An off-duty Garda was shot dead. They were convicted of capital murder — the murder of a Garda acting in the course of his duty.
f.held: The Garda was acting in the course of his duty even though he was off duty, but the couple did not know he was a Garda, so while there was intent to murder there was no intent to commit capital murder. The Supreme Court substituted a conviction of murder for the husband; the wife was retried and convicted of murder. Later cases treat Murray as the leading Irish authority on recklessness (e.g. Phelan v Ireland, High Court, 2024).

d: Where a decision affects fundamental rights, proportionality is part of judging whether it is reasonable, and the decision must show it engaged with the relevant material.

d: A search warrant for a solicitors' offices was properly issued — but the search was leaked to the media, and journalists were waiting when Gardaí arrived. The High Court found the leak deliberate and, as a matter of probability, from Gardaí: an outrageous interference with the firm's privacy and constitutional rights. £100,000 damages.

f.facts: In 1997 a special Garda unit investigating money laundering and drug trafficking (Operation Pineapple) obtained a warrant under s.64 of the Criminal Justice Act 1994 to search a Dublin solicitors' firm for files on property transactions linked to two clients. Gardaí chose a warrant over a production order because they feared the documents could be lost if the clients learned of the investigation. Anonymous calls were made to the media, and journalists were outside the offices before Gardaí arrived. The firm challenged the warrant and sued the District Judge, the Garda Commissioner and the State.
f.held: High Court, 14 November 1997 (Kinlen J): the warrant was properly issued, so the challenge to it failed. But the leak was a deliberate, wilful act intended to embarrass and distress the firm, and as a matter of probability it came from Gardaí. It was an outrageous interference with the firm's privacy and constitutional rights, causing considerable and probably irreparable harm. The firm was awarded £100,000. The judge also criticised the Garda approach to investigating the leak, which he said could be a criminal offence.

n: Shortt v Commissioner of An Garda Síochána
d: Two Gardaí conspired to fabricate evidence, and perjured Garda evidence led to a man's conviction and 27 months in prison. After a miscarriage of justice was certified, the Supreme Court raised his damages to about €4.6 million — including €1 million in exemplary damages to mark the gravity of the misconduct.

f.facts: The plaintiff ran a licensed premises in Co Donegal. In 1995 a jury convicted him of permitting the sale of drugs there, on evidence that two Gardaí — a Superintendent and a Detective Garda — had conspired to fabricate; perjured Garda evidence was given at trial. He served 27 months. The conviction was later quashed, and the Court of Criminal Appeal certified a miscarriage of justice. In 2005 the High Court awarded him €1,923,871 against the Garda Commissioner and the State. He appealed.
f.held: Supreme Court, 21 March 2007 (Murray CJ, for a unanimous court with Denham, Hardiman, Geoghegan and Fennelly JJ): appeal allowed in part. The officers' conspiracy to concoct false evidence was the gravest dereliction of duty and abuse of power. General damages (including aggravated) went up to €2,250,000, and a separate €1,000,000 in exemplary damages marked the Court's disapproval; special damages were unchanged. Total: €4,623,871. The conduct was not to be taken as reflecting on the force as a whole.

why: Evidence must be true, complete and disclosed. Fabricating or suppressing evidence destroys lives, costs the State millions and ends careers — and the courts will punish it with exemplary damages.

n: Simple Imports Ltd v Revenue Commissioners
d: Search warrants that didn't show the statutory condition was met — a reasonable suspicion, assessed by the issuing judge — were invalid on their face and quashed, and the seized goods had to be returned. Because warrants authorise the forcible invasion of property, the conditions the legislature sets must be strictly met.

f.facts: District Judges issued warrants under s.205 of the Customs Consolidation Act 1876 and s.5(1) of the Customs and Excise (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1988 for Customs officers to search shops in Dublin, Cork and Limerick for allegedly indecent or obscene imported material and related documents. Officers seized magazines, videos, discs and documents. The warrants were standard forms with handwritten blanks and recited that the officer 'hath cause to suspect and doth suspect' — not the statutory standard of reasonable cause. The High Court (Shanley J) refused judicial review in 1998.
f.held: Supreme Court, 19 January 2000 (Keane J, Barrington J agreeing; Barron J dissenting): appeal allowed. The legislation required the District Judge to be satisfied, on sworn information, that the officer's suspicion was reasonable; it wasn't enough that the officers thought they had cause. Warrants showing on their face that they were issued on a basis the statute doesn't authorise are invalid and must be quashed. The warrants were quashed and the goods ordered returned.

why: Every word of a warrant matters. The information and the warrant must show the statutory test — usually reasonable grounds — was met by the issuer, not just that you suspect. Use the current statutory form and check it before you execute.
topic: Warrants invalid on their face
st: Yes. Still cited for the strict approach to search warrants. Read with Damache v DPP (2012) on who may issue a warrant and People (DPP) v JC (2015) on whether evidence is excluded.

d: Possession — control plus knowledge — can be inferred from the circumstances. A man found in a Dublin duplex set up to make cannabis sweets and grow cannabis, with his passport and bank card there and no account of why he was present, must face all ten charges. Inferences under ss.18–19 of the Criminal Justice Act 1984 can be weighed at a s.4E dismissal application, but using one to prove possession itself risks circularity.

f.facts: Gardaí searched a Dublin duplex under warrant and found the accused with two others. The kitchen-living area appeared to be used to make cannabis-infused jelly sweets — moulds, syringes, food colouring, a pot of green gelatinous substance, bags of dried cannabis, secateurs — and there were separate grow areas with heating and lighting. His bank card and passport were in the room. He faced ten charges. On his s.4E application the Circuit Court dismissed the five grow-area charges; the Court of Appeal restored them ([2024] IECA 252).
f.held: Supreme Court, 4 June 2025 (Charleton J, for Dunne, O'Malley, Murray and Donnelly JJ): appeal dismissed; all ten charges go to trial. Possession has no single definition and is often inferred from circumstances. His presence, the production apparatus, the dried cannabis, his personal effects, phone and passport, and the lack of any account of why he was there gave a rational prospect of conviction — and, for the grow areas, a possible common design to possess and cultivate. Inferences under ss.18 and 19 can be considered, but using an inference to prove possession itself risks circularity. Whether possession is proved is for the jury's common-sense assessment.

why: Possession cases are built on circumstances. Photograph and record exactly where everything was and what links the suspect to the place — documents, phone, keys, clothes — and put specific facts (presence, objects, marks) to the suspect under ss.18/19 with proper warnings, rather than only asking 'are these yours?'.
topic: Proving possession from circumstances; inferences at the s.4E stage
st: Yes. Current Supreme Court authority (June 2025) on proving possession and on using ss.18/19 inferences at a s.4E dismissal application.

d: Using CCTV from homes, businesses, a bus and public places to investigate a murder didn't breach the accused's rights under the Constitution, the ECHR, the EU Charter or data protection law. Processing footage is lawful where necessary and proportionate to investigate crime, and there's no realistic expectation of privacy in public. Gardaí get a significant margin early in an investigation — and failing to seek available CCTV could be a grave dereliction of duty.

f.facts: In June 2018 a man was killed in an unprovoked stabbing in Tallaght, Dublin. Gardaí gathered CCTV from private homes, local businesses, a Dublin bus and public places including footpaths, roads, a park and a shopping centre. The accused, then 17, was convicted of murder by a jury. At trial and on appeal he argued that using the CCTV breached his privacy and data protection rights.
f.held: Court of Appeal, 30 January 2024 (Edwards J giving judgment): appeal dismissed. Processing CCTV data is lawful where necessary and proportionate for preventing, detecting, investigating or prosecuting crime; a person in a public place has no realistic expectation of privacy, and CCTV there is widely known. That some footage proved irrelevant was apparent only in hindsight, and Gardaí must get a significant margin, especially early on. The admissibility challenge was 'quite simply, misconceived'.

why: Collect CCTV early and widely — the courts back Gardaí who do. Keep it necessary and proportionate: record why each source was sought, the time window taken, and how it was downloaded and stored, so the collection can be justified.
topic: CCTV evidence, privacy and data protection
st: Yes. The Court of Appeal's answer (January 2024) to privacy and data protection challenges to CCTV evidence. DPP v Thompson (2024), decided the same day, rejected a similar argument.

d: Counselling records attract a high level of constitutional protection. Disclosure needs a compelling basis — that the records are likely to be of real forensic value to the defence, not a theoretical possibility — and a complainant's consent must be fully informed: she should see the records and be able to take advice before consenting. Conviction upheld.

f.facts: The accused was convicted in Kerry Circuit Criminal Court of one count of sexual assault. Before trial the defence sought wide disclosure, including counselling records. A rape crisis centre told Gardaí it held none for the complainant, and she was asked to sign consents to disclosure without seeing any material. After the trial it emerged that she had attended counselling there; a record of the first session suggested the abuse happened more than once, which differed from her evidence. The Court of Appeal obtained a statement from her under s.3(3)(a) of the Criminal Procedure Act 1993 — she maintained there was one incident — and dismissed the appeal in May 2023.
f.held: Supreme Court, 2 May 2025 ([2025] IESC 16, Collins J): appeal dismissed. Under s.19A of the Criminal Evidence Act 1992 a compelling basis must be shown before counselling records are disclosed: they must be likely to be of real forensic value to the defence, and materiality is not a bare or theoretical possibility. A complainant's consent must be fully informed — she should see the records and be able to get advice, with consent the final step. The Court of Appeal was entitled to use s.3(3)(a) instead of ordering a retrial.

why: Counselling records are highly protected. Never ask a complainant to sign a blanket consent: explain what is sought and why, let her see the records and get advice first, and record each step. Be precise when asking services whether records exist — a wrong 'no records' answer can unsettle a conviction.
topic: Disclosure of counselling records in sexual offence cases
st: Yes. The leading Supreme Court decision (May 2025) on s.19A of the Criminal Evidence Act 1992, read with DPP v WC (2024). A presumption of non-disclosure for counselling notes was approved for the Criminal Law and Civil Law (Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill 2026 in February 2026 — check whether it has been enacted.

d: Covert recording of a conversation in a fast-food restaurant the day after a murder, approved by a superintendent under the urgency route in the Criminal Justice (Surveillance) Act 2009 without going to a judge, was lawful: the trial court accepted he genuinely believed delay would lose the chance to plant the device. Privilege over the identities of National Surveillance Unit officers was upheld. Murder conviction affirmed.

f.facts: In 2013 a man was shot dead in a pub car park in Co Meath. The next day the accused met others at a fast-food restaurant in Dublin, and Gardaí covertly recorded the conversation with a listening device; remarks included concern about the heavy Garda presence and being followed. A superintendent approved the surveillance himself rather than applying to a District Judge. The Special Criminal Court convicted the accused of murder in February 2019, relying also on a co-accused who became a State witness.
f.held: Court of Appeal, June 2026 (Kennedy J, with O'Moore and MacGrath JJ): appeal dismissed on every ground pursued (51 were originally advanced). The superintendent said he considered going to court but feared losing the chance to place the devices before the meeting; the trial court's finding that he believed it was an emergency was impossible to upset. Key passages of the recording were audible and intelligible. The accomplice's inconsistencies and admitted lies didn't make the conviction unsafe, and privilege over the identities of eight surveillance officers was rightly upheld.

why: Covert surveillance is only as good as its authorisation. If the urgency route is used, the approving officer must genuinely believe delay would lose the evidence — and must record that reasoning at the time, because the court will test it.
topic: Urgent surveillance approval without a judge; protecting surveillance officers' identities
st: Yes. A recent Court of Appeal decision (June 2026). For the earlier Supreme Court challenge by the same accused, on s.30 detention extensions, see Braney v Special Criminal Court.

d: Audio from a court-authorised listening device that recorded an IRA 'inquiry' was admissible. Section 10 of the Criminal Justice (Surveillance) Act 2009 — on storing and accessing surveillance material — doesn't require ministerial authorisation for Gardaí and prosecutors to use recordings in an investigation and trial. A JC exclusion inquiry isn't needed where a breach after collection hasn't affected the evidence's integrity or probative value.

f.facts: On 7–8 August 2015 an IRA-organised 'inquiry' questioned suspected informants at a house in Castleknock, west Dublin. The Garda National Surveillance Unit had placed listening devices there under a District Court authorisation (s.5 of the 2009 Act). The recordings were copied, transcribed, shared among investigators and enhanced by commercial firms, then disclosed and played at trial. In June 2018 the Special Criminal Court convicted five people of IRA membership or assisting the IRA. It and the Court of Appeal held the handling breached s.10 (no ministerial regulations) but admitted the evidence.
f.held: Supreme Court, 4 May 2021 (O'Malley J; Charleton J concurring): appeals dismissed. Read as a whole, the Act doesn't give the Minister exclusive power over access to surveillance material; 'otherwise authorised by law' covers those working for the DPP and the Garda Commissioner, and s.10 — mainly about secure storage of old material — has no relevance to investigation and trial. There was no relevant breach. A JC inquiry isn't appropriate where a post-collection breach hasn't affected integrity or probative value, though handling that seriously breached an accused's rights could still lead to exclusion.

why: Surveillance evidence is won or lost on authorisation and handling. Keep the authorisation tight, preserve a master, and record every copy, transcript, enhancement and person given access — the courts will look at the chain.
topic: Handling surveillance recordings: s.10 of the Surveillance Act and admissibility
st: Yes. The leading Supreme Court decision (May 2021) on s.10 of the Criminal Justice (Surveillance) Act 2009 and on breaches after evidence is gathered.

d: An alibi under s.20 of the Criminal Justice Act 1984 is about geography — evidence that the accused was somewhere else, not where someone else was. Rebuttal evidence was properly admitted in answer to evidence covered by an alibi notice, and objections not raised at trial couldn't be raised for the first time on appeal. A conviction for facilitating a criminal organisation's serious offence by driving a vehicle was upheld.

f.facts: In 2016 gunmen carried out a gangland shooting at a Dublin hotel and were driven away in a convoy of vehicles. The prosecution alleged the accused drove one of them, facilitating a serious offence by a criminal organisation by providing a motor vehicle, contrary to s.72 of the Criminal Justice Act 2006. His defence was that he wasn't driving it at the relevant times, supported by two alibi witnesses; the prosecution called rebuttal evidence under s.20(4) of the Criminal Justice Act 1984. The Special Criminal Court convicted him on 17 April 2023 and imposed eight and a half years.
f.held: Supreme Court, July 2026 ([2026] IESC 38, Hyland J): appeal dismissed. The objections to the rebuttal evidence, and to what counts as 'evidence in support of an alibi' under s.20(8), weren't raised at trial, with no reason given, and the interests of justice didn't require them to be heard for the first time on appeal. Section 20(8) is concerned with geography — evidence that the accused was elsewhere — so one witness's evidence about another person's whereabouts wasn't alibi evidence. Even so, the rebuttal evidence was properly admitted, there was no unfairness, and the trial court's independent findings meant the point wouldn't have changed the outcome.

why: When an alibi notice is served, investigate it promptly and thoroughly — the witnesses, times, places, CCTV and phone data. The prosecution can call rebuttal evidence, but only if Gardaí have gathered it.
topic: Alibi notices and rebuttal evidence
st: Yes. Recent Supreme Court authority (July 2026) on s.20 of the Criminal Justice Act 1984.

d: A murder conviction for the killing of a detective garda during a 2013 credit union robbery was upheld on all of nearly 50 grounds. Admissions the accused made to two people in the US were properly admitted (by video-link, under arrangements that weren't ideal but weren't unfair); the prosecution was rightly allowed to treat a resiling witness as hostile; and the claim that his deportation from the US was a disguised extradition was 'entirely without foundation'.

f.facts: On 25 January 2013 a detective garda was shot dead during a credit union robbery in Co Louth. The accused later lived in the US, where, two witnesses said, he admitted the killing; he was deported to Ireland in 2018. In August 2020 a jury convicted him of murder and he was sentenced to life imprisonment with a 40-year minimum term. He appealed on nearly 50 grounds.
f.held: Court of Appeal, 11 July 2024 (Edwards J, 363-page judgment): appeal dismissed on every ground. The trial judge properly considered Covid-19 in letting the trial proceed. The video-link arrangements for the US witnesses may not have been ideal but weren't an error, and claims that one witness was induced by US authorities were for cross-examination and the jury. The second witness was properly treated as hostile when she resiled. Interruptions by a witness's partner didn't create a real risk of an unfair trial, given the judge's warnings. The deportation argument was entirely without foundation.

why: Cases can turn on admissions made to friends and associates, sometimes abroad. Trace and secure those witnesses early, take their statements in a form usable under s.16 of the Criminal Justice Act 2006 if they later resile, and arrange overseas evidence through formal channels.
topic: Admissions to witnesses abroad; hostile witnesses; deportation is not extradition
st: Yes. A Court of Appeal decision (July 2024) upholding the conviction.

d: Admissions a mother made to a court-appointed psychologist during child-care (wardship-type) proceedings — assessments that used a polygraph — were admissible at her criminal trial. The assessment wasn't arrest, detention or a criminal investigation; the polygraph wasn't used oppressively; and the lack of a police-style caution didn't make the statements unfair. (Later: after a 2024 retrial, the Court of Appeal in July 2025 held the admissions should have been excluded and quashed the conviction.)

f.facts: The accused's three children, who have special needs, were abused by others, who were later convicted. She was arrested and interviewed under caution and denied any knowledge; the DPP decided not to prosecute her at that stage. In later wardship-type proceedings a psychologist interviewed her five times to assess her capacity to care for the children, using a polygraph. She allegedly made admissions, which were shared with the relevant agencies, and she was charged. The trial judge excluded the admissions on fairness grounds and directed an acquittal; the Court of Appeal reversed ([2022] IECA 248).
f.held: Supreme Court, 13 October 2023 (Charleton J, for Dunne, O'Malley, Woulfe and Murray JJ): appeal dismissed — the trial judge was wrong to exclude the statements. The polygraph was used to verify information, not as a tool of oppression, and answers weren't tied to threatened consequences for the children. The interviews weren't equivalent to arrest, detention or being placed under authority for a criminal investigation; they were a measured assessment of risk. In those circumstances the absence of police-style cautions didn't make the statements unfair. The Court sought further submissions on whether to order a retrial.

why: Admissions can come from outside the interview room — to social workers, psychologists, doctors and others. Find out early whether such assessments took place and seek the records lawfully; admissibility will turn on fairness and how the statements were obtained.
topic: Admissions made outside Garda custody: psychologist interviews and polygraph
st: The 2023 principle stands — admissions made in non-criminal assessments aren't automatically excluded — but on the facts it was overtaken: at the 2024 retrial the psychologist accepted the polygrapher's remarks could have been inducements, and in July 2025 the Court of Appeal held the admissions should have been excluded and quashed her conviction.

d: Gardaí who knew the accused recognised him on CCTV years after a gangland murder. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction: the recognition process — each Garda viewing the footage separately, with the process recorded — was excellent in many respects, and the identifications were firm and untainted, even though some Gardaí had checked PULSE beforehand and the footage showed the date of the killing.

f.facts: In December 2012 a man was shot dead in north Dublin. In 2018 Gardaí viewed CCTV and identified the accused, whom they knew, as a 'spotter' for the gang. In November 2021 the Special Criminal Court convicted him of murder, finding he met the gang on the day, acted in concert with them and coordinated with them afterwards; he was acquitted of possessing a handgun. He got life imprisonment. On appeal he argued the case came down to Garda identification from CCTV, which was contaminated: some Gardaí had looked him up on PULSE before viewing, and the footage showed the date of the killing.
f.held: Court of Appeal, December 2023: appeal dismissed. The identification process was excellent in many respects — the Gardaí viewed the footage individually and the process was recorded — and the identifications were firm and untainted. Given the six-year gap, the date-stamp didn't create unfairness, and the trial court was entitled to distinguish what the Gardaí knew at the time of the killing from what they knew in 2018. Its credibility findings weren't perverse, and detailed circumstantial evidence of planning, advance surveillance and practice runs proved joint enterprise and intent.

why: Recognition from CCTV is identification evidence and will be attacked. Have each Garda view the footage separately, record the whole process, and note what each knew about the suspect and the incident before viewing — don't brief them first.
topic: Garda recognition of a suspect from CCTV
st: Yes. A Court of Appeal decision (December 2023) on the process for Garda recognition evidence. Read with the identification cases in this app, People (AG) v Casey (No 2) and R v Turnbull.

n: Corcoran v Commissioner of An Garda Síochána
d: A s.10 search warrant for a journalist's home was quashed because the sworn application didn't tell the District Judge he was a journalist who had claimed privilege over his sources, or that the search aimed to identify them. Protection of sources is integral to a free press, and Gardaí must put all highly relevant facts before the issuing judge.

f.facts: On 16 December 2018 armed men attacked security staff and set vehicles alight at a property in Co Roscommon. A local journalist, tipped off by a source, filmed and photographed the aftermath and published it. Interviewed under caution, he gave Gardaí a USB of his material but refused to reveal his sources, claiming journalistic privilege. In April 2019 a Garda sergeant obtained warrants under s.10 of the Criminal Justice (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1997 for his home and the newspaper's premises, without telling the District Judge he was a journalist or had claimed privilege. His phone was seized; he refused the PIN and sought judicial review. The High Court upheld the warrant; the Court of Appeal quashed it in 2022.
f.held: Supreme Court, 22 June 2023 (seven judges; O'Donnell CJ, Hogan and Collins JJ giving judgments): the Commissioner's appeal was dismissed unanimously and the warrant stayed quashed. Highly relevant information — his journalistic status, his privilege claim and the aim of identifying his sources — wasn't before the District Judge, who couldn't perform an independent role without it. Gardaí, bound by Article 10 ECHR, must disclose such facts. Hogan J identified serious, systemic shortcomings in search-warrant law needing urgent legislation; the Court declined to decide the full constitutional scope of journalistic privilege.

why: A warrant is only as good as the information behind it. Put every highly relevant fact before the issuing judge — especially anything that weighs against granting it, such as journalistic, legal or other privilege — and record what you told them.
topic: Warrants and journalists: full disclosure to the issuing judge
st: Yes. Leading Supreme Court authority (June 2023) on candour in warrant applications and protection of journalistic sources. Check for any new legislation on search warrants.

d: Under a s.26 Misuse of Drugs Act warrant, other Gardaí may use its powers only while accompanied by the Garda named in it. The named Garda left to search other properties, so cocaine found by a colleague in the meantime was unlawfully seized. The District Court shouldn't have dismissed the charge automatically — admissibility is a JC question — but the prosecution never asked for that assessment, so the acquittal stood.

f.facts: A Garda obtained a s.26 warrant to search a house in Co Offaly, along with separate warrants for two nearby properties. She and a colleague began the search at about 7.40am; she then left to search the other properties and later returned. While she was away the colleague kept searching and found suspected cocaine near the end of the search. In October 2023 the District Court held the seizure unlawful — the colleague wasn't 'accompanied by' the named Garda — and dismissed the possession charge. The DPP appealed by case stated.
f.held: High Court, 12 February 2026 (O'Higgins J): the colleague was not in any sense accompanied by the named Garda, so the search and seizure were unlawful; s.26 intends the named Garda to exercise a general supervisory role. The District Judge erred in dismissing the charge automatically — admissibility should have been assessed under People (DPP) v JC — but the onus was on the prosecution to seek that assessment, it didn't, and gave no adequate reason, so the point couldn't be raised on appeal. Appeal dismissed; the acquittal stood.

why: The Garda named on a warrant must stay with the search. If you're named and have to leave, pause the search until you're back. And if evidence may have been obtained unlawfully, the prosecution must argue admissibility under JC at trial — it can't be raised for the first time on appeal.
topic: Executing a s.26 warrant: 'accompanied by' the named Garda
st: Yes. A High Court decision (February 2026) on s.26 of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1977 and on raising JC at trial.

d: A suspect has no right to be arrested and interviewed so that his account can be put before the jury. A trial judge was wrong to stop an endangerment trial — before hearing any evidence — because Gardaí hadn't interviewed the accused. Fairness at the investigation stage matters for whether a trial can be fair, but it isn't a free-standing right that makes a trial unlawful.

f.facts: In December 2016 the accused allegedly drove dangerously during a Garda chase. He was arrested, cautioned and charged with summary road traffic offences, for which there was no power to detain him for questioning. In February 2017 he was charged with reckless endangerment, an indictable offence; Gardaí could then have detained him for interview but didn't, and he made no reply to the charge. At trial in November 2017 the judge, before any evidence, dismissed the charge: without an interview memo he'd have to give evidence to put his version, so it wasn't a trial in due course of law. The Court of Appeal allowed the DPP's appeal.
f.held: Supreme Court, October 2022 ([2022] IESC 39, MacMenamin J): appeal dismissed. The trial judge shouldn't have ruled on a hypothetical basis before evidence was heard. Fair trial rights don't apply in full at the investigation stage; the question is whether the investigation was fair enough for a trial to take place. There is no right to be arrested and detained for questioning, and whether an unsworn statement is admitted is for the trial judge under the rules of evidence. This wasn't a lost-evidence case — a hypothetical lost opportunity isn't enough — and he could have given Gardaí a statement or a written response before trial.

why: Not interviewing a suspect won't by itself sink a prosecution — but give a fair chance to respond. Caution at charge and record any reply word for word, and note any offer to take an account, so fairness can be shown.
topic: No right to be interviewed: how the accused can put his account
st: Yes. Supreme Court authority (October 2022).

d: A breach of the 2013 custody regulations on interpretation — the custody record said nothing about whether a foreign national needed an interpreter — didn't make a drink-driving detention unlawful. Whether the breath evidence is admitted is for the trial judge's discretion under the ordinary rules for evidence obtained through illegality (not a constitutional breach); the lack of any causal link between the breach and the breath specimen is relevant.

f.facts: At about 1am on 13 December 2013 a Garda in Dublin stopped a car dragging a parking cone, noticed signs of intoxication and arrested the driver for drink driving. At the station he got his rights notice and provided two breath specimens (55 micrograms per 100ml). The defence disputed his English, which the Garda said was good; the custody record's foreign-nationals section said nothing about whether an interpreter was needed, and he didn't ask for one. The Circuit Court judge found a breach of the 2013 Interpretation and Translation Regulations and stated a case.
f.held: Court of Appeal, 11 November 2020 (Ní Raifeartaigh J, with Birmingham P and Edwards J): the breaches didn't render the detention unlawful. Admissibility of the breath evidence is a matter for the trial judge's discretion, applying the ordinary principles for evidence obtained through illegality rather than breach of a constitutional right. The absence of a causal link between the breaches and obtaining the specimen is relevant, and all relevant factors must be weighed.

why: For any detainee who may not speak English well, the member in charge must assess the need for an interpreter, tell the person the decision, and record it — even if it seems obvious. A blank box hands the defence an argument.
topic: Interpreters in custody: a recording breach and the breath evidence
st: Yes. Court of Appeal authority (November 2020) on the 2013 interpretation regulations.

d: A child's video-recorded interview was the core of a sexual assault case. By the trial, four and a half years later, she couldn't remember the incident and relied on the video. With a single brief incident, no supporting evidence, and the dispute being whether it happened at all, the accused couldn't meaningfully cross-examine — a real risk of an unfair trial. Conviction quashed, though expressly not a bright-line rule.

f.facts: In October 2016 a six-year-old child complained the next day that the accused had touched her while sitting beside her. A formal video-recorded interview in December 2016 became her evidence-in-chief. The first trial collapsed in October 2019 over non-disclosure and the second was abandoned because of Covid-19; the trial went ahead in May 2021. Cross-examined at 11, she said she couldn't remember the incident or its circumstances — only what was on the video — though she maintained the accused was lying. The trial judge admitted the video and left the delay to the jury. He was convicted and sentenced to four years.
f.held: Court of Appeal, March 2023 ([2023] IECA 65, Ní Raifeartaigh J): conviction quashed. Her memory was significantly impaired and she was relying on the video, so the accused couldn't effectively cross-examine on her evidence-in-chief — a real risk of an unfair trial that a jury warning couldn't cure. Key factors: her young age, a single brief incident, no other supporting evidence, and a dispute about whether the touching happened at all. Not a bright-line rule: forgetting details doesn't require a trial to stop, and refreshing memory from the video isn't wrong in itself.

why: In child cases the video interview may end up as the only evidence — and time erodes the child's ability to be cross-examined. Look hard for supporting evidence from the start, and get the case trial-ready without delay; a trial collapsed by a disclosure failure costs time the case may not have.
topic: Child witnesses: delay, lost memory and fair cross-examination
st: Yes. Court of Appeal decision (March 2023). Expressly not a bright-line rule, and the concern doesn't generally arise in historic cases where all the evidence is given live.

n: Hyland v Commissioner of An Garda Síochána
d: Material on a garda's phone, lawfully seized under a criminal search warrant, could be used to start a disciplinary inquiry after the DPP decided not to prosecute. His privacy rights weren't exhausted by the seizure, but using the knowledge was lawful and proportionate. Copying data after the no-prosecution decision and his demand for the phone's return wasn't permitted. Two of five judges dissented.

f.facts: A garda in a Dublin traffic unit was investigated over a video clip he allegedly forwarded on WhatsApp in 2019. Gardaí searched his office, home and car under warrant, and he handed over his phone and passcode. In May 2020 the DPP decided not to prosecute. Disciplinary processes followed, relying on material from the phone — including images of Garda computer screens, PULSE entries and CCTV stills from investigations — and other allegations. The Court of Appeal reversed the High Court in his favour, and the Commissioner appealed.
f.held: Supreme Court, 6 November 2025 ([2025] IESC 54, Murray J; O'Donnell CJ and Dunne J agreeing; Woulfe and Hogan JJ dissenting): he couldn't insist on the return of material unlawfully held on the phone, which could be removed first. The Commissioner was entitled to use knowledge from the lawful search to start the disciplinary inquiry — his privacy rights weren't exhausted by the seizure, but the use was lawful and proportionate. Material copied after the no-prosecution decision and his demand for return shouldn't be used; earlier copies raise further questions. The dissent said internal use needed independent authorisation.

why: Anything on your phone can end up in a disciplinary file. Never store images of PULSE, Garda systems or case material on a personal device. And when you seize a device, handle the data strictly within the purpose and stage of the investigation.
topic: Using data from a seized phone in Garda discipline
st: Yes. Supreme Court decision (November 2025) by a 3–2 majority; the dissent's call for independent authorisation may be argued again.

d: Evidence that a complainant told others about sexual abuse — a doctor, his mother, a counsellor, a friend — can show consistency, not prove the abuse happened. Where it's admitted, the jury must be told its limited purpose. With no such direction, and the prosecution relying on it, six sexual assault convictions were quashed.

f.facts: The accused, a school chaplain, was convicted in March 2022 of six counts of sexual assault under s.2 of the Criminal Law (Rape) (Amendment) Act 1990. The complainant said he didn't report at the time because he'd been told not to tell anyone. He first disclosed in 2017 to a doctor, then to his mother; a priest gave evidence of disclosures at counselling sessions in late 2017; and he told a lifelong friend in May 2018. This complaint evidence was admitted and relied on by the prosecution in closing, but the trial judge gave no direction on its limited purpose, and the defence didn't ask for one.
f.held: Court of Appeal, June 2023 ([2023] IECA 127, Kennedy J): convictions quashed. Complaint evidence admitted as an exception to the hearsay rule shows consistency; it doesn't prove the facts. The jury must be told how it may be used, or it may treat the complaints as confirming the account. Given its clear importance to the prosecution case, the omission was an oversight or error of substance raising a real risk of injustice, so the new ground was allowed despite the lack of a requisition.

why: Statements from first-complaint witnesses can be central at trial — but only for consistency. Record precisely when and how each disclosure was made, to whom, in what words and in what circumstances, so the prosecution and the judge can use it correctly.
topic: Recent complaint evidence: consistency, not proof
st: Yes. Court of Appeal decision (June 2023) on directing juries about complaint evidence.

d: Rape ordinarily merits a headline sentence of about seven years, with custody all but inescapable; a more serious category merits 10–15 years, and some cases up to life. The circumstances of the crime — violence in the home, breach of trust, domination, a background of abuse — are aggravating and must be considered, not the rape in isolation. The original 10-year total for a man who raped and later attacked his wife was restored.

f.facts: After the couple separated, the accused, during a row in May 2014, produced a knife, threatened to cut his wife's face, and raped her overnight. He threatened her again the next day, and over the following weeks confronted her at work and at their child's creche, telling her he'd next come armed with a hammer. In August 2014 he struck her several times on the head with a hammer at her parents' home, also striking her mother. He pleaded guilty to the hammer attack and was convicted of rape and threats. The Central Criminal Court imposed 10 years in total; the Court of Appeal cut it to eight and a half years, treating the rape and earlier threat in isolation.
f.held: Supreme Court, 6 December 2019 ([2019] IESC 85, Charleton J): the Court of Appeal was wrong to consider the rape and the earlier threat in isolation. The circumstances of a crime are relevant, but events entirely separate in time and character, or offences acquitted or never charged, can't aggravate the sentence. The Court set rape sentencing bands (about seven years ordinarily; 10–15 years for a more serious category; up to life in some cases) and named aggravating factors including domestic violence, breach of trust, domination and a background of abuse. Consecutive sentences mustn't punish twice for one crime, subject to totality. After further submissions, the Court restored the 10-year sentence in 2020.

why: Sentence reflects the whole picture. In domestic sexual violence, gather and record the full context — earlier threats, violence, control, breach of trust — and charge each distinct offence, so the court can take it into account.
topic: Sentencing rape: headline bands and the context of domestic abuse
st: Yes. The Supreme Court's framework for rape sentencing (December 2019). Section 40 of the Domestic Violence Act 2018 also makes an intimate relationship with the victim an aggravating factor.

d: A driver charged with drink driving has the right to apply to have his expert inspect the breath-testing machine. Refusing that application without reasons was a substantial error, and he didn't have to give reasons for wanting the inspection. Because breath specimens are transitory, the chance of independent assessment is critical to fair procedures.

f.facts: The applicant was convicted on 5 June 2009 of drink driving under s.49 of the Road Traffic Act 1961 (as amended), for an alleged offence in Co Roscommon on 21 July 2008. Before trial he asked for his expert to examine the evidential breath-testing machine and for its servicing history. The District Judge refused without giving reasons. The High Court (Charleton J) refused to quash the conviction, holding that he had to establish reasons for an inspection.
f.held: Supreme Court, 29 February 2016 (Hardiman J, with Laffoy and Dunne JJ): appeal allowed. He had a right to apply for inspection of the machine, and the District Judge fell into substantial error by refusing without reasons. The High Court erred in requiring him to establish reasons, which would offend fair procedures and constitutional justice. Because breath specimens are transitory and none can be kept for independent analysis, the opportunity for independent assessment is critical.

why: The breath-testing machine is evidence too. Keep its service, calibration and maintenance records complete and available, and expect defence requests to inspect them.
topic: Inspecting the breath-testing machine: fair procedures
st: Yes. Supreme Court authority (February 2016) on defence access to evidential breath-testing equipment.
