d: Section 40 of the Domestic Violence Act 2018 is victim-centred: where the offender has a close relationship with the victim, the offence is aggravated because of the extra psychological harm, and the judge must take that into account expressly — but without a fixed percentage uplift. Offences taken into consideration are valid if the sentence reflects them. An eight-year headline for false imprisonment and assault of a partner was upheld.

f.facts: Over about an hour and forty minutes in Dublin, the accused slapped his partner in public, forced her into the boot of her car for about ten minutes, punched her repeatedly while she drove, punched the windscreen and assaulted her again. A witness filmed the first incident and alerted Gardaí. He pleaded guilty to false imprisonment and assault, with an assault causing harm taken into consideration. The trial court imposed three years after mitigation from a five-year headline; the Court of Appeal raised the headline to eight years, discounted by two and a half years.
f.held: Supreme Court, December 2025 ([2025] IESC 53, O'Malley J): appeal dismissed. Section 40 doesn't impose mandatory punishment but requires a more severe sentence where the offender is in a specified relationship with the victim, reflecting the additional harm; the s.40(5) exception may apply if none was caused. It should be weighed in assessing gravity and referred to expressly, but not as a percentage uplift. Offences taken into consideration are valid, but there must be no 'free ride'. The false imprisonment facilitated the assaults, so separating them would be entirely artificial; the trial court's headline was too low.

why: In DV cases, evidence of the relationship and of the harm — fear, ongoing distress, control — directly raises the sentence. Record it, take a victim impact statement, and secure independent evidence such as witness footage and 999 calls.
topic: Domestic violence sentencing: s.40 DVA 2018 and offences taken into consideration
st: Yes. Supreme Court authority (December 2025) on s.40 of the Domestic Violence Act 2018. Check the judiciary's 2026 sentencing guideline for domestic violence offences too.

d: When Gardaí lawfully detain a vehicle under s.41 of the Road Traffic Act 1994 (here, untaxed and uninsured), they have lawful possession and control of it — including opening the boot and taking items found, such as evidence of crime. No separate search power was needed; drugs found in the boot at the Garda compound were admissible.

f.facts: In February 2017 the accused was driving on the M7 in a vehicle that was untaxed and uninsured. Gardaí detained it under s.41 of the Road Traffic Act 1994 and the 2011 regulations, and it was removed and stored. At the Garda compound a Garda opened the boot and found a large quantity of amphetamines, worth about €137,000. He was convicted in the Circuit Court in 2023 of possession for sale or supply (s.15A Misuse of Drugs Act 1977). In October 2024 the Court of Appeal quashed that conviction because hearsay about a tip-off had been wrongly admitted, and sent the case back to the Circuit Court. The Supreme Court gave leave on whether opening the boot was authorised by law.
f.held: Supreme Court, 2025 ([2025] IESC 22, O'Donnell CJ giving the lead judgment): the accused's appeal on the boot point was dismissed. Detention under s.41 gives Gardaí lawful possession and control of the vehicle, which includes opening its compartments and taking items found, including evidence of a crime. It was unnecessary to rely on a separate common-law search power or on s.23 of the Misuse of Drugs Act. The evidence was admissible.

why: A lawful s.41 detention lets you open and check the detained vehicle — but only if the detention itself is lawful. Record the grounds (no tax, no insurance), the vehicle's chain to the compound, and exactly where and when each item was found. And explain a stop or search by what you yourself saw and checked: telling the jury about a tip-off another Garda received is hearsay, and it cost this conviction.
topic: Opening a vehicle detained under s.41 RTA 1994
st: Yes on the search point: Supreme Court authority (2025) on what a lawful s.41 vehicle detention allows. But the conviction itself was quashed by the Court of Appeal in October 2024 because hearsay about a tip-off was wrongly admitted — check the current position of the case.

d: Gardaí who didn't start a prosecution can still present it in the District Court. Overturning a 2022 High Court ruling that had put thousands of cases at risk, the Supreme Court held that s.8 of the Garda Síochána Act 2005 contemplates different Gardaí instituting and conducting summary prosecutions, and that the District Court rule allowing court presenters was valid.

f.facts: In August 2021 a man was prosecuted in the District Court for possessing a small quantity of cannabis. A Garda other than the one who instituted the prosecution presented the case, under a District Court rule permitting this. In May 2022 the High Court (Bolger J) held the rule invalid: s.8(2) of the 2005 Act confined the role to the Garda who instituted the prosecution. Thousands of District Court prosecutions were put at risk, and emergency legislation was enacted the next day to let any Garda conduct a prosecution. The DPP appealed.
f.held: Supreme Court, 14 July 2023 (Dunne J for a five-judge court): appeal allowed and the High Court overturned; the appeal wasn't moot despite the emergency legislation. The ordinary meaning of s.8(2) clearly contemplates different Gardaí instituting or conducting summary proceedings. Gardaí had acted as prosecutors since at least 1948, and ending that would have been a radical step needing explicit words. Rights of audience fall within the District Court Rules Committee's powers; the rules have the force of law unless declared invalid, and a consultative case stated is the wrong route to challenge them.

why: Court presenters can run cases they didn't start — but the case still rests on the investigating Garda's file. Make sure the file, statements and evidence are complete and clear enough for a colleague to present.
topic: Garda court presenters: who can prosecute in the District Court
st: Yes. Supreme Court authority (July 2023). The Garda Síochána Act 2005 has since been largely replaced by the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024; check the current provision on Garda prosecutions.

d: An IRA membership conviction was quashed. The accused had already been arrested on suspicion of membership and released; re-arresting him for membership without a District Court warrant was unlawful, even though the second arrest related to a different incident. And a senior Garda's belief evidence — given with privilege claimed over its basis — needed strong independent support, which 'grave suspicion' about his role in buying a car didn't provide.

f.facts: In September 2012 the accused was arrested on suspicion of IRA membership over his presence at a funeral and released without charge. In December 2012 he was arrested again, without a warrant, during the investigation into the murder of a prison officer in Northern Ireland; it was alleged he had bought the car used in the shooting. In 2017 the Special Criminal Court convicted him of IRA membership, relying on a Detective Chief Superintendent's belief evidence (with privilege claimed over its basis) and other evidence, and imposed five years. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal.
f.held: Supreme Court, 10 February 2022 (O'Malley J for a unanimous five-judge court): conviction quashed. The Act provides a clear route — a District Court warrant — where the limits on re-arrest apply, and the Special Criminal Court was wrong to hold no warrant was needed because the second arrest concerned a different incident; leaving that to trial would gravely weaken the protection against abuse of arrest powers. Belief evidence needs strong independent support: there were grounds for grave suspicion about his role in sourcing the car, but not enough to prove membership beyond reasonable doubt.

why: Before re-arresting anyone already arrested and released, check whether a warrant is needed — and get it. In membership cases, belief evidence alone won't carry a conviction: build independent supporting evidence.
topic: Re-arrest without a warrant; belief evidence needs support
st: Yes. Supreme Court authority (February 2022) on re-arrest and on the support belief evidence needs.

n: Hegarty v Commissioner of An Garda Síochána
d: The Commissioner's power under s.14(2) of the Garda Síochána Act 2005 to dismiss a member to maintain public confidence is separate from the disciplinary regulations. It survived the end of disciplinary proceedings in which the Appeal Board imposed only a fine, and the Board's findings didn't bind the Commissioner — but it is an extreme power for wholly exceptional cases, and it is reviewable.

f.facts: In March 2017 a garda, on duty taking a statement from a woman at a Garda station, engaged in a sexual act with her and didn't record the statement. A Board of Inquiry under the 2007 Discipline Regulations recommended that he retire or resign for discreditable conduct; the Commissioner ordered resignation, but the Appeal Board substituted a four-week pay deduction. The Commissioner didn't implement that, suspended him, and in March 2020 dismissed him under s.14(2) as necessary to maintain public confidence. The High Court quashed the dismissal as fundamentally unfair, and the Court of Appeal agreed.
f.held: Supreme Court, July 2025 ([2025] IESC 36, Murray J giving the lead judgment): Commissioner's appeal allowed and relief refused. Section 14(2) is a distinct protective power, usable only in the most unusual and extreme circumstances, where the Commissioner forms the view that dismissal is necessary to maintain public confidence — wrongful, disgraceful or briefly angering conduct isn't enough, and the threshold is higher for lower ranks. Board or Appeal Board findings don't bind the Commissioner, and where the facts are admitted no prior fact-finding is needed. Decisions are reviewable on ordinary public-law grounds, with no special deference.

why: Your conduct on duty — especially with victims and witnesses — goes to public confidence in the whole force. Abuse of position can end a career even after a disciplinary process has imposed a lesser penalty.
topic: Garda discipline: the Commissioner's dismissal power and public confidence
st: The leading Supreme Court decision (July 2025) on s.14(2). The 2005 Act and 2007 Discipline Regulations have since been largely replaced by the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024 and new conduct rules — check the current provisions.

d: Convictions for a machete attack were quashed because Gardaí never retrieved CCTV covering the scene — a householder told canvassing Gardaí her system worked and they could view it, but no one went back — and kept no notes of their CCTV enquiries. Seeking out and preserving CCTV is an established duty; the failure removed a realistic prospect of a defence, so the judge should have directed an acquittal.

f.facts: On 17 December 2017 a 74-year-old man was attacked with a machete near a yard in Rathkeale, Co Limerick, where many people and vehicles were present. A woman whose house camera covered the scene told canvassing Gardaí her system was working and they could view it; they never returned. The defence's engineer said there were about 30 cameras in the area. In November 2021 a jury at Limerick Circuit Criminal Court convicted the accused of assault causing serious harm and violent disorder, acquitting him of producing a machete and threats to kill. He got 10 years.
f.held: Court of Appeal, 16 February 2024 (Burns J speaking for the court): convictions quashed. The Garda duty to seek out and preserve CCTV is established, and there were significant failings in how it was handled — footage the owner offered was never retrieved, and there were no notes of the CCTV enquiries. That unfairness in the investigation removed a realistic prospect of a defence, so the trial judge should have directed an acquittal.

why: If someone offers you CCTV, take it — there and then, or at a fixed return time — and record every CCTV enquiry, including dead ends. Unretrieved footage can sink a strong case.
topic: Failing to retrieve offered CCTV: convictions quashed

d: Sentences for a participant in the November 2023 Dublin riots — throwing bags at Gardaí, stamping on a patrol car, setting another alight, and a racially motivated attack on a building housing international protection applicants — were upheld: a 10-year headline for arson and six for riot. The riot's unique gravity, the attack on Gardaí, the escalation and his removal of forensic traces meant it was far from opportunistic.

f.facts: On 23 November 2023 a large crowd gathered in Dublin city centre after an incident at a school earlier that day. CCTV showed the accused throwing rubbish bags at Gardaí, stamping on a patrol car and breaking its windscreen, then placing a burning box in a second patrol car, which caught fire; he wiped the door handle afterwards. He also threw a bicycle saddle at a centre housing about 90 international protection applicants, which he admitted was racially motivated. He admitted his involvement in interview and pleaded guilty to riot, arson and criminal damage, with violent disorder and further criminal damage taken into consideration. Headlines of 10 years (arson), 6 (riot) and 4 (criminal damage) were reduced by 35% for mitigation.
f.held: Court of Appeal, May 2026 ([2026] IECA 105, Butler J): appeal dismissed. The offending was part of the gravest public disorder incident in the history of the State. The attack on Gardaí was extremely frightening, the attack on the centre racially motivated, and the arson — the first that evening — an escalation. He had returned with his face covered intending to take part and removed forensic traces, so it wasn't simply opportunistic and impulsive. Other riot sentences were of limited value as comparators, and no error in principle was shown.

why: In public disorder, CCTV and methodical identification work carry the case — and attacks on Gardaí, racial motivation and forensic clean-up all aggravate. Preserve footage from every source and link each act to each person.

d: A van parked untaxed and uninsured in a residential car park was lawfully seized under s.41 of the Road Traffic Act 1994 — the car park was a public place — and lawfully crushed after notices went unanswered. The Gardaí acted in good faith and without negligence, so s.41(5) protected them, and an allegation of discriminatory policing failed for lack of evidence.

f.facts: In October 2022 the plaintiff bought a van but didn't register as owner. It was parked, untaxed and uninsured, in a residential car park in Dublin, where a Garda seized it under s.41 and had it towed to a contractor's compound. Notices went to the registered owner, who didn't respond, and after the statutory period it was crushed. The plaintiff, who had reported it stolen, sued for theft, destruction of property and discrimination, pointing to his nationality and to another uninsured vehicle nearby that wasn't seized.
f.held: High Court, 4 December 2025 ([2025] IEHC 698, Gillane J, ex tempore, on appeal from the Circuit Court): claim dismissed. The car park, accessible to vehicles by permission, was a public place, and the seizure was lawful; the Garda didn't know the owner's identity or nationality. Disposal followed the statutory notice and waiting process, and a Garda had phoned the plaintiff and told him the van could be crushed. There was no negligence, so s.41(5) applied. Racism, if proven, is odious — but an allegation not founded in evidence is an ugly one, and there was no evidence of discriminatory motive.

why: s.41 seizures are routine but generate complaints. Record why the place is a public place, the tax and insurance checks, the notices sent and the disposal dates — and keep any contact with the person on record.
topic: s.41 seizure and disposal of vehicles; good-faith immunity
st: Yes. High Court decision (December 2025). Read with DPP v Noonan (2025) on opening a vehicle detained under s.41.

n: GW v Commissioner of An Garda Síochána
d: A member in charge refused station bail to a man arrested for a second alleged breach of a protection order, for case-specific reasons: he was already on bail for an earlier breach, and court-imposed conditions were needed. His claim that a (since rescinded) Garda HQ directive on domestic violence had fettered the member's discretion failed — he couldn't prove the directive influenced the decision.

f.facts: The applicant was arrested for a second time over an alleged breach of a protection order under the Domestic Violence Act 2018, and station bail under s.31 of the Criminal Procedure Act 1967 was refused. The member in charge relied on two reasons: he was already on bail for an earlier alleged breach, and conditions only a court can impose (such as no contact) were needed. He sought judicial review, arguing that a 2017 Garda HQ directive, since rescinded, required refusal of station bail in domestic violence cases and unlawfully fettered the statutory discretion. He had previously been granted station bail.
f.held: High Court, 2025 ([2025] IEHC 336): relief refused. The evidence of the arresting Garda and the member in charge showed case-specific reasons, and he didn't show the directive influenced the decision. His affidavits were incomplete and contradicted by objective evidence, and he didn't seek cross-examination. The burden lies on the challenger and the threshold is high; a mere coincidence between a policy and an unfavourable decision isn't enough. The Court didn't need to rule on the directive's validity.

why: Station bail is a personal statutory discretion. Decide each case on its own facts and record the specific reasons — especially where you refuse because only a court can impose the conditions needed (no contact, stay away) in domestic violence cases.
topic: Station bail: a case-by-case discretion, not a blanket policy
st: Yes. High Court decision (2025) on the member in charge's discretion under s.31 of the Criminal Procedure Act 1967.

n: Roche (Dumbrell) v Governor of Cloverhill Prison
d: The Bail Act 1997 is not a complete code: the courts keep their common-law powers to grant and revoke bail. Bail revoked for breaches of conditions (residence, passport) was lawful, and the challenge wasn't a matter for habeas corpus — a detention isn't unlawful under Article 40.4 merely because some defect is alleged.

f.facts: The applicant was charged with violent disorder in November 2013 and refused bail in the District Court. The High Court granted bail with conditions — a specified residence, a curfew, daily signing at a Garda station and no contact with co-accused — and later revoked it for breaches. He got bail again on relaxed conditions, went to Portugal, returned early, didn't surrender his passport and didn't live at the agreed address; Gardaí sought a warrant and bail was revoked again. He brought an Article 40 challenge, arguing the Bail Act 1997 was a complete code that excluded any power to revoke bail.
f.held: Supreme Court, 31 July 2014 (Charleton J, with O'Donnell and MacMenamin JJ): appeal dismissed. The 1997 Act added statutory grounds for refusing bail and amended the law, but courts keep their common-law power to grant and revoke bail (People (AG) v O'Callaghan). The High Court is a full jurisdiction on bail, and applications may be revisited on a relevant and appropriately probative change of circumstances. A detention isn't unlawful for Article 40 purposes merely because some defect attaches to it, so this wasn't a matter for habeas corpus.

why: Bail conditions only protect if they're enforced. Check compliance (signing, residence, curfew, passport), record each breach with evidence, and bring it to court promptly — the court can revoke bail.
topic: Revoking bail for breach of conditions
st: Yes. Supreme Court authority (July 2014) that courts keep common-law powers over bail alongside the Bail Act 1997.

d: CCTV footage is real evidence, not hearsay: it must be proved — where it came from and that it's authentic — but its weight is for the jury, and it shouldn't have been excluded. The trial judge also misread s.19 of the Criminal Justice Act 1984 in excluding an interview. Both rulings were wrong in law, so the directed acquittal on burglary and arson charges was set aside and a retrial ordered.

f.facts: In early 2014 the accused was tried at Dublin Circuit Criminal Court for burglary, endangerment and arson. In a voir dire the trial judge ruled CCTV footage inadmissible, and excluded the memo of a Garda interview on the basis that Gardaí had wrongly invoked s.19 of the Criminal Justice Act 1984, casting doubt on voluntariness. With no other evidence of value, the jury was directed to acquit. The DPP appealed under s.23 of the Criminal Procedure Act 2010, arguing compelling evidence had been wrongly excluded.
f.held: Supreme Court, December 2016 (McKechnie J for a unanimous four-judge court): appeal allowed and a retrial ordered. CCTV is generally real evidence, not hearsay; it carries no presumption of reliability and must be proved, including its provenance and authenticity, but its weight is for the jury. The judge misread s.19 in holding the Gardaí couldn't invoke it, so voluntariness didn't arise. Both rulings were erroneous in law, the excluded material was compelling evidence, and a fair retrial was possible — recollection unimpaired and exhibits preserved.

why: CCTV is only as good as its proof. Record where each recording came from, who extracted it, how, and how it was stored — so provenance and authenticity can be proved. And know the statutory basis before invoking an inference provision in interview.
topic: CCTV as real evidence; s.19 inferences; retrial after a wrongful acquittal
st: Yes. Supreme Court authority (December 2016) on CCTV as real evidence and on s.23 prosecution appeals.

d: When a suspect refuses a formal identification parade, Gardaí may run an informal one. An elderly robbery victim watched seven men walk along a station corridor and recognised the accused instantly; his speaking to a Garda as he passed didn't matter, because the identification had already happened. Excluding it was wrong: the directed acquittal was set aside and a retrial ordered.

f.facts: An elderly woman was robbed at the back door of her home in Co Laois; the robber was alleged to have followed her home. The suspect refused a formal identification parade. At Portarlington Garda Station Gardaí ran an informal parade: without his knowledge, seven men including him walked with a Garda along a corridor while she watched, ready to squeeze her daughter's hand if she recognised the robber. She identified him. CCTV and clothing fibres were said to support the identification. The trial judge excluded the identification — he had spoken to a Garda as he walked past — and directed an acquittal. The DPP appealed under s.23 of the Criminal Procedure Act 2010.
f.held: Court of Appeal, 29 July 2022 (Kennedy J for a three-judge court): appeal allowed, the acquittal set aside and the accused returned for retrial. His speaking to a Garda wasn't significant because she had already recognised him before he spoke. Nor did he need to be told that an informal parade would be held if he refused a formal one — that information might induce a suspect to agree to a formal parade.

why: If a suspect refuses a formal parade, an informal one is a lawful alternative — but it must be run to a high standard: a fair group, no interaction between the suspect and Gardaí, and a full record of what the witness did and said, and when.
topic: Informal identification when a suspect refuses a parade
st: Yes. Court of Appeal decision (July 2022). The accused can't be named for legal reasons. Read with People (AG) v Casey (No 2) and People (DPP) v Murphy (2023) on identification.

d: A man who took in a postal package of methamphetamine was acquitted after the trial judge excluded his guilty pleas to other drug offences found in the same search. That exclusion was wrong — the evidence was probative of knowledge and intent — but the Supreme Court still refused a retrial: after a full jury trial in a routine case, the DPP must show a distinct public-interest reason, and correcting the legal error was enough.

f.facts: The accused accepted a postal package containing about €6,000 of methamphetamine addressed to a housemate. In the same search, drugs were found in his bedroom, and he had pleaded guilty to cannabis and amphetamine supply charges arising from them. At trial on the remaining counts, the judge excluded references to those pleas and related items as more prejudicial than probative, and the jury acquitted. The DPP appealed under s.23 of the Criminal Procedure Act 2010; the Court of Appeal found the exclusion wrong, quashed the acquittal and ordered a retrial.
f.held: Supreme Court, 11 July 2025 ([2025] IESC 32, O'Malley J, with O'Donnell CJ, Woulfe, Hogan and Murray JJ): a point-of-law appeal lay, and the exclusion was wrong — the evidence was reliable, probative of knowledge and intent, and compelling. But a retrial wasn't in the interests of justice under s.23(12): the case was over five years old, there was no identifiable victim, the quantity was routine and below the s.15A threshold, he had been punished for the related offences, and correcting the error on appeal served the systemic purpose. The acquittal was reinstated.

why: In drugs cases, related finds — other drugs, scales, bags, cash, messages — can prove knowledge and intent. Record exactly where each item was found and link it to the suspect, so the prosecution can argue it's admissible.
topic: Related drug finds as evidence of intent; retrial after a jury acquittal
st: Yes. Supreme Court authority (July 2025) on s.23 prosecution appeals after a jury acquittal.

t: Have you recorded every related find in the search and linked each to the suspect, with the evidence of intent (scales, bags, cash, messages) gathered?

d: Gardaí lost items bearing fingerprints from a 1983 kidnap scene — but photographs survived and the forensic examination was done before the loss, so there was no real risk of an unfair trial. Delay didn't justify prohibition either without specific prejudice. Prohibition was refused, though the later trial collapsed when the Garda evidence was ruled inadmissible.

f.facts: In late 1983 a businessman was kidnapped and held in Co Leitrim; during the rescue a Garda recruit and a soldier were shot dead, and the kidnappers escaped, leaving objects bearing fingerprints. The applicant was a suspect but was in custody in Northern Ireland for many years. In 1998 he was arrested in the State and charged with false imprisonment and firearms offences. Gardaí had lost the fingerprinted items. He sought to prohibit the trial for loss of evidence and delay, and the High Court prohibited it on the lost evidence.
f.held: Supreme Court, 2006 ([2006] IESC 11): no real risk of an unfair trial from the lost items — photographs of the prints survived and the forensic examination was complete before the loss. Supreme Court, 5 March 2008 ([2008] IESC 7, Kearns J, unanimous): delay didn't justify prohibition — waiting for his release in Northern Ireland was legitimate, and an accused must show specific prejudice or delay well outside the norm, weighing length, reasons, assertion of the right and prejudice (Barker v Wingo; DPP v Byrne).

why: Exhibits can be lost; the evidence they carry needn't be. Photograph and record exhibits fully, complete forensic examination promptly, and keep the results and photographs securely — they can save a case when the original goes missing.
topic: Lost exhibits and delay: when a trial can still go ahead
st: Yes on the principles. In 2010 the European Court of Human Rights found that Ireland lacked an effective remedy for excessive delay in criminal proceedings.

t: Are exhibits photographed in detail and forensically examined promptly, with results stored securely — so the evidence survives even if the item is lost?

d: A man brought to a Garda station and then to hospital under the Mental Health Act 2001 was lawfully detained under the admission order despite defects: the application for a medical recommendation was signed by his brother instead of a Garda, the GP's examination was 'too informal', the consultant saw him seven hours later, and the Mental Health Commission was notified late. None justified release — but each was a breach to avoid.

f.facts: The applicant, who had a mental illness, had stopped his medication; his brother told a consultant he had a samurai sword and feared for everyone's safety, and raised concerns with Gardaí. Next morning two Gardaí asked him to come to the station, and he went voluntarily. They called a retired GP, who spoke with him for about ten minutes behind the station and recommended hospital care. The application for the recommendation was signed by the brother, not a Garda. At hospital the consultant phoned to say he should be admitted but didn't see him for over seven hours, and the admission order reached the Mental Health Commission late. He sought release.
f.held: High Court, 28 July 2008 (Peart J): release refused; he was lawfully detained under the admission order. Despite a somewhat unusual sequence, the brother's signature on the application didn't justify release; the GP's examination was too informal, but there was no reason to doubt the basis of the recommendation; 'as soon as may be' allowed latitude for the seven-hour delay; and the late notice to the Commission was a technical breach that didn't fundamentally affect his rights.

why: Under s.12 the Garda must make the application for a medical recommendation — not a family member — and should make sure the doctor carries out and records a proper examination. Move promptly and get the paperwork right.
topic: Mental Health Act 2001, s.12: Garda custody and the recommendation process
st: Yes on the approach to procedural defects. Mental health law has been under reform; check the current Act, forms and procedure.

d: A drunk 17-year-old who dropped his trousers in Dublin city centre while a Garda spoke to him, and didn't stop when told, was rightly convicted of offensive conduct under s.5 of the Criminal Justice (Public Order) Act 1994. Unlike s.8, s.5 doesn't require a warning that continuing is an offence, and the conduct was self-evidently criminal.

f.facts: On 18 April 2013 a 17-year-old was drinking with a group in Dublin city centre. Two Gardaí approached; he was very drunk and was warned about intoxication in public. While a Garda spoke to him he pulled down his trousers and underwear; told to stop, he didn't, and ran off. He was later summonsed, convicted in the District Court of offensive conduct under s.5, and given six months' probation. The question whether a warning was required went to the High Court.
f.held: High Court, June 2015 (Kearns P): the conviction stood. Section 5 doesn't specifically require a warning before the offence applies — unlike s.8(2), where failing to comply with a direction is an offence only after a warning. The conduct was so self-evidently and notoriously criminal that no warning was needed.

why: For s.5 outside midnight to 7am, the request to desist is part of the offence — make it clearly and record it: what you said, the time and the response. A warning isn't required by s.5, but it does no harm and strengthens the case.
topic: Offensive conduct (s.5): request to desist, no warning required
st: Yes. High Court decision (June 2015). The accused was a minor and isn't named.

d: A man charged with rape failed to stop his trial on the basis that Gardaí hadn't sought out statements about the complainant's previous sexual history. Prohibition is exceptional: the applicant must show a real or serious risk of an unfair trial, judged on the whole situation — not one element in isolation.

f.facts: The applicant was charged with rape. Prosecution witnesses had referred to the complainant's previous sexual history, and he argued that Gardaí had failed to seek out and make available witness statements about it. The High Court refused leave for judicial review to prohibit the trial, and he appealed.
f.held: Supreme Court, 21 November 2005 (Denham J, with McGuinness and McMenamin JJ): appeal dismissed. Prohibition succeeds only in exceptional circumstances, where there is a real or serious risk of an unfair trial. The onus is on the applicant, and the court must look at the whole situation rather than pick out one element and infer a mere possibility of unfairness. He hadn't shown even an arguable case of such a risk, and courts should be slow to interfere with the DPP's decision to prosecute.

why: The duty to seek out evidence is real but not unlimited, and the courts look at fairness overall. Pursue reasonable lines of enquiry — including ones that may help the accused — and record why any others weren't pursued.
topic: Prohibiting a trial: 'real or serious risk of an unfair trial'
st: Yes. The standard test for prohibition: a real or serious risk of an unfair trial, with the onus on the applicant. Evidence of a complainant's sexual history is also restricted by statute.

src.t: Wikipedia — D.C. v Director of Public Prosecutions

t: Have reasonable lines of enquiry — including those that may help the accused — been followed, with reasons recorded for any not pursued?

d: A driver's solicitor was told the DPP wouldn't prosecute her over a fatal crash. After the deceased's family asked for a review, the DPP reversed the decision — with no new evidence and no warning that it could be reviewed. The Supreme Court (4–1) held this breached fair procedures, and the prosecution was stopped. The DPP may review a decision, but must act fairly.

f.facts: In June 1998 the applicant's car collided with another car in Co Cork, and the other driver died. Her engineers said a deflated tyre had caused the car to go out of control. In early December 1998 her solicitor was told the DPP had decided not to prosecute. The deceased's family wrote asking the DPP to reconsider; the decision was reviewed, and on 23 December 1998 a summons for dangerous driving causing death issued. The DPP's office gave no reasons. The High Court (Kearns J) found the reversal arbitrary and perverse and restrained the prosecution.
f.held: Supreme Court, 31 July 2002 (Keane CJ, Denham, McGuinness and Geoghegan JJ; Murphy J dissenting): DPP's appeal dismissed. The DPP may review an earlier decision not to prosecute and reach a different view. But there was no new evidence or change of circumstances, and she hadn't been told the decision could be reviewed, so reversing it denied her fair procedures. McGuinness and Geoghegan JJ held that once she was told without qualification there would be no prosecution, reversal breached fair procedures. Murphy J would have let the DPP change his mind.

why: Only the DPP (or a Garda prosecuting under the DPP's directions) decides whether to prosecute. Never tell a suspect or solicitor there'll be no prosecution unless that decision has actually been made and you're authorised to pass it on — and say in writing that it may be reviewed, especially in fatal cases.
topic: Reversing a decision not to prosecute: fair procedures
st: Yes. A leading authority on fair procedures when the DPP reverses a communicated decision not to prosecute. Victims can now ask for a review of a decision not to prosecute (EU Victims' Rights Directive, 2012), so how a decision is passed on matters even more.

t: If a decision not to prosecute is passed on, has the suspect been told in writing that it may be reviewed?

d: Blameworthy delay by the prosecution side doesn't by itself stop a trial, but it goes into the balance. A man charged with historic gross indecency had his trial halted because about 34 months of delay, which the DPP couldn't adequately explain, added significantly to his anxiety. The court weighs that against the public interest in prosecuting crime.

f.facts: The applicant was charged with three counts of gross indecency against a relative, alleged to have happened between 1982 and 1985 when the complainant was a teenager. The complaint came years later; he was arrested and questioned in July 1999 and later charged. He sought to prohibit the trial because of the complainant's delay in reporting and further delay by the prosecuting side. The High Court refused to stop the trial for the complainant's delay but halted it for blameworthy prosecutorial delay. The DPP appealed.
f.held: Supreme Court, 5 April 2006 (Kearns and Geoghegan JJ giving judgments; Murray CJ, Denham and Hardiman JJ agreeing): DPP's appeal dismissed, so the trial stayed halted. Blameworthy prosecutorial delay alone doesn't entitle an accused to stop a trial. The court balances the accused's interest in being protected from stress and anxiety caused by unnecessary and inexcusable delay against the public interest in prosecution. Serious blameworthy delay is a factor in its own right, and prejudice to the defence isn't always needed. Here, about 34 months of inadequately explained delay caused significant extra anxiety.

why: Delay after a complaint — by Gardaí or the DPP — counts against the prosecution. Keep files moving, chase directions, and record the reason for every gap: unexplained State delay, plus anxiety to the accused, can stop a trial.
topic: Blameworthy prosecutorial delay: the balancing test
st: Yes, as refined. In Devoy v DPP (2008) the Supreme Court approved PM but let that prosecution go ahead; Nash v DPP (2015) stresses the strong public interest in trials on the merits. Prohibition for delay is exceptional.

d: In historic child sexual abuse cases the court no longer asks why the complainant delayed in reporting. The question is whether the delay has caused prejudice giving a real or serious risk of an unfair trial — and the accused must show it. A former teacher facing 50 charges from the 1960s had to stand trial.

f.facts: A former teacher faced 50 charges of indecent assault involving four boys, aged about 7 to 10, in his care in the mid-1960s. Complaints to Gardaí came more than 30 years later, and charges followed from 2001. He sought to stop the prosecutions because of the lapse of time. The High Court (Ó Caoimh J) refused in July 2004.
f.held: Supreme Court, 31 July 2006 (Murray CJ for a unanimous court of five): appeal dismissed; the prosecutions could proceed. The earlier approach — requiring the prosecution to explain the complainant's delay, often with psychiatric or psychological evidence — was set aside. The test is whether the delay has caused prejudice giving rise to a real or serious risk of an unfair trial, which the applicant must establish. Otherwise only wholly exceptional circumstances would make a trial unfair. Neither was shown.

why: Gardaí no longer have to justify why a victim of historic abuse took years to report. Put the effort into what can still be found — records, documents and witnesses from the time — and record what has been lost and when, because that's what any delay challenge will be about.
topic: Delay in historic sexual abuse cases: the prejudice test
st: Yes. The leading test for delay in historic child sexual abuse prosecutions: prejudice causing a real or serious risk of an unfair trial, or wholly exceptional circumstances.

d: The Sallins mail train robbery (1976). In 1980 the Court of Criminal Appeal quashed a 1978 Special Criminal Court conviction: the confession wasn't shown to be voluntary — it had been obtained under oppression — and refusing him a solicitor was 'inexcusable'. In July 2026 the Court of Appeal certified a miscarriage of justice after the DPP accepted he had no part in the robbery.

f.facts: In March 1976 the Dublin–Cork mail train was robbed at Sallins, Co Kildare, and about £200,000 taken. The accused was arrested and held in Garda custody, where he was denied access to a solicitor. He said he was assaulted and eventually signed a confession; Gardaí denied any ill-treatment. In 1978 the Special Criminal Court convicted him and two co-accused, Kelly and McNally, largely on their statements. He was sentenced to 12 years.
f.held: Court of Criminal Appeal, May 1980 (Finlay P presiding): the convictions of Breathnach and McNally were quashed. The court couldn't be satisfied their statements were voluntary; his confession had been obtained under oppression, and the denial of a solicitor was inexcusable. He had served about 18 months. On 21 July 2026 the Court of Appeal (Kennedy J for a three-judge court) granted a certificate of miscarriage of justice under s.9 of the Criminal Procedure Act 1993, relying on a newly discovered fact and the DPP's concession that he had no part in the robbery — which, the court said, implies actual innocence.

why: A confession is only as good as the conditions it was taken in. Get the suspect a solicitor promptly, record interviews in full, keep the custody record accurate, and test every admission against independent evidence. A confession obtained under oppression is worthless — and here it cost an innocent man his liberty and took 50 years to put right.
topic: Oppression, solicitor access and false confessions (Sallins)
st: Yes. An early landmark on oppression and access to a solicitor; the modern protections go further (see People (DPP) v Gormley and White, 2014). Certified a miscarriage of justice in July 2026, and calls for a public inquiry followed.

d: An IRA membership conviction (2017) rested partly on a senior Garda's belief evidence. He assured the court his belief didn't depend on the book of evidence — which he hadn't seen — and the conviction was quashed over 'double counting'; he was acquitted at a retrial. A 2021 miscarriage of justice certificate was quashed by the Court of Appeal in July 2026: carelessness, though regrettable, wasn't enough.

f.facts: In December 2014 Gardaí saw the accused driving in convoy with a man found with two improvised explosive devices. In 2017 the Special Criminal Court convicted him of IRA membership, relying in part on a senior officer's belief evidence; the officer said his belief wasn't affected by the book of evidence, which he hadn't seen. The Court of Appeal quashed the conviction in 2018 over the risk of double counting, and he was acquitted at a 2019 retrial after 14 months in prison. In April 2021 the Special Criminal Court certified a miscarriage of justice (s.9 Criminal Procedure Act 1993); the High Court refused to quash the certificate in December 2023.
f.held: Court of Appeal, 31 July 2026 (O'Moore J giving judgment): the DPP's appeal was allowed and the certificate quashed. Granting it was not an option reasonably open to the Special Criminal Court; the officer's carelessness, though regrettable, wasn't a basis for a certificate, and there was no finding of deliberate wrongdoing by the State. The acquittal stands.

why: Belief evidence is only as good as the officer's grasp of what it rests on. Before swearing that a belief is independent of the evidence in the case, check the book of evidence. A careless assurance here lost a conviction and led to more than a decade of litigation.
topic: Belief evidence, double counting and miscarriage of justice certificates
st: The acquittal stands. The certificate was quashed by the Court of Appeal in July 2026 — reported as the first time it has overturned such a certificate. Check for any further appeal.

d: A DNA sample taken under s.13 of the Criminal Justice (Forensic Evidence and DNA Database System) Act 2014 was admissible despite the complaint that the sergeant and superintendent hadn't stated their grounds: the reasonable grounds were 'plainly and unequivocally present' and were tested in cross-examination. A Garda's search warrant application heard in a judge's chambers needn't be recorded. Murder conviction upheld.

f.facts: In September 2019 a man was killed at his home in Cork, after a long-running dispute over a family home that was before the civil courts. The accused was found to have used a billhook: his blood was on the handle and the victim's on the blade. A taxi driver found blood in his cab after carrying the accused and a co-accused, and a DNA sample taken from the accused by Gardaí matched it. Search warrant applications were heard in a District Judge's chambers, with no recording. In December 2021 a jury at the Central Criminal Court in Cork convicted him of murder and burglary; he got life imprisonment.
f.held: Court of Appeal, 26 March 2026 ([2026] IECA 65; McCarthy J, with Collins and Owens JJ): appeal dismissed. The defence said the sample breached s.13 of the 2014 Act and his right to bodily integrity because the grounds for authorisation weren't stated. The court held the reasonable grounds were plainly present, the superintendent had sufficient grounds, and the Garda evidence was tested in cross-examination, so the trial judge was entitled to admit it. There's no requirement that a warrant application be recorded; the District Judge properly heard it and rightly granted the warrants.

why: The sample survived because the grounds existed and Gardaí could prove them under cross-examination — don't rely on that. Record the grounds for any sample authorisation at the time: the suspicion, and why the sample will confirm or disprove it. And make sure the oath is properly administered when swearing information for a warrant, wherever the application is heard.
topic: DNA sample authorisation; warrant applications in chambers
st: Yes. Recent Court of Appeal authority (March 2026).

n: DPP v Unnamed (oath on warrant information, 2024)
d: A detective's oath, worded to cover answers to the judge's questions rather than the information itself, didn't invalidate a search warrant. The oath was taken before the information was read to the judge, so the statutory requirement was met; quashing a murder conviction over a formula of words would be 'an absurd triumph of form over substance'. No legal requirement to record the application.

f.facts: In September 2019 a man was killed in Cork after a long-running family dispute over the family home. A search warrant was issued on 10 September 2019 on a detective's sworn information; the application wasn't recorded. In December 2021 the man's sister was convicted of his murder at the Central Criminal Court sitting in Cork and received the mandatory life sentence. She argued on appeal that the information hadn't been sworn as the law requires — the words of the oath covered answers to any questions the judge might ask, not the information itself — and that the application should have been recorded.
f.held: Court of Appeal, 6 June 2024 (Ní Raifeartaigh J for a three-judge court): appeal dismissed. The detective took an oath before the information was read to the judge, so the requirement of information on oath was met. The oath's purpose — impressing the duty to tell the truth — was achieved, and it implicitly covered the information read. Recording the basis for granting a warrant is best practice, but there's no legal requirement to note everything said, and the lack of a recording caused no harm.

why: The warrant survived on substance, but the argument shouldn't have been possible. When swearing information, make sure the oath covers the information itself and is taken before you read it, and keep your own note of the application: when, where, before which judge, who administered the oath, and what was asked.
topic: The oath on sworn information for a search warrant
st: Yes. Court of Appeal authority (June 2024). The co-accused's separate appeal, on DNA sampling and warrant applications in chambers, failed in March 2026 (DPP v O'Hara).

d: Gardaí didn't take a statement from the accused's wife, who he said would contradict part of the complainant's account; she died before trial. The Court of Appeal held that was the investigators' fault — an effort should have been made to speak to her — but the trial wasn't unfair: the defence never challenged the complainant on the point, the jury heard what he said she'd have said, and the judge warned about lost evidence.

f.facts: The accused was charged with two sexual assaults in summer 1991 in the West of Ireland. He said his wife would confirm that the complainant didn't stay at their home on the night between the two incidents, undermining her account of the second assault. Gardaí didn't take a statement from the wife, saying she was unwell, and she died before the trial. In 2024 a jury at Galway Circuit Court convicted him on both counts, and he was sentenced to two years.
f.held: Court of Appeal, 5 May 2026 (Burns J for a three-judge court): the ground failed. The missing statement was the fault of the investigating force, and an effort should have been made to speak to her. But it was uncertain her statement would have been admissible after her death; his account of what she'd say was before the jury; the judge warned the jury about delay and lost evidence; and the complainant was never challenged on whether she stayed at the house — an 'insuperable difficulty for the appellant'. The trial was imperfect, but no unfairness arose.

why: When a suspect names a witness who could support his account, make a real effort to get a statement — and record every attempt, and why it failed. A witness being unwell is a reason to try another way or another day, not to drop it. Here the conviction survived only because of how the defence ran the trial.
topic: Failing to interview a potential defence witness
st: Yes. Recent Court of Appeal authority (May 2026). Read with the duty to seek out and preserve evidence (Braddish v DPP, Dunne v DPP).

d: A change of member in charge partway through a detention doesn't by itself make the detention unlawful. Where nothing has happened to change the original reason for detaining the suspect, it continues lawfully — the trial judge was wrong to exclude a statement because the incoming member in charge hadn't re-satisfied himself. (The acquittal stood: the DPP's reference was without prejudice.)

f.facts: On Christmas Eve 2007 a man was arrested in Carrick-on-Suir, Co Tipperary, while travelling in a car with three others; a rucksack beside him held six bars of cannabis resin. He was detained at a Garda station. At a change of shift a new member in charge took over and didn't satisfy himself that continued detention was necessary. The trial judge ruled the man's statement inadmissible on that ground, and he was acquitted. The DPP referred the point to the Supreme Court, without prejudice to the acquittal.
f.held: Supreme Court, July 2015 (4–1): the detention was lawful. Nothing had happened during the detention to change the original reason for it, so the change of member in charge didn't make the continued detention unlawful, and the trial judge was wrong on that point. The acquittal wasn't affected.

why: Detention doesn't lapse at a shift change — but don't invite the argument. At handover the incoming member in charge should review the custody record, confirm the grounds still apply and note it with the time. If anything changes the grounds, deal with it at once.
topic: Change of member in charge during detention
st: Yes. Supreme Court authority (2015) on handover between members in charge.

t: At each change of member in charge, is there a timed note that the grounds for detention were reviewed and still apply?

d: Gardaí took no details or statements from two people who brought a rape complainant to the station — one sat with her while she made her statement — and the defence learned of them only at sentencing. That breached the duty to seek out and preserve evidence, and the accused couldn't be required to prove what unknown evidence would have shown. But judged on the trial as a whole there was no lost chance of acquittal, so the conviction stood.

f.facts: The accused was convicted of rape in the Central Criminal Court; his defence was consent. The evidence included medical and forensic evidence and texts he sent soon afterwards, one apologising. About 20 hours after the incident the complainant met a work colleague and his girlfriend, who went with her to the Garda station; the girlfriend stayed with her while she made her statement. Neither was asked for details or a statement, and the defence learned of them only from her victim impact statement at sentencing. The Court of Appeal accepted Gardaí should have sought them out, but held any unfairness 'entirely speculative' and dismissed the appeal.
f.held: Supreme Court, 31 March 2023 ([2023] IESC 8; Baker J, with Dunne, Charleton, O'Malley and Woulfe JJ): appeal dismissed. The duty to seek out, preserve and disclose evidence is central to fair trial rights, and the State must take reasonable and proportionate steps; here it plainly fell short. Where the State's failure kept the defence unaware of the evidence, the accused can't be required to show what it would have said. The court looks at the trial as a whole and asks whether there was a lost chance of acquittal. Recent complaint evidence goes only to consistency, its value would have been limited, and the other evidence was strong.

why: Anyone who brings a complainant to the station, or heard the first account, is a potential witness. Take their names and details, take statements where relevant, and tell the prosecutor. The conviction survived here, but the Supreme Court found a clear breach of duty.
topic: Uncollected evidence on appeal: the 'lost chance of acquittal' test
st: Yes. The leading Supreme Court authority (2023) on how appeal courts treat evidence Gardaí failed to collect.

d: A detective who knew the accused recognised him on good-quality CCTV of a 2010 armed robbery. No notes or record were kept of how the footage was shown, but the recognition evidence was properly admitted: the trial court weighed the criticisms, warned itself of the dangers, and could test the evidence against the footage and stills. Recognition is distinct from identification of a stranger.

f.facts: In March 2010 two raiders hid in the ceiling of a bookmaker's in Swords, Co Dublin, then robbed it; a passing car was hijacked at gunpoint and later abandoned in Finglas. A phone dropped at the scene was linked to the accused. A detective who had worked in Finglas for 17 years, and had dealt with and arrested the accused before, viewed the CCTV at a Garda station; no suspect was named to him, and he said he was '100 per cent certain' it was the accused. No contemporaneous notes or record of the viewing were kept. The Special Criminal Court convicted him in May 2021.
f.held: Court of Appeal, 23 July 2024 ([2024] IECA 218; Edwards J, with McCarthy and Kennedy JJ): appeal dismissed. Recognition evidence is distinct from identification evidence (DPP v Tynan, 2017). The recognition evidence was relevant and probative and properly admitted. The trial court acknowledged the criticisms of the procedure, warned itself of the dangers of recognition evidence, and could test the witness's reliability against high-quality CCTV and stills. Its approach was 'impeccable'.

why: When a Garda views CCTV to see if they recognise someone, record the whole process: who showed it, when, what the viewer was told, what was shown, and their exact words and basis of knowledge. The evidence survived here on the strength of the footage and the phone — don't rely on that.

st: Yes. Court of Appeal authority (July 2024) on recognition evidence from CCTV.

d: A 'one witness case': a Garda recognised the accused on a bookmaker's CCTV, and he was convicted of violent disorder. In 2017 the Court of Appeal upheld the conviction, treating it as recognition evidence. Then another man came forward as the attacker; UK experts compared the images, the conviction was quashed (2018), and in 2023 it was certified a miscarriage of justice. The Garda's opinion was honest — and wrong.

f.facts: In December 2012 three men attacked customers in a bookmaker's in Tallaght in a feud. The only evidence against the accused was a Garda's identification of him from the bookmaker's CCTV. A Garda bulletin with the CCTV hadn't produced an identification of him, and an internal email naming other suspects wasn't disclosed. He was convicted in the Circuit Criminal Court and sentenced in January 2017 to four years, the last suspended. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal in July 2017. Months later another man came forward claiming to be the third attacker, and the case was referred to UK identification experts.
f.held: Court of Appeal, April 2018: conviction quashed under s.2 of the Criminal Procedure Act 1993, the DPP not opposing; no retrial. He had served about 11 months. Court of Appeal, 28 July 2023 (McCarthy J): certificate of miscarriage of justice granted. The UK Metropolitan Police experts' comparison of photographs and CCTV stills confirmed his innocence; the core problem was the Garda identification process and a lack of material that could have helped the defence test its reliability. The court made no criticism of the investigation: the Garda's opinion was honestly held and in good faith.

why: A sincere, confident recognition by a Garda can still be wrong. Record every step of a CCTV viewing — including earlier occasions when the same person wasn't recognised — disclose internal emails or intelligence naming other suspects, and look for evidence that supports or undermines a single recognition before relying on it.
topic: Recognition from CCTV and a wrongful conviction
st: Yes, as a warning. The 2017 recognition-evidence approach is still followed (DPP v Byrne, 2024), but this conviction was quashed in 2018 and certified a miscarriage of justice in 2023.

d: The original s.12 of the Immigration Act 2004 — making it an offence for a non-national to fail to produce a passport on demand 'without satisfactory explanation' — was unconstitutional. The undefined 'satisfactory explanation' was too vague and open to arbitrary application by individual Gardaí, and silence could be treated as guilt. Section 12 was amended in 2011 and now has a defence of reasonable cause.

f.facts: In April 2008 the applicant arrived at Dublin Airport with children she said she had been asked to bring. She was arrested and charged under s.12 of the Immigration Act 2004 with failing to produce a passport or equivalent document and failing to give a satisfactory explanation. She later applied for asylum and challenged s.12 by judicial review; the Irish Human Rights Commission appeared as amicus curiae.
f.held: High Court, 25 March 2011 (Kearns P): s.12 declared inconsistent with Articles 38.1 and 40.4.1 of the Constitution. 'Satisfactory explanation' was undefined, creating uncertainty and scope for arbitrary application; the explanation seemed to be part of the offence rather than a defence; and silence could count as failing to explain, risking self-incrimination. The State's right to control non-nationals was accepted, and a criminal sanction wasn't in itself disproportionate; on the facts, s.11 (entry requirements) would have been more appropriate.

why: A power to demand ID must be clear — and so must your reason for using it. Under the amended s.12, demand a passport or ID only to establish that the person's presence is lawful, don't use it on under-16s or EU free-movement cases, and remember the person has a defence of reasonable cause.
topic: Demanding a passport from a non-national (s.12 Immigration Act 2004)
st: The original s.12 was struck down (2011). The amended s.12 (Civil Law (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2011, s.34) applies — check the current text before relying on it.

d: A Chief Superintendent's belief that the accused was an IRA member (s.3(2) of the Offences Against the State (Amendment) Act 1972) was admissible even though privilege was claimed over its sources, limiting cross-examination. The right to cross-examine can be restricted where strictly necessary to protect informants. There was enough other evidence — but the trial court should have explained the weight it gave the belief.

f.facts: The accused was convicted of IRA membership by the Special Criminal Court in November 2003 and jailed for four years. The prosecution relied in part on a Chief Superintendent's belief that he was a member; the officer claimed privilege over the sources of that belief without further explanation, so the defence couldn't test them. The Court of Criminal Appeal certified the point for the Supreme Court.
f.held: Supreme Court, 2006 (Fennelly J for a unanimous court of five): appeal dismissed. The right to cross-examine one's accusers is essential to a fair trial, but can be restricted in the interests of overall balance. Belief evidence was justified because it applies only to dangerous organisations, senior officers are presumed to have high integrity, and the Special Criminal Court applies high standards of fairness. Restricting access to the sources to protect informants went no further than strictly necessary. There was sufficient other evidence of membership. The trial court should have explained the weight it gave the belief, but there was no overall unfairness.

why: Belief evidence is lawful but limited, and it won't carry a case on its own. Investigators need independent evidence of membership; a senior officer giving belief evidence must be ready to justify any claim of privilege through the prosecutor.
topic: Belief evidence and privilege over its sources
st: Yes. Read with Redmond v Ireland (2015), which upheld s.3(2) as constitutional, and the Connolly certificate case (2026) on double counting.

d: Section 3(2) of the Offences Against the State (Amendment) Act 1972 — making a Chief Superintendent's belief evidence of membership of an unlawful organisation — is constitutional. Belief evidence is merely admissible: it can be challenged and rejected like any other evidence, there's a practice of not convicting on it alone, and privileged material can be examined by the court and may yield if it could raise a reasonable doubt.

f.facts: The applicant was convicted of IRA membership by the Special Criminal Court. The trial focused on forensic evidence linking him to weapons, but the court also relied on a Chief Superintendent's belief that he was a member, whose sources were privileged. He didn't challenge the belief, seek the material or give evidence. He then argued s.3(2) breached his right to a fair trial (Article 38.1): the informants would never testify, and an officer could be misled by bogus information yet still appear credible.
f.held: Supreme Court, December 2015 (Charleton J giving judgment): s.3(2) upheld. Belief evidence has no special status; credibility and expertise can be tested in cross-examination. The statute doesn't require corroboration, but a practice has developed of not convicting on belief evidence alone. Undisclosed material doesn't by itself make a trial unfair: the defence can ask the court to examine it, and privilege can yield where it could raise a reasonable doubt. The provision is confined to membership charges in the Special Criminal Court; the court must be satisfied of guilt beyond reasonable doubt on all the evidence.

why: Belief evidence is a support, not a substitute: build the membership case on independent evidence (forensics, surveillance, association, conduct). A senior officer giving belief evidence should expect cross-examination on credibility and expertise, and should have the underlying material organised so the court can examine it if asked.
topic: Constitutionality of belief evidence (s.3(2), 1972 Act)
st: Yes. The leading Supreme Court authority (2015) upholding belief evidence. See also People (DPP) v Kelly (2006) and the Connolly certificate case (2026).

d: A gangland murder conviction built on CCTV from many locations, fingerprints and DNA in two cars, and Garda recognition evidence was upheld. Challenges to the recognition evidence — undated statements, no notes of the basis for recognition, other footage viewed first — and to the quality of the footage failed, and collecting CCTV breached no privacy right: no one in public can expect to be 'immune from CCTV observation'.

f.facts: In July 2016 a man was shot dead outside a shop in Dublin 8. The prosecution relied on CCTV from multiple locations showing four vehicles operating together before and after the shooting; the accused's car passed the shop about four minutes beforehand. His fingerprints and DNA were found in two cars used in the attack, and inferences were drawn from his silence in interview. Gardaí gave evidence recognising him on footage: one officer's statements were undated, he kept no notes of the basis for his recognition, and he had viewed other footage first; another's statement was dated about four months after the killing. The Special Criminal Court convicted him of murder in 2018.
f.held: Court of Appeal, 30 January 2024 ([2024] IECA 22; Ní Raifeartaigh J, with Birmingham P and Edwards J): appeal dismissed on all grounds. The arguments about the quality of the footage and the lack of Garda records of the identification were rejected, and the CCTV was admissible. There was no breach of privacy: people walking on a public street, driving on a public road or eating in a public restaurant can't reasonably expect their movements to be immune from CCTV observation.

why: The conviction survived, but the recognition evidence was attacked on exactly the gaps Gardaí control: undated statements, no note of the basis for recognition, and no record of what was viewed first. Date every statement, record the basis for recognition at the time, and log each viewing.
topic: Garda recognition from CCTV; CCTV and privacy
st: Yes. Court of Appeal authority (January 2024). Decided the same day as DPP v Dunbar, which also rejected a CCTV privacy challenge.

d: An unaccompanied learner permit holder who produced an insurance certificate couldn't be convicted of driving without insurance (s.56(1) Road Traffic Act 1961) just because he had no full licence. The question is whether the policy actually covered him, which turns on its wording; the prosecution must prove any breach of a policy condition with admissible evidence. An insurer's remark relayed by the Garda was hearsay.

f.facts: In September 2018 a Garda stopped the accused in Co Clare. He held a learner permit, not a licence, and no qualified driver was with him. He produced a certificate of insurance. The Garda said an insurer's employee had told him the insurer would compensate a third party but seek to recover the cost from the driver. He pleaded guilty to unlicensed driving but denied no insurance. The District Judge took the view that a learner permit is a conditional licence and, the condition not being met, he wasn't insured — and stated a case to the High Court.
f.held: High Court, June 2020 ([2020] IEHC 362, Humphreys J): he couldn't be convicted under s.56(1) on that evidence. The real question is whether an approved policy was in force covering the user, which depends on the policy's wording, not on whether he held a valid licence. Any breach of a policy condition must be proved in each case by admissible evidence. The insurer's employee's account was inadmissible hearsay — and in any event showed only that the insurer would seek recovery, not that it would refuse to indemnify.

why: Don't assume an unaccompanied learner is uninsured. Get the policy, identify the exact condition said to be breached, and prove it with admissible evidence from the insurer — not a phone call relayed in your own evidence. Deal with the licensing offence separately.
topic: No-insurance charges against unaccompanied learners
st: Yes. High Court authority (2020). The judge noted that s.56(1)'s replacement (s.34 of the Road Traffic Act 2004) hadn't been commenced — check the current wording before relying on it.

d: A learner driving without L-plates or a qualified accompanying driver is liable for driving without a licence (s.38 RTA 1961): the permit only authorises driving in line with its conditions. But he was still insured — the certificate wasn't conditional on complying with the permit's terms — so there was no no-insurance offence (s.56).

f.facts: In November 2012 a Garda stopped the accused driving in Kilrush, Co Clare. He produced a learner permit and an insurance certificate; he had never held a full licence, and had no L-plates and no qualified driver with him. The certificate covered him 'provided that the person holds a licence to drive such a vehicle'. He was charged with driving without insurance (s.56), failing to produce insurance (s.69) and driving without a licence (s.38). The District Judge stated a consultative case to the High Court.
f.held: High Court, 20 November 2014 ([2014] IEHC 558, McDermott J): a learner permit has effect in accordance with its terms and conditions, so driving without L-plates or a qualified accompanying driver left him liable to conviction for driving without a licence. But the insurance certificate wasn't conditional on compliance with the permit's terms, so he was insured on the day and there was no s.56 offence. A Northern Irish authority (McGimpsey v Carlin, 1969) was distinguished.

why: For an unaccompanied learner, the licensing offence is the straightforward charge. Charge no insurance only if the policy itself makes cover depend on complying with the permit — and be ready to prove that wording.

d: Gardaí who pursued a speeding motorcycle that failed to stop weren't liable for injuries to its pillion passenger when it crashed. The failure to stop gave a reasonable, genuinely held suspicion of crime; pursuing it in the course of duty breached no duty to the occupants; and the injuries were caused by the motorcyclist's own driving.

f.facts: In August 1994 Gardaí running a radar check recorded a motorcycle at 80 mph. It didn't stop but sped up. Gardaí pursued it; it went around an attempted roadblock and on through Cashel. The pursuing car lost sight of it, then found it had crossed onto the wrong side on a bend and hit an oncoming car. The plaintiff, the pillion passenger, was severely injured. Gardaí had no information that the occupants had committed a crime. The High Court found for her, holding that the pursuit caused the excessive speed.
f.held: Supreme Court, 23 February 2007 ([2007] IESC 8; Kearns J, with Hardiman and Finnegan JJ): the State's appeal was allowed. The failure to stop gave the Gardaí a reasonable and genuinely held suspicion of criminal activity, and pursuing the vehicle in the course of their duty to detect and prevent crime breached no duty owed to its occupants. The trial judge was wrong to treat the pursuit as one seamless process; there was no breach in its final stretch either. In any event, the injuries were caused by the motorcyclist's driving.

why: Pursuing a vehicle that fails to stop is lawful police work, but each stage is judged on its facts. Follow the Garda Code and current pursuit policy, weigh the suspected offence against the risk to everyone on the road, and record why you started, continued and ended the pursuit.
topic: Garda pursuits: duty of care to a fleeing vehicle's occupants
st: Yes. The leading Supreme Court authority on liability for Garda pursuits, applied in Galazka (2024). Check the current Garda pursuit policy.

n: Galazka v Minister for Public Expenditure and Reform
d: The State was fully liable when an Armed Support Unit car making a 'compliant stop' cut across a motorist's path before a roundabout and was struck. His car had nothing to do with the burglary being investigated. There was no good reason to stop him there rather than tail him, and he wasn't at fault for missing a Garda car in his blind spot. Damages €10,070.

f.facts: Gardaí responding to an aggravated burglary followed two vehicles, one of them the plaintiff's car; neither was involved. An Armed Support Unit Audi Q7 approached from his right rear to make a 'compliant stop' and, he said, cut across his path as he neared a roundabout; his car struck its left rear wheel. He said he didn't see the flashing lights, which the court accepted given how briefly the Garda car had been behind him. The case came to the High Court on appeal from the Circuit Court.
f.held: High Court, 2024 ([2024] IEHC 266, O'Connor J): the State was fully liable, and €10,070 was awarded. Applying Hayes v Minister for Finance, a breach of policy isn't automatically negligence, and Gardaí must balance catching suspects against protecting the public. But there was no satisfactory explanation for stopping him before the roundabout instead of letting him through it: under the Garda Code the risk wasn't imperative, and too little regard was paid to the Code's advice to tail suspects and to the road conditions. Judged without hindsight, he wasn't contributorily negligent.

why: A stop must be necessary at that moment and in that place. Unless it's imperative, tail the vehicle and pick a safe location — not the approach to a roundabout or junction — and give the driver time to see your lights.
topic: Compliant stops: Garda liability for a collision
st: Yes. High Court authority (2024) applying Hayes v Minister for Finance (2007). Check current Garda policy on stopping vehicles.

d: A bus driver who cut the corner turning at a T-junction and knocked a cyclist off her bicycle — she died of head injuries — was rightly convicted of careless driving causing death. No evidence of a phone or other distraction was needed: the question is whether the driving fell appreciably below the standard of a reasonably prudent driver. 'Far from a marginal case.'

f.facts: On a November night in 2014 a double-decker bus turning at a T-junction in Dublin 4 appeared to cut the corner and knocked a cyclist off her bicycle; she died two days later from head injuries. The driver was convicted of careless driving causing death in the Dublin Circuit Criminal Court in October 2018 and disqualified for four years. On appeal he argued that the judge's re-charge, using terms like 'appreciable', 'due care and attention' and 'prudent', confused the jury; that there was no evidence of any distraction; and that the verdict was perverse.
f.held: Court of Appeal, 19 October 2021 ([2021] IECA 271; Edwards J giving judgment): appeal dismissed. No requisitions were raised on the re-charge, and the directions — including 'appreciable' — were adequate. Careless driving needs no proof of intention or recklessness; the question is whether the driver fell below the standard of care of a reasonably prudent driver in the circumstances. There was evidence capable of supporting the verdict, and the perversity ground was rejected without hesitation.

why: In a fatal collision the case is built on the manoeuvre itself. Map the scene, the vehicle's line through the turn and the cyclist's position, recover CCTV and vehicle data quickly, and get a collision reconstruction. You don't need to prove a phone or distraction to show careless driving.

d: A man seen handing over a package in a Phibsboro pub — it held 400 fake €50 notes — had keys to a unit in Co Meath with offset printers, finished notes and part-finished notes with a face value of about €2 million. On his plea to having counterfeiting materials (s.36 of the 2001 Act), the Court of Appeal set an eight-year headline, re-sentencing him because the judge's reasons on mitigation were too thin.

f.facts: In February 2014 Gardaí surveilling suspected IRA members saw the accused exchange a package with a man in a pub in Phibsboro, Dublin. The man was stopped and found with 400 counterfeit €50 notes (€20,000 face value). The accused had genuine cash and a set of keys, which opened a leased unit in Dunboyne, Co Meath, holding two offset printers, printing materials, completed counterfeit €50 notes (about €189,000) and part-finished notes (about €2 million). He declined to answer questions. f.held: Court of Appeal, 28 July 2016 ([2016] IECA 239; Edwards J, with Sheehan and Mahon JJ): sentence appeal allowed. The judge's reasons were too thin to show adequate credit for mitigation — a significant error of principle. Re-sentencing, the court took a headline of eight years to reflect the gravity of the offending, allowed 30 months for mitigation, and suspended a further 18 months for his progress towards rehabilitation.

d: Making it an offence to refuse Gardaí the password or biometric access to a lawfully seized device (s.49 of the Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001) is constitutional. Compelled access does engage the privilege against self-incrimination, so the act of unlocking can't be used to prove ownership or control — but what's already on the device can be used. The warrant must justify searching the digital space, following Quirke.

f.facts: On 9 January 2024, in a Garda Economic Crime Bureau investigation, two smartphones and a computer were seized at the applicant's home under a District Court warrant (s.48(2) of the 2001 Act). The District Judge was satisfied, following Quirke, that there were reasonable grounds to search the digital space as well as the physical one. Gardaí asked for the passwords under s.48(5)(b)(i); he refused, was arrested, and was charged with three offences under s.49(1)(c) of failing, without lawful excuse, to provide them. He sought to prohibit the prosecution and have s.49 declared invalid. The High Court (Bradley J) refused, holding the privilege wasn't engaged, and he appealed directly to the Supreme Court.
f.held: Supreme Court, November 2025 ([2025] IESC 47, Charleton J giving judgment): appeal dismissed; s.49 is valid and compatible with Article 6 ECHR. Unlike the High Court, it held that giving a passcode or using a biometric can show possession and use, so the privilege is engaged — but the key safeguard is that the compelled act can't be used against the suspect. Material already on the device isn't compelled and can be used. The suspect's choice is like opening the door to a room or safe during a physical search; refusing exposes him to a much lesser offence. Searching the digital space needs reasonable justification put before the issuing judge, showing necessity and proportionality.

why: Device evidence now turns on two things you control: a warrant application that justifies searching the digital space, and independent proof of who owns and uses the device. Ask for passwords under the warrant power, record the request and the answer — but never rely on the unlocking itself to prove ownership.

st: Yes. The leading Supreme Court authority (November 2025) on compelled access to seized devices under the 2001 Act, and on warrants covering the digital space after Quirke.
