n: McDonagh v Governor of Cloverhill Prison
d: A District Judge refused bail on his own fear that the accused 'would go out and murder someone' — not on the Garda's evidence, which named no witnesses. The Supreme Court ordered release: a s.2 Bail Act refusal must rest on evidence, the court must consider the s.2(2) matters, and the accused must be told a s.2 objection is being made and get a fair chance to answer it.

f.facts: Two men were charged with assault causing harm after a New Year's Day shooting in Coolock, Dublin, that left a man seriously injured; the Garda described an ongoing feud between two families. At the bail hearing the Garda objected on the seriousness of the charge and a fear that witnesses would be intimidated, but identified and called no witnesses. The defence objected that this was hearsay and that no s.2 objection had been made. The District Judge refused bail, saying the test was whether the accused would go out and murder someone. The High Court refused to order release.
f.held: Supreme Court, 28 January 2005 (McGuinness J, with Hardiman and Fennelly JJ): appeal allowed; both men had already been released. The judge hadn't ruled on the prosecution's objection or the hearsay point, hadn't considered the mandatory s.2(2) matters, and refused bail on an apprehension he raised himself, with no evidence. A refusal must rest on relevant evidence, and an accused must be told a s.2 objection is being made and have a proper chance to answer it. The hearing was unfair, so the detention wasn't in accordance with law.

why: A bail objection is only as good as the evidence behind it. State which grounds you rely on (O'Callaghan, s.2 or both), give the evidence — specific witnesses, incidents, and why they're at risk — and address the s.2(2) factors. A general fear of intimidation, with nobody identified, won't do.

d: Bail was refused because four complainants withdrew their statements, which the High Court read as plain intimidation. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal: there was no evidence that the accused had intimidated anyone or was likely to interfere with witnesses. Refusing bail on the risk of interference needs evidence — not an inference from withdrawn statements alone.

f.facts: The accused was arrested in August 2013 on six charges — including demanding money with menaces, violent disorder, wrongful intimidation and criminal damage — after he and three others allegedly demanded €8,000 over a drug debt at a house in Finglas. Bail was refused in the District Court and the High Court. Before a later bail hearing all four complainants withdrew their statements. The High Court refused bail on the O'Callaghan grounds, finding the complainants had plainly been intimidated and that there was a risk of interference with witnesses.
f.held: Supreme Court, 25 February 2014 ([2014] IESC 18; Dunne J, with Denham CJ and MacMenamin J): appeal allowed and the matter remitted to the High Court. There was no evidence that, as a matter of probability, the accused would interfere with witnesses, and none that he was involved in any intimidation. The finding that the witnesses had plainly been intimidated lacked evidential support, so the refusal couldn't stand.

why: If witnesses withdraw, find out why and record it. To oppose bail on the risk of interference you need evidence connecting the accused to it — what the witnesses say, contacts, threats, messages — not the withdrawal alone.

d: Inferences from a failure to account for presence (s.19 CJA 1984) can be used only at a trial for the offence the suspect was questioned about when the section was invoked. A man arrested and warned about a firearm discharge, but tried for burglary, had his conviction quashed.

f.facts: After a firearm was discharged at a house in Blanchardstown, Dublin, on 3 June 2009, the accused was arrested under s.30 of the Offences Against the State Act 1939. In interview Gardaí invoked s.19 of the Criminal Justice Act 1984, asking him to account for his presence at named places on the basis that he was there to take part in the firearm discharge. He was never charged with a firearms offence: he was charged with burglary (s.12(1)(b) of the 2001 Act), involving an assault causing harm. The trial judge allowed reliance on s.19, and the Court of Appeal upheld the conviction.
f.held: Supreme Court, 13 July 2017 ([2017] IESC 53; Denham CJ, with McKechnie, O'Donnell, Clarke and O'Malley JJ): appeal allowed, conviction quashed. The wording of s.19 is clear: it can be relied on only where the offence charged is the offence the accused was questioned about when the section was invoked. The caution related to the firearm offence, not the burglary, so no inference could be drawn. Any change would need legislation; a retrial was for the DPP.

why: Inference provisions are offence-specific. Name in the inference warning every offence you may charge, and if the investigation moves to a different offence, take advice on re-arrest or a fresh warning for that offence before relying on the suspect's silence.
topic: Inferences are tied to the offence named when they were invoked

d: Harassment by 'communicating with' a person (s.10 NFOAPA 1997) doesn't require the victim to be addressed directly: an anonymous campaign of abusive letters, emails and leaflets to a State solicitor's home, workplace and neighbourhood was enough, and the persistence requirement was clearly met. A majority held 'besetting' needs some physical presence or action. Conviction of a Detective Sergeant upheld.

f.facts: Between 2011 and 2013 the accused, a Detective Sergeant, sent abusive letters and emails over about 18 months to the home and workplace of a State solicitor in the DPP's office, whom she didn't know; one email purported to come from a dangerous criminal, and leaflets were placed on cars and pillars in the victim's neighbourhood. In 2017 a Dublin Circuit Criminal Court jury convicted her of harassment, and she was sentenced to three years; in 2019 the Court of Appeal suspended the balance for an error in principle. The Supreme Court considered the meaning of 'communicating with' and 'besetting' in s.10.
f.held: Supreme Court, 24 July 2020 ([2020] IESC 45; O'Donnell J giving the lead judgment, with MacMenamin, O'Malley and Baker JJ; Charleton J dissenting on besetting): appeal dismissed. 'Communicating with' takes its ordinary meaning and doesn't necessarily require the victim to be directly addressed; the jury could find the conduct amounted to communicating with her. Persistence can be shown by a number of incidents or a single continuing action. A majority held besetting requires some physical presence or action. All five judges called 'besetting' archaic and urged that s.10 be updated.

why: Harassment is proved by the whole course of conduct. Gather every communication — letters, emails, posts, leaflets, messages to third parties — prove who sent them, and show how they reached and affected the victim. They don't need to be addressed to the victim directly.

d: A Garda Superintendent, as SPSV licensing authority, may take into account an allegation that ended in acquittal when deciding whether a taxi licence applicant is suitable (s.10 Taxi Regulation Act 2013) — it can bear on the safety of passengers. But fair procedures require telling the applicant the material relied on so he can answer it. Refusal quashed and sent back.

f.facts: In 2017 the applicant faced an allegation of sexual assault; his conviction was quashed on appeal and he was acquitted by a jury at the retrial. He applied for a small public service vehicle (taxi) driver licence. At an interview the licensing authority told him only that it had 'one side of the events', without identifying the documents or statements it relied on. On 7 November 2023 the application was refused because of concerns arising from the 2017 allegation. He sought judicial review.
f.held: High Court, 28 April 2025 ([2025] IEHC 244, Phelan J): under s.10(1) a licence shall not be granted unless the authority is satisfied the applicant is suitable, and the s.10(2) matters (such as good character and Garda concerns) aren't exhaustive. Considering an allegation that ended in acquittal was within the authority's discretion, given the safety of vulnerable passengers. But fair procedures require the applicant to be told the material behind adverse concerns so he can respond; that wasn't done, so the refusal was quashed and remitted for reconsideration with notice of all material relied on.

why: In SPSV vetting you can weigh more than convictions — but you must show the applicant what you're relying on and let them respond before refusing. Identify the specific statements or records, give the applicant a fair chance to answer them, and record your reasons.
topic: SPSV driver licensing: acquitted allegations and fair procedures

d: After the District Court allowed an appeal against a Garda refusal of an SPSV licence, Gardaí granted it with a condition restricting the driver to working for one named business. The High Court quashed the condition: licence conditions must be rational, reasonable and proportionate, must respect the right to earn a living, and can't effectively override the District Court's decision.

f.facts: Gardaí refused the applicant a small public service vehicle licence; he had previous drugs convictions. He won an appeal in the District Court, which granted the licence. Gardaí then issued it with a condition restricting him to working for one named private-hire business run by a relative. He sought judicial review of the condition.
f.held: High Court, July 2023 (Meenan J): the condition was quashed. The power under the Taxi Regulation Act 2013 to attach conditions has limits: conditions must be rational, reasonable and proportionate, balanced against the constitutional right to earn a living. This one was so restrictive it effectively overrode the District Court's decision, and it was fragile — a change of business name would void the licence. Supervision-type conditions might have been reasonable given his record. The application went back to An Garda Síochána to grant the licence.

why: Licence conditions must answer a specific risk in a proportionate way. Record the risk, the condition chosen and why less restrictive options won't do — and don't use conditions to undo a District Court decision.
topic: SPSV licence conditions must be reasonable and proportionate

d: Carrying a passenger 'for hire or reward' without an SPSV licence doesn't need a fare agreed in advance or paid on the spot. A phone booking, turning up at the agreed time and place, and asking for a fare after the journey showed an expectation of payment — enough. The District Court's acquittal was overturned and the case sent back.

f.facts: The National Transport Authority prosecuted the accused under the Taxi Regulation Act 2013 for carrying a passenger for hire or reward in an unlicensed vehicle. The journey was arranged in a phone call that treated him as a taxi service; he arrived at the agreed time and place; there was no prior fare agreement and no payment up front, but he asked for a fare after the journey. He stopped the activity afterwards. The District Court acquitted him.
f.held: High Court, 21 April 2020 ([2020] IEHC 224, Barr J): the acquittal was overturned and the case remitted. The District Court applied too narrow a test by focusing on a prior fare agreement or immediate payment. Looking at all the circumstances — the booking, the arrival, the fare request after the journey and the cessation afterwards — there was an expectation of payment, which was enough for 'hire or reward'.

why: In unlicensed-taxi cases, prove the whole arrangement: how the journey was booked, what was said, the pick-up, and any request for or expectation of payment. A fare agreed in advance isn't required.

d: A taxi owner was liable when an unlicensed person drove his vehicle, without proof that he knew or consented: the High Court treated the owner's offence under the Taxi Regulation Act 2013 as strict liability, aimed at public safety and an orderly taxi service. As reported, an owner who took all reasonable steps to prevent unauthorised use has a defence.

f.facts: The National Transport Authority prosecuted the owner of a taxi that had been driven by a person without the required licence. The owner argued that, as with possession offences, he couldn't be liable without knowledge or consent.
f.held: High Court, 2020 ([2020] IEHC 301, Barr J): the offence (reported as s.22(4) of the Taxi Regulation Act 2013) is one of strict liability. The Act is regulatory, aimed at public safety and an orderly taxi service. Operating a vehicle concerns control and the owner's duty to prevent unauthorised use — unlike possession offences, where knowledge is part of the offence (DPP v Ebbs). As reported, an owner can avoid liability by showing all reasonable steps were taken to prevent unauthorised use.

why: When an unlicensed driver is found operating a taxi, consider the owner too — you don't have to prove the owner knew. Record who owns the vehicle, who was driving, and anything the owner did or didn't do to control its use.
topic: Taxi owners: strict liability for unlicensed drivers

d: A taxi driver with temporary immigration permission was refused renewal of his SPSV licence. The refusal was valid — an adverse immigration finding could be weighed as a 'red flag' on good character — but the judge had grave reservations about a Garda policy of refusing all such applicants, introduced ad hoc. A time-limited licence was invalid: SPSV licences run for five years, though conditions can be attached.

f.facts: Since February 2020 the Garda licensing authority in the Dublin region had refused SPSV driver licences to people holding temporary immigration permission while a residence application was pending. The applicant had temporary permission to live and work in Ireland while an application to retain residence was pending. He was given a time-limited SPSV licence that expired in April 2020, when his permission lapsed. On renewal he was refused as not a 'suitable person', after an adverse immigration finding. He sought judicial review.
f.held: High Court, April 2022 (Simons J): the refusal to renew was valid — the authority could treat the adverse immigration finding as a 'red flag' bearing on good character, even though it was under review. But the judge had grave reservations about the policy: the authority hadn't justified systematically refusing family members of EU citizens while immigration matters were pending, and such changes should be made by the National Transport Authority through regulations. The original time-limited licence was invalid, because SPSV licences must last five years; conditions (such as renewed immigration permission) can be attached instead.

why: SPSV licensing decisions must be individual and lawful: assess each applicant's suitability on the evidence, don't apply blanket policies that the regulations don't support, and issue licences for the statutory period — using conditions, not shorter terms, to manage risk.

n: JM v Commissioner of An Garda Síochána (diversion, 2022)
d: Children considering whether to accept responsibility for admission to the Garda Youth Diversion Programme (s.23 Children Act 2001) aren't entitled to see the Garda investigation file first. The programme is supportive diversion, not a disclosure process; they'd been told the allegations in interview and their solicitors had enough to advise them. Four challenges dismissed.

f.facts: Four children, represented by their parents and solicitors, were interviewed by Gardaí with legal representation and then considered for the Garda Youth Diversion Programme, which requires the child to accept responsibility. They asked for access to the Garda investigation files before deciding whether to accept responsibility; access was refused. They sought judicial review, relying on s.23(1)(a) of the Children Act 2001, constitutional fair procedures and EU Directive 2012/13/EU.
f.held: High Court, 1 February 2022 ([2022] IEHC 149, Heslin J): all four applications dismissed. Read literally, s.23 gives no entitlement to the files. The programme's purpose is supportive diversion, not access to prosecution evidence, and the Director's admission decision is independent of any later prosecution. The children had been told the allegations and the complainants' identities in interview, and their solicitors had enough information to advise them.

why: For diversion, the child needs to understand the allegation, not see the file. Put the allegation clearly in interview, make sure the child has had the chance to consult parents or guardians and get legal advice, and record that before any acceptance of responsibility.
topic: Youth diversion: no right to the Garda file before accepting responsibility
st: Yes. High Court authority (2022), summarised from a published commentary — check the judgment before relying on detail.

n: Unnamed v DPP (juvenile delay and diversion, 2023)
d: A youth alleged to have committed an assault at 16 wasn't summonsed for almost four years. The High Court found the delay culpable, but it didn't tip the balance enough to stop the prosecution. The case also exposed a risk: he'd made a partial admission under caution at the diversion consideration stage, then was refused entry and prosecuted.

f.facts: In May 2017, when he was 16, the applicant allegedly committed an assault. At the stage of being considered for the Garda Youth Diversion Programme he made a partial admission, under caution, to a Juvenile Liaison Officer. He was refused entry and wasn't summonsed until February 2021. By then he had come to Garda attention as an adult and served a custodial sentence on unrelated matters. The prosecution pointed to the investigating Garda's caseload and difficulty serving him at the address given. He sought to restrain the prosecution.
f.held: High Court, 4 July 2023 ([2023] IEHC 384): there was culpable prosecutorial delay, but it didn't tip the balance of justice in favour of restraining the prosecution. Loss of anonymity as a child wasn't prejudicial, as he'd come to Garda attention as an adult, and the delay after he turned 18 caused no additional prejudice. The application was refused.

why: Process youth files promptly — a Garda's caseload won't excuse delay. And take care at the diversion stage: an admission made under caution while a child is being considered for the programme may later be used if they're refused entry and prosecuted.

n: S v Director of the Garda Juvenile Diversion Programme
d: The Director of the Garda Youth Diversion Programme wrongly applied a blanket rule that anyone over 18 by the time of the decision couldn't be admitted, whatever their age at the time of the offence. That misread s.23 of the Children Act 2001. The refusal, given without reasons, was quashed and sent back for reconsideration.

f.facts: S was 17 when the offences were committed in 2017 and was arrested after turning 18. He was charged with child sexual exploitation and child pornography offences. His solicitors argued he met the criteria for diversion; Juvenile Liaison Officers recommended against admission. In July 2018, and again in September 2018 after further submissions, the Director found him unsuitable without giving reasons.
f.held: High Court, November 2019 ([2019] IEHC 796, Simons J): the Director's decision was amenable to judicial review and, in the circumstances, required reasons. There was a prima facie case that it rested on a mistaken reading of the eligibility criteria — a blanket policy excluding anyone who had turned 18, regardless of age at the time of the offence. Refusing reasons was a 'Sphinx-like approach'. Certiorari granted; the matter was remitted for reconsideration, and the order restraining the prosecution stayed in place.

why: Eligibility for diversion turns on the person's age when the offence was committed, not when it comes to light. If a youth offence surfaces after the suspect turns 18, consider diversion properly, record the reasons for any recommendation, and expect the decision to need reasons.
topic: Youth diversion: age at the time of the offence; giving reasons

d: An interview that ran to four hours should have been stopped or adjourned under the Custody Regulations (reg. 12(4)), and Gardaí kept no contemporaneous note of an earlier interview — but neither breach of itself made the later statement inadmissible. Privilege over the source behind a search warrant was upheld to protect a civilian contact. Murder convictions stood.

f.facts: Two applicants, armed with knives, killed a man in a stabbing after a long-running family dispute and were convicted of murder. The first applicant's interview ran to four hours; she declined an offer to adjourn it. Gardaí hadn't kept a contemporaneous note of her first interview. For the second applicant, privilege was claimed over the source of information behind a search warrant; Gardaí had offered her access to a solicitor and made calls for her. The jury also learned that she had been in prison.
f.held: Court of Criminal Appeal, 4 December 1995 (Blayney J, with Flood and Kinlen JJ): leave to appeal refused. The four-hour interview should have been interrupted under reg. 12(4) of the 1987 Custody Regulations, but the failure didn't of itself render the statement inadmissible; nor did the missing note of the first interview, as the later statement complied with the Judges' Rules. Privilege over the warrant source was upheld because disclosure could endanger a civilian contact. The reference to prison shouldn't have happened but caused no miscarriage of justice given the strength of the evidence. There is no defence in law of 'flawed intent'.

why: Breaches of the Custody Regulations won't automatically exclude a statement — but each one hands the defence an argument. Stop or adjourn interviews at four hours, keep a contemporaneous note of every interview, and record each offer of a solicitor and break.
topic: Custody Regulations breaches: four-hour interviews and missing notes

n: Rochford (civil claims over arrest and device warrant, 2025)
d: A protester's claims against Gardaí for false imprisonment, malicious prosecution and maliciously procuring a search warrant all failed. The public order arrest was lawful — reasonable cause to suspect a s.6 offence, and a s.8 direction disobeyed — and an acquittal on appeal didn't show malice. The later warrant for his devices expressly covered digital devices, as Quirke requires.

f.facts: In February 2016 the plaintiff was arrested at a sod-turning ceremony attended by a Government minister. The Garda observed insults, the plaintiff touching a Garda's epaulette, threats about the minister, and a refusal to obey a s.8 direction to leave. He was convicted in the District Court but acquitted on appeal. In 2017, after a Garda complained of harassment through Facebook posts, a s.10 (1997 Act) warrant was issued for 'electronic devices capable of forwarding messages on social media'; devices were seized and examined, and the DPP directed no prosecution. He sued for €500,000.
f.held: High Court, 2025 ([2025] IEHC 251, Simons J): all claims dismissed. The arrest under s.24 of the Criminal Justice (Public Order) Act 1994 was lawful: there was reasonable cause to suspect a s.6 offence, and a valid s.8 direction had been given and disobeyed. The acquittal satisfied the first element of malicious prosecution, but there was no lack of reasonable cause and no malice — the Garda's observations and a Superintendent's review gave objective grounds. There were reasonable grounds for the warrant, which specified the search of digital devices as Quirke requires, and no malice.

why: A public order arrest stands on what you saw and did at the time. Record the words and actions, the s.8 direction you gave and how it was disobeyed, and the grounds for arrest. For device warrants, say expressly that you seek electronic devices and why.
topic: Civil claims after a public order arrest and a device warrant

n: Unrepresented accused at bail hearings (High Court, 2026)
d: During the 2026 legal aid solicitors' dispute, many accused faced District Court bail hearings without a solicitor. The High Court released people whose hearings were a 'fundamental denial of justice' — including a man whose bail was refused and revoked over €3.60 of shoplifting without his being heard. Lack of representation alone doesn't make a hearing unlawful; what matters is whether the accused had a real chance to answer the case for detention.

f.facts: From June 2026 criminal defence solicitors withdrew District Court services in protest at a new 'one accused, one fee' legal aid model (a fixed €520 fee from 1 July). Many accused were remanded in custody after bail hearings at which they had no solicitor, and brought Article 40 (habeas corpus) challenges. In one case a man charged with stealing two cans of cola (€3.60) had bail refused and existing bail revoked; he couldn't question the Garda and wasn't heard before the decision.
f.held: High Court, 29 July 2026 (Gearty J): 11 accused released; their unrepresented bail hearings were a fundamental denial of justice, though not the fault of the District judges. 5 August 2026 (Twomey J): Article 40 refused where a solicitor declined to act over fees; appeal was the remedy. 18 and 26 August 2026 (Simons J): the €3.60 case 'did not constitute a hearing', and the man was released; Twomey J had misread the case law — no solicitor can cause another person's detention, but lack of representation doesn't of itself make a hearing fundamentally flawed, and two applicants who'd had a meaningful chance to answer the case were refused relief.

why: When you object to bail and the accused has no solicitor, the fairness of the hearing rests partly on you. State your grounds clearly, give your evidence so the accused understands it, expect and allow questions, and make sure they're heard before bail is refused or revoked. Keep the objection proportionate to the charge.
topic: Bail hearings for unrepresented accused (2026 solicitors' dispute)
st: Developing. High Court rulings (July–August 2026) conflicted on the route to relief; written judgments and any appeals may change the position. Check the latest before relying on it.

d: A Peace Commissioner's search warrant for stolen property was upheld: the sworn information was enough for him to be satisfied stolen goods would be found, issuing a warrant isn't the administration of justice, and an invalid clause purporting to authorise arrest could be cut out without bringing down the rest. Once a warrant has been executed, its effect on the evidence is for the trial court.

f.facts: In November 1985 a Peace Commissioner issued a warrant under s.42(1) of the Larceny Act 1916 to search a house in Swords, Dublin, for stolen property, on a Garda's sworn information about stolen electric cookers. Stolen equipment was found in a bedroom, and the applicant, who lived there, was arrested and charged with burglary, larceny and receiving. He sought judicial review: the information didn't justify the warrant, the warrant wrongly purported to authorise arrest, and the Peace Commissioner's power (s.88(3)(b) of the Courts of Justice Act 1924) was unconstitutional.
f.held: High Court, 9 October 1987 (Hamilton P): application dismissed. Issuing a search warrant isn't the administration of justice in a criminal matter (following Ryan v O'Callaghan), and s.88(3)(b) wasn't inconsistent with Article 40.5. The sworn information was sufficient for the Peace Commissioner to be satisfied stolen property would be found. The arrest wording was severable. In any event the court would have refused relief in its discretion: the warrant was spent, and admissibility was for the trial court.

why: The person issuing a warrant must be satisfied on your sworn information, so put the facts behind your suspicion in it. Don't add powers the statute doesn't give — a clause that oversteps may be cut out, but it invites a challenge.
topic: Peace Commissioner warrants: sufficiency of information; severing a bad clause
st: Older authority. The Larceny Act power has been replaced (theft-related warrants now come under s.48 of the Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001), and after Damache (2012) the issuer must be independent. The severance and discretion points are still cited.

t: Does the sworn information set out the facts behind your suspicion, and does the warrant claim only powers the statute gives?

d: A search warrant obtained for a neighbouring flat — because a suspect might escape through it — was technically invalid: the warrant power was about finding property, not blocking escape routes. But no damages lie for acting on a warrant that looked valid unless there was a deliberate or conscious violation of rights; an innocent, unknown defect in a warrant sought in good faith isn't enough.

f.facts: In August 1995 Gardaí obtained warrants under s.42(1) of the Larceny Act 1916 for several flats in Dún Laoghaire after a burglary suspect was identified. The warrant for the plaintiff's flat was sought because the suspect might move there from next door over the rear balconies. Gardaí broke down her door to arrest the suspect. She sued for personal injuries and breach of constitutional rights, saying she was injured in her home; the court found she was probably injured outside, when a crowd turned on the Gardaí as they left.
f.held: High Court, 13 April 2006 (Clarke J): claim dismissed. The warrant was technically invalid — the statute concerns property in someone's possession on the premises, not a possible escape route — though failing to strike out a 'District Judge' description didn't itself invalidate it. Applying People (AG) v O'Brien, no damages arise from acting on a warrant that appeared valid but was technically defective unless there was a deliberate or conscious violation of rights: for example, a false basis given to get the warrant, knowledge that the basis didn't justify it, or Gardaí executing it knowing of the defect. The sergeant's belief was genuine and reasonable, and the warrant was sought and granted in good faith.

why: Use each power for its own purpose: a search warrant is for finding property or evidence, not for covering an escape route — entry to arrest needs its own power (now s.6 of the Criminal Law Act 1997). Acting in good faith protects you from damages, but not from losing the evidence.
topic: Damages for executing a defective warrant: deliberate violation needed
st: Yes, on civil liability for defective warrants. The Larceny Act power has since been replaced, and entry to arrest is now governed by s.6 of the Criminal Law Act 1997.

d: The member in charge is whoever is actually in charge of the station when a duty under the Custody Regulations arises — a question of fact. A Garda who took over and did all the member-in-charge duties was the member in charge even though he hadn't signed the station diary as a local directive required. A drink-driving charge wrongly dismissed on that ground was sent back.

f.facts: The accused was charged with drink driving (over 80mg per 100ml of blood). At about 1am a Garda relieved the member in charge who had been on since 10pm, and performed all the duties — completing the custody record and informing the accused of his rights — but didn't sign the station diary as a Superintendent's directive required. The relieved Garda stayed in the day room. The District Judge dismissed the charge, holding he couldn't be member in charge without the diary entry, and stated a case.
f.held: High Court, 31 July 1996 (Kelly J): the District Judge was wrong in law. Under reg. 4(1) of the 1987 Custody Regulations the member in charge is the member actually in charge of the station when a duty arises — a question of fact. The Superintendent's directive was at most an administrative way of identifying that person; failing to follow it didn't change who was in charge. Obiter, under s.7(3) of the Criminal Justice Act 1984 a breach of the Regulations doesn't automatically exclude evidence — there must be a causal link to prejudice. Case remitted to the District Court.

why: Who is member in charge is a matter of fact, but don't invite the argument: at each handover, record who is taking over and when, in the custody record and any station diary, and make sure the incoming member actually performs the duties.
topic: Who is the member in charge? (Custody Regulations, reg. 4)
st: Yes. Still cited on the member in charge and on s.7(3) of the Criminal Justice Act 1984. Read with DPP v Roche (2015).

d: A drink-driving suspect who chooses to give urine must get a reasonable opportunity to provide it before a blood sample is taken instead. After about 15 minutes, with the doctor under pressure to leave, blood was taken; the District Judge dismissed the charge, and the High Court wouldn't interfere. Being allowed to give urine is a condition precedent to any obligation to give blood.

f.facts: The accused was charged with driving with excess alcohol. At the station he was offered the choice of giving blood or urine (s.13(1)(b) of the Road Traffic Act 1994) and chose urine, but couldn't produce a sample within about 15 minutes despite attempts to help him. The doctor, under pressure to attend another station, then took blood. The District Judge dismissed the charge, finding he hadn't been given a reasonable opportunity to give urine, so the later blood sample wasn't a proper option. The DPP appealed by case stated.
f.held: High Court, 10 July 1998 (Geoghegan J): appeal refused. Being allowed to provide urine, if it can be provided, is a condition precedent to any absolute obligation to give blood. The District Judge wasn't laying down a rule that 30 minutes must always be allowed; he assessed the time against all the circumstances, including the pressure on the doctor and the accused's distress. His view was open to him, so no question of law arose. The certificate showing he was well over the limit was irrelevant to whether the option had been properly offered.

why: If the person opts for urine, give them a genuine, reasonable chance to provide it — and record the times, the attempts and any help given — before moving to blood. The doctor's schedule is not a reason to cut it short.
topic: Station procedure — reasonable opportunity to give urine before blood
st: Older authority under the 1994 Act; the blood-or-urine option continues under the Road Traffic Act 2010 — check the current section.

d: When requiring a blood or urine specimen, a Garda needn't cite the section of the Act, as long as the requirement and the consequences of refusing are explained and the person complies. Arrest is different: the operative power generally has to be invoked, because it takes away liberty.

f.facts: The accused was seen driving erratically in Dublin in October 1993 and arrested for drunk driving under s.49 of the Road Traffic Act 1961. At the station a doctor was called. The Garda told him he had to allow a blood specimen or, at his option, give urine, and that refusing was an offence punishable by imprisonment, a fine or both — closely paraphrasing the statute without naming the section. He gave urine and was convicted, fined £75 and disqualified for 12 months. The High Court upheld the conviction on a case stated.
f.held: Supreme Court, 1 November 1995 (O'Flaherty J, with Hamilton CJ and Denham J): appeal dismissed. Where a valid requirement is made, the person is told of it and of the consequences of refusal, and complies, there's no need to invoke the actual section, and no encroachment on constitutional rights. DPP v McGarrigle, where the section had to be invoked because non-compliance was the charge, was distinguished; so was arrest, where the operative power generally must be invoked.

why: Explain the specimen requirement and the consequences of refusing in plain words, and record what you said. Citing the section isn't required where the person complies — but if refusal may be the charge, be precise.
topic: Specimen requirement — no need to cite the section
st: Yes, as older Supreme Court authority; the specimen provisions are now in the Road Traffic Act 2010.

t: Were the specimen requirement and the consequences of refusing explained in plain words and recorded?

d: A man arrested after a Garda saw him swap from the driver's seat to the back as a passenger slid across was convicted of refusing to give breath specimens — even though the District Judge wasn't sure he'd been driving. Driving isn't a prerequisite to a conviction for refusal without good and substantial reason; the requirement was lawfully made.

f.facts: A Garda allegedly saw the accused move into the back seat of a car as a passenger took the driver's seat. He was arrested for drink driving and at the station refused to give two breath specimens. He said he wasn't the driver, and his girlfriend told Gardaí and the court that she was. In January 2007 the District Court convicted him under the Road Traffic Act 1994 of refusing the specimens; the judge had doubts about whether he was driving but didn't find that he wasn't.
f.held: High Court, November 2008 (Clark J): the requirement for breath specimens was lawfully made, and he couldn't attack the arrest on the basis that his driving hadn't been proved. Driving was not a prerequisite to a conviction for refusing a breath specimen without good and substantial reason. The conviction stood, with costs to the DPP.

why: A refusal charge rests on a lawful arrest and a lawful requirement — not on proving the driving. Record exactly what you saw that founded your opinion (here, the seat swap), the grounds for arrest, and the requirement and refusal in full.
topic: Refusing breath specimens: driving needn't be proved
st: Yes, as older authority; refusal offences are now in the Road Traffic Act 2010.

n: DPP v Moran (no roadside test before arrest, 2014)
d: A roadside (preliminary) breath test isn't a precondition to a drink-driving arrest. Under s.9(2) of the Road Traffic Act 2010, where a Garda has formed the opinion that the driver should be arrested, the duty to carry out a preliminary test doesn't arise. Erratic driving onto a verge, a strong smell of alcohol and slurred speech made the opinion entirely reasonable.

f.facts: At about 3.30pm on 6 January 2013 a Garda saw the accused's car being driven erratically, failing to keep a steady course and veering onto a grass verge. On stopping him the Garda noticed a strong smell of alcohol and slurred speech, and arrested him for an evidential breath test at the station without a roadside test. He was charged under s.4 of the Road Traffic Act 2010. The defence argued the arrest was unlawful because no preliminary breath test had been done, and the District Court referred the question.
f.held: High Court, 4 July 2014 (Kearns P): s.9(2) of the Road Traffic Act 2010 is clear and unambiguous — where a Garda forms the opinion that a person should be arrested on suspicion of an offence, the mandatory duty to carry out a preliminary breath test doesn't arise. The Garda's opinion was entirely reasonable on the driving, the smell of alcohol and the slurred speech. This reading didn't offend strict construction of penal statutes. Questions answered in favour of the prosecution.

why: You can arrest without a roadside test if your opinion is soundly based — but record every observation that founded it: the driving, smell, speech, balance, eyes, admissions. The opinion stands or falls on what you wrote down.
topic: No roadside breath test needed before arrest (s.9(2) RTA 2010)
st: Yes. High Court authority (2014) on s.9(2) of the Road Traffic Act 2010.

d: A drink-driving charge was wrongly dismissed for lack of evidence that the place where the driver was stopped, tested and arrested was a public place. The prosecution needn't prove the vehicle was still in a public place when stopped, unless there's evidence to the contrary — the driving on the public road was what mattered.

f.facts: At about 3am in November 1996 Gardaí saw a car leave a pub in Kilkenny with its lights off and driving on both sides of the road. They followed with flashing lights; the driver didn't stop for about half a mile and was blocked in near his home. A Garda noticed a smell of alcohol, the roadside test was positive and he was arrested. The District Judge dismissed the charge because the Garda's evidence didn't describe the place where he was spoken to, tested and arrested as a public place.
f.held: High Court, 15 December 1998 (O'Higgins J): the DPP's appeal was allowed and the case remitted. The prosecution didn't need to offer evidence that the vehicle was still in a public place when it was stopped, unless there was evidence to the contrary. The District Judge was wrong to dismiss the charge.

why: Prove the public-place element where the driving happened: name the road and describe it as a public road in your evidence. Note too where the vehicle stopped, and whether it was private property.
topic: Drink driving: proving the 'public place' element
st: Yes, as older authority; the offences are now in the Road Traffic Act 2010.

n: DPP v Sheehan (location in the summons, 1998)
d: A drink-driving charge was wrongly dismissed because of doubt over exactly where the car was stopped — a defence map put it about 15 feet before the junction the Garda named. The District Court can amend a summons, and a case shouldn't be dismissed unless there's a possibility of injustice that an adjournment or amendment can't remedy.

f.facts: In December 1996 a Garda stopped the accused's car in Co Limerick; he reportedly admitted drinking four pints, the roadside test was positive and he was arrested. At the hearing the defence used a photocopied map to argue the stop happened a short distance from the junction the Garda had identified. The Garda couldn't read the map, and the prosecution asked for time. The District Judge, having a substantial doubt about where the offence occurred, dismissed the charge and stated a case.
f.held: High Court, 14 October 1998 (Kelly J): the District Judge wasn't justified in law in dismissing the charge. The District Court has power to amend a summons, and a case shouldn't be dismissed on its merits unless there is a possibility of injustice not capable of being remedied by an adjournment or an amendment. The DPP's appeal was allowed and the case remitted.

why: Get the location right in your notes, statement and summons — a landmark, junction or distance. If a discrepancy surfaces in court, ask for an amendment or adjournment rather than letting the case be dismissed.
topic: Discrepancy in the location: amend, don't dismiss
st: Yes, as older authority on amending summonses in the District Court; check the current District Court Rules.

d: Gardaí looking for a man who had skipped bail forced their way into a woman's home without a warrant after an officer saw 'movement' at an upstairs window; she was injured. Under s.6(1) of the Criminal Law Act 1997, forcible entry to arrest needs reasonable cause to believe the person is inside. Mere movement wasn't enough — the home has the highest protection. Her damages claim was sent back for assessment.

f.facts: A man arrested on a European Arrest Warrant had been bailed to the plaintiff's address; she said he left for Poland on the morning of his High Court date in July 2012. In August 2012 four Gardaí came looking for him. She said he wasn't there, asked for a warrant and refused consent to a search; they had none. An officer reported movement at an upstairs window — the plaintiff said it was likely her dog. A detective pushed the door open against her foot, she fell and injured her ankle, and nobody else was found. The High Court dismissed her claim; the Gardaí's account was that a hand had been seen at the window.
f.held: Court of Appeal, August 2018 ([2018] IECA 289, Hogan J): appeal allowed. Section 6(1) permits forcible entry to arrest only if the person is in the house or the Garda has reasonable cause to believe they are, read against Article 40.5, under which the home enjoys the highest level of protection. Once the court accepted the officer had reported only 'movement', the basis for the belief simply disappeared, and the Gardaí hadn't shown reasonable cause. The claim was remitted to the High Court to assess damages for trespass, personal injury and breach of constitutional rights.

why: Before forcing entry to a home to arrest, you need specific grounds to believe the person is inside — and they must be recorded at the time. Movement at a window, without more, isn't enough. If in doubt, watch the property and get a warrant.
topic: Forcible entry to arrest: reasonable cause to believe the person is inside
st: Yes. Court of Appeal authority (2018) on s.6(1) of the Criminal Law Act 1997 and the home.

n: GE v Commissioner of An Garda Síochána
d: A man detained by Gardaí for 25 days on immigration grounds was released because of technical defects in the warrant, and was awarded €7,500 for false imprisonment. The State argued he should get only nominal damages, since he'd have been detained lawfully anyway (the UK 'Lumba' approach). The Court of Appeal (2021) and Supreme Court (2022) rejected that: an unlawful loss of liberty attracts real, compensatory damages.

f.facts: In August 2011 the plaintiff, an asylum applicant without a valid passport or visa for Northern Ireland, his intended destination, was arrested in Dundalk and detained for 25 days. He was released after an Article 40 application succeeded on appeal to the Supreme Court because of technical defects in the warrant. He sued for false imprisonment; the High Court awarded €7,500, reflecting his lack of credibility about his right to remain. The State appealed, arguing for nominal damages because he would have been lawfully detained had proper procedures been followed.
f.held: Court of Appeal, April 2021 ([2021] IECA 113, Murray J): appeal dismissed. The Lumba principles have never been part of Irish law; the 'but for' test negates the essence of the cause of action. Because liberty is a constitutional right, compensatory damages — with a vindicatory element — are the starting point. Supreme Court, December 2022 ([2022] IESC 51, Hogan J for a court of five): both appeals dismissed and the €7,500 upheld. Nominal damages suit only the most technical or fleeting cases; his own conduct (leaving without permission, lack of credibility) reduced the award, but didn't justify detention under a defective warrant.

why: A technically defective detention order still costs real damages, even if the person could lawfully have been detained. Check the warrant or order before you detain on it — the right person, the right power, correctly completed — and fix defects before acting.
topic: Damages for unlawful detention: no 'would have been detained anyway' discount
st: Yes. Court of Appeal (2021) and Supreme Court (December 2022) authority on damages for unlawful detention.

n: Harford v Commissioner of An Garda Síochána
d: A man arrested after going inside a Garda cordon at a fire scene in Dublin 1 — to retrieve his bicycle — and keeping a piece of crime scene tape tried to stop his public order prosecution, saying he'd never been given a direction to leave. Leave for judicial review was refused: whether a direction was given is a factual question for the District Court, and wrongful arrest claims belong in a damages action.

f.facts: Late at night in Dublin 1 a Garda cordon was extended after a fire. The applicant entered the cordon to retrieve his bicycle and kept a piece of crime scene tape. He was arrested, searched and detained at Store Street Garda Station, then released on bail, and charged under the Criminal Justice (Public Order) Act 1994 and, over the tape, the Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001. His central complaint was that he was never directed to leave. He sought declarations that his arrest was unlawful, prohibition of the prosecution, compensation, and preservation of CCTV and body-camera footage.
f.held: High Court, 26 August 2025 ([2025] IEHC 476, Egan J): leave refused. Prohibition is exceptional and needs an unavoidable risk of an unfair trial that the trial judge can't cure; none was shown. Judicial review while criminal proceedings are pending is for wholly exceptional cases. Whether a direction was given, and where he was standing, are factual disputes for the District Court. A wrongful arrest or false imprisonment claim belongs in a plenary action for damages.

why: At a cordon, give a clear direction to leave in plain words, note who you gave it to and the response, and record when the cordon was set and extended. Preserve CCTV and body-camera footage — that's what any later dispute about a direction will turn on.
topic: Crime scene cordons and directions; challenging a prosecution by judicial review
st: Yes. High Court leave decision (2025), summarised from a published commentary. The merits of the public order charge were left to the District Court.

src.t: Casemine — Judicial review is not a shortcut to halt pending prosecutions (Harford v Commissioner [2025] IEHC 476)

n: McGuinness v Commissioner of An Garda Síochána
d: A businessman whose truck yard in Swords was searched under warrant in 2014 couldn't get the sworn information behind the warrant: he hadn't shown it was relevant to his claim, and public interest and informer privilege were properly upheld after the judge read it. His damages claim over the search failed on all 16 grounds in 2025 — the applying Garda's evidence was unchallenged and the search was on a genuine warrant.

f.facts: In August 2014 Gardaí searched the plaintiff's truck business yard in Swords, Co Dublin, on foot of a search warrant; the yard had been linked to a vehicle seen there that was used in an attack on a company's premises. He sued the Commissioner and the State, alleging harassment, that the information used to get the warrant was untrue, unnecessary damage to gates cut with an acetylene torch, and the seizure of company documents. He sought discovery of the sworn information supporting the warrant; the High Court refused in October 2016, after viewing the document and upholding privilege claims, and later dismissed the action in May 2024.
f.held: Court of Appeal, January 2018 (Edwards J): appeal on discovery dismissed. He hadn't shown the document was relevant to his pleaded claim, and even if he had, public interest and informer privilege had been claimed and the High Court judge was right to view the document before upholding them. Court of Appeal, January 2025 (Allen J): all 16 grounds of appeal dismissed; he had never pleaded that the search was without a warrant, the copy warrant was genuine, and the evidence of the detective sergeant who applied for it went unchallenged.

why: Write the sworn information knowing a court may read it later, and identify informant material so privilege can be claimed properly. Keep a clear record of the search — who, what was seized, any damage caused and why — because civil claims can follow years later.
topic: Privilege over warrant information; civil claims after a search
st: Yes. Court of Appeal authority (2018 and 2025) on discovery of warrant information and civil claims over searches.

Echo — Brother loses appeal over search on business premises (28 January 2025)

d: Armed Gardaí intercepting a burglary had the suspect face down and handcuffed on a lawn, then questioned him before arresting him; he said the gun was 'in the bag'. Those answers were inadmissible: Gardaí could restrain him for safety, but should have arrested him under their powers before questioning him to gather evidence. 'He was not arrested. Yet he was not free.' Conviction quashed, no retrial.

f.facts: Gardaí moved in on a suspected break-in at a house in Templeogue, using a loud bang as a distraction. The accused ran onto the lawn, was made to lie down, overpowered and handcuffed face down. A Garda searched him (gloves, balaclava, car keys, phone; no weapon) and then questioned him; with no notebook, he later wrote the questions and answers on an A4 sheet. The Garda said the accused told him he had no gun, that the gun was 'in the bag', and that the car was full of items from the house. Only then was he arrested; at the station he answered 'no comment'. He was convicted of possessing a firearm and sentenced to seven years.
f.held: Court of Criminal Appeal, 16 December 2008 (Fennelly J, with Budd and Hanna JJ): appeal allowed, conviction quashed, no retrial. The questioning took place in highly unusual circumstances. Gardaí were entitled to subdue him for safety, but should have arrested and detained him under their statutory powers before questioning him to gather evidence. He was physically restrained, face down and handcuffed, with armed Gardaí present — not arrested, yet not free.

why: Once you have someone restrained, arrest them before you question them about the offence — then caution, and record the questions and answers in your notebook at the time. Questioning a person who is held but not arrested invites exclusion.
topic: Questioning a restrained suspect before arrest
st: Yes. Court of Criminal Appeal authority (2008) on questioning a suspect who is restrained but not arrested.

t: If the suspect is restrained, have you arrested and cautioned them before asking about the offence?

d: At a checkpoint a Garda formed the opinion a driver was drunk, then asked him to pull over — and he drove a short distance into a park before being arrested. The arrest was lawful and the Garda's opinion wasn't undone by the request. But the judge said that, as a matter of practice, you shouldn't ask a driver you believe is drunk to drive on: have them pull in first, or arrange removal of the vehicle after arrest.

f.facts: In November 2003 a driver was stopped at a checkpoint on the Templeogue Road, Dublin. The Garda noticed a smell of alcohol and slurred speech and formed the opinion he was intoxicated to the extent of being incapable of proper control of the vehicle. The Garda then asked him to pull over to the side; he drove a short distance into a nearby park, was arrested, and later gave a breath sample. He was charged with drink driving under s.49 of the Road Traffic Act 1961, and the District Judge stated a consultative case.
f.held: High Court, 27 July 2006 (Dunne J): the arrest was lawful — all the ingredients of a valid s.49 arrest were present, the arrest didn't depend on the request, no evidence was obtained because of it, and there was no prejudice. The Garda's opinion was a finding of fact that later events couldn't undo. Applying Lynch v Attorney General, the court wouldn't interfere with an otherwise proper procedure because it disapproved of one step. But in practice the Garda shouldn't have asked the driver to move.

why: Once you've formed the opinion that a driver is over the limit or impaired, don't ask them to drive on. Have them pull in before you deal with them, or arrest and arrange for the vehicle to be moved.
topic: Asking a suspected drunk driver to move the car
st: Yes, as older authority; the offence is now under the Road Traffic Act 2010.

t: After forming the opinion that the driver is impaired, did you avoid asking them to drive again?

d: Interviews about IRA membership, where an inference provision was to be invoked, were excluded as tainted with unfairness: they were held at a station without video recording, the explanation of the inference provision wasn't recorded, the accused wasn't told the focus had shifted or reminded of his right to legal advice, the questions were compound and loaded, and his call to his solicitor was made in a public office.

f.facts: The accused was arrested under s.30 of the Offences Against the State Act 1939 on suspicion of possessing explosives. After about 11.5 hours of questioning on that offence his detention was extended. On 2 July 2003 he was interviewed twice about IRA membership, with s.2 of the Offences Against the State (Amendment) Act 1998 (inferences) to be invoked, at a station without video recording facilities — chosen for its proximity to his family and solicitors. The Gardaí's verbal explanation of s.2 wasn't recorded, the questions were compound and loaded, and his phone call to his solicitor was made in a public office.
f.held: Special Criminal Court, 26 November 2004 (O'Donovan J presiding): the arrest was lawful and the extension couldn't be invalidated, but the two interviews were excluded as tainted with unfairness. Where an inference provision is to be invoked, fairness requires taking the prisoner to a station with video recording where possible (though there was no statutory duty), telling him the focus of questioning has changed, and reminding him of his right to legal advice. The questioning was unfair, the unrecorded explanation of s.2 was a problem, and the public-office call to his solicitor breached his privacy.

why: When you invoke an inference provision, the interview must be scrupulously fair: record it, record the explanation of the provision in full, tell the suspect when the questioning moves to a different offence, remind them of their right to a solicitor, ask one clear question at a time, and let them consult their solicitor in private.
topic: Fairness when invoking inference provisions in interview
st: Yes, as a ruling on interview fairness. Electronic recording is now the norm; the fairness points about inference warnings remain.

t: Is the inference warning recorded word for word, with the change of focus explained and the right to a solicitor repeated?

n: Finnegan v Member in Charge (Santry Garda Station)
d: A murder suspect held under s.30 of the Offences Against the State Act was released because the District Court's order for a third 24-hour extension was made at 11.20pm — 25 minutes after his detention had expired at 10.55pm. Starting the application in time wasn't enough: once lawful detention ended, the court had no jurisdiction, and the order couldn't be backdated.

f.facts: The applicant was arrested at 10.55pm on 5 March 2006 under s.30 of the Offences Against the State Act 1939 in connection with a murder by shooting in Coolock, and was detained for 24 hours and then a further 24 hours (unchallenged). Towards the end of the second period Gardaí sought a third extension from the District Court under s.30(4). The hearing began before expiry (10.26pm on the warrant; 10.35pm on Garda evidence), but the order and warrant weren't made until 11.20pm, after the detention expired at 10.55pm.
f.held: High Court, 8 March 2006 (O'Neill J), on an Article 40 inquiry: the detention after 10.55pm was unlawful and he was ordered released. Statutory detention periods can't be extended by the courts or by implication, and starting the application within the period didn't stop it expiring. A District Court extension under s.30(4A) requires continuing lawful detention under s.30(3); once that ended, there was no jurisdiction. The suspension provision in s.4(8A) of the Criminal Justice Act 1984 didn't apply to s.30 detention — 'a significant and express omission' — so the illegality couldn't be cured.

why: Never let an extension run to the wire. Diary the expiry time, apply for any extension early enough that the order is made before expiry, and if it won't be, release or re-arrest only where the law allows. Know which suspension provisions apply to the detention power you're using.
topic: Detention extension made after expiry — release
st: Yes, on the strictness of detention periods. Check whether s.30 has since been amended to address applications heard close to expiry.

src.t: Irish Times law report — District Court has no jurisdiction to extend detention after statutory period has expired (3 April 2006)

t: Is the detention expiry time diaried, and will any extension order be made before it expires?

d: A murder suspect released without charge was lawfully re-arrested on a District Court warrant under s.10 of the Criminal Justice Act 1984: a witness's identification of him from a photo album, and his remarks to his landlord, were new information since his release. But judgment came at 8.30pm — 15 minutes after his detention had expired — and the court couldn't stop the clock, so he went home.

f.facts: The suspect was arrested on suspicion of murdering his wife, held at Santry Garda Station and released without charge the same day. Gardaí then applied to the District Court for a re-arrest warrant under s.10 of the Criminal Justice Act 1984, relying on a witness who said she saw a man near where the body was found and identified him from a photo album; a landlord's account of remarks he made about being accused of the murder; and evidence that a bag of clothing linked to the couple was thrown into a river, while he couldn't account for his movements early that morning. He was re-arrested at his home and challenged the lawfulness of the re-arrest.
f.held: High Court, September 1996 (Kelly J): the re-arrest was lawful. A s.10 re-arrest needs a District Court warrant, on the judge being satisfied that new information has come to the Gardaí since the release about the suspect's participation in the offence. The identification was new information that amply justified the application; the landlord's account, though less compelling, was new too. But judgment was delivered at 8.30pm, 15 minutes after a six-hour extension had expired, and the judge had no jurisdiction to stop the clock — so the suspect was no longer detained and was free to go.

why: A released suspect can be re-arrested for the same offence only on a District Court warrant based on genuinely new information since release — set it out specifically. And the detention clock keeps running even while a court considers a challenge: plan interviews and any extension so time doesn't run out.
topic: Re-arrest on new information (s.10 CJA 1984); the clock keeps running
st: Yes, as older authority on s.10 re-arrest warrants; check the current wording of s.10.

t: For a re-arrest, is the new information since release set out specifically — and is the remaining detention time planned?

d: A Detective Superintendent issued a s.26(2) Misuse of Drugs Act warrant for a truck wash yard — a third party's commercial premises — when no judge or Peace Commissioner was available; cannabis worth about €2 million was found in a van there. The accused couldn't rely on Damache: he had no proprietary or constitutional interest in someone else's commercial premises. Conviction upheld.

f.facts: After surveillance of the accused in Rathcoole, Co Dublin, a warrant under s.26(2) of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1977 was issued by a Detective Superintendent for a truck wash and parking business owned by a third party, after Gardaí learned a judge wouldn't be available for some hours and a Peace Commissioner wasn't at home. Cannabis resin worth about €2 million was found in a white van there. The accused argued the issuer wasn't independent, that any urgency was self-created, that the warrant was issued within a minute, and that his arrest was unlawful. He was convicted of possession for sale or supply and jailed for 13 years.
f.held: Court of Appeal, 9 March 2015 ([2015] IECA 46, Sheehan J for the court): appeal dismissed. Damache v DPP was distinguished — it concerned a warrant for the applicant's home; here the premises were commercial and owned by someone else, so he couldn't invoke any proprietary or constitutional interest. The warrant's authority wasn't exceeded, and the claim that evidence was contrived was rejected. The trial was fair: he hadn't shown missing CCTV would have helped him, and the judge's intervention and charge dealt with any prejudice.

why: Superintendent-issued warrants are for genuine urgency: record why a judge or Peace Commissioner couldn't be reached, and keep the issuer independent of the investigation where possible. Who can challenge a warrant depends on their interest in the premises — but don't rely on that; get the warrant right.
topic: Urgent Superintendent warrants; standing to challenge a search of someone else's premises
st: Yes, as Court of Appeal authority (2015) on standing; read with Damache (2012) and check the current rules on who may issue s.26 warrants.

src.t: vLex Ireland — People (DPP) v Boggans [2015] IECA 46

t: If a Superintendent issued the warrant, are the urgency and the attempts to reach a judge or Peace Commissioner recorded?

d: Gardaí got a District Court drugs warrant for a suspect's registered flat, learned on arrival that he had moved to another flat in the same building, and went back to court for a second warrant rather than going in. The sworn information for the second was almost a copy of the first with the flat number changed. Held valid: the judge heard both applications, asked questions and was clearly satisfied.

f.facts: In a 2015 investigation into cocaine posted to two Dublin hostels, a co-accused was arrested carrying the accused's driving licence and receipts in his name. Gardaí got a s.26 Misuse of Drugs Act 1977 warrant for the accused's registered flat. On arrival the owner told them he had recently moved to another flat in the building because of renovations. Gardaí didn't enter that flat; they went back to the District Court for a second warrant, whose sworn information was almost identical to the first apart from the flat number. Cocaine was found. In November 2017 a Circuit Court jury convicted him of conspiracy to import (s.71 Criminal Justice Act 2006), possession, and possession for sale or supply; he got five years.
f.held: Court of Appeal ([2019] IECA 93, Kennedy J): appeal dismissed. The District Judge heard sworn evidence on both applications, was fully aware of the circumstances of each, asked further questions, and was clearly satisfied on oath that there were reasonable grounds for suspicion under s.26(1)(a). There was no reason for the wording to change much when the only difference was the flat. The trial judge was entitled to find the information properly prepared and the warrant valid, so the search evidence was admissible.

why: Re-using the wording of an earlier information isn't fatal if it's true for the new application — but update it to the latest facts and the right premises. What helped here: the gardaí didn't enter before the second warrant, and the judge's questions were answered on oath.
topic: Second warrant after a suspect moves flat; re-used sworn information

d: A drunk-in-charge suspect was observed for 27 minutes, not 20, before the Intoxilyser test, and no reason was given for the extra seven. The Supreme Court held the detention stayed lawful: not every delay is unreasonable, and only an unreasonable one needs to be justified.

f.facts: He was found in a car parked on a Dublin footpath with the engine running, smelling of drink and slurring his speech. He was arrested for being in charge of a vehicle with excess alcohol and brought to a Garda station at 2.40am. Instead of the usual 20-minute observation before the breath test he was observed for 27 minutes; the reading was 66 µg per 100ml. The garda gave no reason for the extra seven minutes. The District Judge held the detention unlawful and the breath evidence inadmissible, and the High Court agreed on a case stated.
f.held: Supreme Court, 22 July 2008 ([2008] IESC 45, Murray CJ; Denham and Hardiman JJ agreeing): DPP's appeal allowed — the question was answered no. The Act sets no fixed time for the procedures, but detention must be processed with reasonable expedition. Following DPP v Finn, not every delay is unreasonable, and a delay that isn't unreasonable needn't be objectively justified. Seven extra minutes, in a process from arrest to charge by 4.45am, was not unreasonable, so the detention stayed lawful and the result was admissible.

why: You don't have to account for every minute, but a long or policy-driven delay will need a reason. Keep the custody timeline tight and record why any step took longer (machine busy, other prisoners, a broken observation) so you can explain it in evidence.

d: Near the end of the 20-minute observation before the Evidenzer test the garda looked away for a moment; unsure whether anything had gone into the suspect's mouth, and with the machine in use anyway, he started a fresh 20 minutes. The District Judge held the second period unjustified and dismissed the charge. The Court of Appeal held that was wrong in law.

f.facts: Arrested under s.4(8) of the Road Traffic Act 2010 in March 2014 and brought to a Dublin Garda station, he was put under a 20-minute observation starting at 00.45. About a minute before it ended the garda briefly looked away and couldn't be sure nothing had been taken by mouth; he had also noticed the Evidenzer was in use. He began a second 20-minute period at 01.12, after which two valid samples showed 64 µg per 100ml. The District Judge held the second period unjustified — the garda should have checked the machine before starting, and a momentary look-away didn't reasonably suggest anything had been taken — and dismissed the charge. On a case stated the High Court said that was a finding of fact it couldn't disturb.
f.held: Court of Appeal, 11 December 2015 ([2015] IECA 284, judgment delivered by the President): DPP's appeal allowed. Whether the second period was justified, and whether the charge should have been dismissed, were questions of law, not fact (citing DPP v Fox). The District Judge was not correct to find the extra 20 minutes unjustified, nor to dismiss the charge.

why: If the observation may have been compromised — you looked away, the machine isn't free — restarting it can be justified. Give the reason at the time, note it, and be ready to explain it in evidence.

d: Arrested at a checkpoint and brought to a rural Garda station, a driver waited about half an hour for a garda trained on the Evidenzer to come from another station before the 20-minute observation began. The District Judge was minded to dismiss for undue delay. The High Court held the wait wasn't unreasonable: it wasn't a Finn-type policy delay, nor the kind that makes detention unlawful.

f.facts: He failed a roadside breath test at an authorised checkpoint and was arrested at 11pm, arriving at Kilrush Garda station at 11.25pm. At 11.40pm a garda trained to operate the Evidenzer was requested from Ennis, about 43km away; he arrived at 11.56pm and began the 20-minute observation at 11.59pm, followed by the test. The arresting garda wasn't then trained on the machine. The District Judge held the wait of about 29 minutes unjustified — 'procedure' was no explanation, and the arresting garda could have started the observation — and was minded to dismiss.
f.held: High Court, 21 November 2016 ([2016] IEHC 723, Ní Raifeartaigh J): both questions answered no — he wasn't detained longer than was reasonable, and the District Judge wasn't correct to dismiss. The case didn't fall within the policy category in DPP v Finn, and the delay wasn't of a kind that would normally bring detention into illegality. No earlier case had directly decided whether waiting for a trained garda to observe and test made detention unlawful.

why: Waiting for a trained operator can be justified — but record when you asked, when they arrived, and why the observation didn't start sooner. Better still, have a trained member available.

d: A District Judge dismissed a drink-driving charge because the garda didn't wait 20 minutes before the roadside breath test, as the device's operating instructions suggested. The High Court held that was wrong: the threshold for the garda's opinion to arrest is low, and the device's instructions form no part of the offence.

f.facts: A garda on mobile patrol in Swords, Co Dublin, at about 2.25am on 2 December 2017 observed a vehicle being driven. He formed his opinion to arrest partly on the result of a roadside breath test on a Dräger device, given without first observing a 20-minute period. The accused was charged under s.4(2) and (5)(a) of the Road Traffic Act 2010 (blood alcohol over 50mg per 100ml; the summons alleged 147mg). The District Judge dismissed the charge because the 20-minute period in the device's operating instructions wasn't observed, and stated a case.
f.held: High Court, 28 April 2020 ([2020] IEHC 235, Meenan J): the District Judge was not correct in law. Agreeing fully with DPP v Slattery [2017] IEHC 442, the court held that the threshold for forming an opinion to arrest is low and that the apparatus's operating instructions form no part of the offence itself. The garda wasn't obliged to observe 20 minutes before the roadside test.

why: A 20-minute wait in a roadside device's instructions isn't a legal precondition to your opinion or the arrest. The station evidential test is a separate step with its own observation procedure — see Stack, Fox and Dardis.
topic: No 20-minute wait needed before a roadside breath test

d: A driver who failed a roadside breath test had mentioned 'a few' drinks, with no time given, and was coming from somewhere five minutes away; the garda didn't know the device's instructions call for 20 minutes after a last drink, and didn't wait or ask. The High Court held the test valid and the arrest lawful.

f.facts: In Cork in August 2021 a garda stopped a driver seen driving at speed and noted a strong smell of alcohol, slurred speech and glassy eyes. A roadside breath test under s.9(2) of the Road Traffic Act 2010 gave a 'fail' and the garda formed the opinion that he couldn't properly control the vehicle. In cross-examination the garda accepted that the driver had volunteered having a few drinks before driving, with no time given and no inquiry made, that he was coming from a property five minutes away, and that the garda didn't know the device's instruction to allow at least 20 minutes after a last drink. The District Court stated a case.
f.held: High Court, 20 December 2023 ([2023] IEHC 734, O'Regan J): both questions answered no — the roadside test wasn't invalid and the arrest wasn't unlawful, though the garda, acting in good faith, didn't know the instruction and didn't wait or ask about timing. The 20-minute period comes from the device's instructions, not statute. As summarised in commentary, a wait is needed only where the garda knows or has reason to suspect drinking within the previous 20 minutes — following Slattery (2017) and Feghiu (2020).

why: No law requires a 20-minute wait before every roadside test. But if you know or have reason to suspect a drink in the last 20 minutes, wait before testing — that's where the risk lies. Know your device's instructions.

t: Did you know or have reason to suspect a drink in the last 20 minutes before the roadside test — and if so, did you wait?

d: After a roadside 'fail' at a checkpoint, a driver argued the garda should have watched him for 20 minutes, or asked whether he'd had a drink in that time, as the device's instructions say. The High Court held the garda was under no obligation to ask; his unchallenged, good-faith opinion stood. Later followed in Feghiu (2020) and Foley (2023).

f.facts: At a mandatory alcohol testing checkpoint in Co Mayo in November 2013, a garda required a roadside breath specimen under s.10(4) of the Road Traffic Act 2010. It gave a 'fail', shown to the driver. The garda formed the opinion that he was incapable of proper control of a vehicle and arrested him; a urine specimen at the station showed 281mg per 100ml. The defence argued that the garda hadn't checked that nothing was taken by mouth for 20 minutes, as the device's instructions require (they say at least 20 minutes should pass, because residual mouth alcohol can distort the reading), and that this was fatal.
f.held: High Court, 4 July 2017 ([2017] IEHC 442, Binchy J): the garda was under no obligation to ask about drinking in the previous 20 minutes. His opinion rested on the breath result and its reasonableness and good faith weren't challenged, so the District Judge had to accept it and the dismissal argument fell away. As later applied in Feghiu, the threshold for the opinion is low and the device's operating instructions form no part of the offence.

why: At the roadside you needn't question every driver about their last drink, and the device manual isn't part of the offence. But your opinion must be genuine and reasonable — record what it rested on — and if you do have reason to suspect a very recent drink, wait.
topic: Roadside test: no duty to ask about a drink in the last 20 minutes
